10.title: best of all time
10.content:
Not being a huge fan of superhero movies, I didn't have much expectations for Batman Begins. However viewing the 2005 Christopher Nolan production, I was pleasantly shocked. Then after my huge expectations for, "The Dark Knight", Christopher Nolan blew my expectations to the dust. Will the same happen with the 3rd and last film, "The Dark Knight Rises"? Quite simply, Yes! My big expectations were once again, blown away. What a production! This is a true cinematic experience, to behold. The movie exceeded my expectations in terms of action, and entertainment. The editing, sound, score, visuals, direction and action are all top notch.

The film contains a fine cast of talented actors. Christian Bale, of course still makes is a great Batman. Michael Cain is fantastic, as he always is. He gives such a powerful performance, he really ought to be considered for an Oscar nomination. Tom Hardy as Bane is utterly terrifying, at times, and completely ominous. Anne Hathaway as Catwoman/Selina Kyle is a scene steal-er. She is completely engrossing. Everyone is so great, the dynamic scenes between the actors are so well done, so well written, and so well directed. The Dark Knight Rises is is emotionally riveting and amazing to view.

At a running time of almost 3 hours, the film never becomes dull, which is pretty impressive. The movie's action sequences are spectacularly well created and very intense. The dialogue between the character's are intelligent and highly believable. The movie's soundtrack is terrific and really exemplify's many of the movie's scenes. Extremely well editing and sound use really develop many of the movie's action scenes, so it's not just explosions and visuals like in many other movies. Nolan creates a grand, dirty, engrossing world, and his action sequences just hum.

In conclusion, this film is a gorgeous reminder that great writing and direction can enhance any movie-going experience, even superhero movies, which are usually thought of as mindless entertainment. I am wholly satisfied with Christopher Nolan's vision and thank all who worked on this film for bringing such an intricate interpretation of its very famous literary source. I cannot recommend this film anymore than I have, I just have to say everyone and anyone should see it. 10/10"

But it's Heath Ledger's iconic performance as the Joker that steals the show. His portrayal is hauntingly brilliant, a chaotic force that challenges the very ideals Batman stands for.

The storytelling is razor-sharp, keeping you on the edge of your seat from start to finish. Nolan's direction combined with the mesmerizing cinematography creates an atmosphere that's both ominous and enthralling. The action sequences are exhilarating, but it's the psychological depth of the characters that truly sets this film apart.

Beyond the action and spectacle, "The Dark Knight" delves into profound themes about society, justice, and the nature of heroism. It's a thought-provoking exploration of the human psyche, showing how even the most virtuous can be pushed to their limits.

Like, it's reputation is ridiculously high, and it's the kind of movie you think would be overhyped, but it really just is that great.

Rewatching Batman Begins last week was disappointing. I used to like it a lot, but I feel like it's aged poorly, even in just 15 years. The Dark Knight, however, gets better and better as time goes on.

It might not be perfect, as there's some logical flaws and inconsistencies. My least favourite is always wondering how the Joker got out of Wayne's penthouse, when Batman clearly got to the ground level quicker than he did.

But everything it does well it does so well that the flaws barely register. Everything is improved on Batman Begins- the action is clearer, the set pieces more memorable, the special effects more seamless, the characters (especially Rachel) are more interesting, the villains are better (even aside from the Joker, who is clearly the standout character in the film), the plot is more satisfying, there are more twists in the story, the world of Gotham City fees more lived in (it also looks completely different than Gotham in the last film), Batman as a character feels less goofy, the tone is better (as it's not as dreary and self-serious), and the attempts at humour are more successful.

But you didn't really need me to tell you all that.

10.title: A symphony of heroism and realism
10.content:
The Dark Knight by Christopher Nolan is an exemplary film that transcends the typical superhero genre, creating an intricate dance between light and dark, not only through its visuals but through its exploration of moral ambiguity, human resilience, and the nature of heroism. This film builds on a fascinating juxtaposition between light and dark, where each action, twist, and confrontation delves deep into the psyche of its characters, leading to a resolution that feels both inevitable and deeply earned. The film is more than a superhero story; it's a portrayal of what a hero could truly be like in our flawed, modern world.

Set in the crime-infested streets of Gotham City, The Dark Knight follows Bruce Wayne, aka Batman (played with restrained intensity by Christian Bale), as he takes on the chaotic and morally ambiguous Joker, portrayed by Heath Ledger in a role that redefined villainy in cinema. Nolan's Gotham isn't just a backdrop; it's a character in its own right, seething with corruption, fear, and desperation. And amidst this tumultuous cityscape, Batman struggles not only with his physical opponents but with his own inner demons and the ethical challenges that confront him at every turn.

One of the most compelling aspects of The Dark Knight is its moral complexity. In most superhero movies, the lines between good and evil are clear, but here they're anything but. The Joker is a master of chaos, someone who doesn't desire wealth or power but exists to show the world how fragile its sense of order truly is. His only aim is to bring Gotham, and Batman himself, to the edge of moral collapse. Ledger's Joker is unnervingly unpredictable, making it impossible to anticipate his next move. Every scene he's in is charged with an anarchic energy, forcing Batman, and by extension, the audience, to confront the uncomfortable question: how far can you go to fight evil without becoming what you despise?

The visual and thematic play of light and dark underscores the film's psychological tension. Gotham is often draped in shadows, neon lights bouncing off wet streets, reflecting the blurred moral boundaries the characters navigate. Wally Pfister's cinematography is phenomenal here, using contrasts in lighting to symbolize Batman's own conflict. The darkened skies and ominous backdrops capture Batman's shadowy world, while harsh, fluorescent lights in the Joker's scenes reinforce his raw, unrelenting chaos.

Nolan's narrative approach is meticulously structured, unfolding like a thriller with each new dilemma adding layers to the characters. Batman's efforts to stop the Joker are not straightforward heroic feats but rather a descent into ethical quagmires. The Joker puts Gotham's heroes-both Batman and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart)-through a crucible of moral compromise. Harvey Dent, once Gotham's "White Knight," succumbs to bitterness and transforms into Two-Face, a tragic embodiment of Gotham's broken ideals. His story arc is one of the film's most haunting, showing how even the noblest individuals can be corrupted by trauma and loss.

The film's resolution is bittersweet, offering neither a victory for Batman nor a clean end to Gotham's suffering. Rather, it's an acknowledgment of the cost of heroism in a flawed world. Batman takes the fall for Harvey's crimes, sacrificing his reputation to preserve the city's hope. This choice underlines the film's profound message about heroism: that it's not about winning but about sacrifice, about carrying burdens no one else can. Batman becomes a scapegoat, embracing the shadows to save Gotham's fragile sense of hope and justice.

Nolan's vision of Batman in The Dark Knight is revolutionary, presenting a hero who isn't invulnerable or morally absolute but conflicted, weary, and human. This Batman is a figure who exists within the darkest parts of our world yet still strives to protect it. His journey forces us to ask ourselves: What would we be willing to give up in the fight for justice? The Dark Knight shows us that in the battle between light and dark, true heroism is not always about overcoming darkness but about enduring it-remaining steadfast even when the world threatens to unravel.

In blending action and resolution, light and dark, The Dark Knight doesn't just redefine the superhero genre; it stands as one of the most sophisticated explorations of heroism in modern cinema. It's a film that resonates beyond its action sequences, leaving a profound impact that reminds us what a hero might truly look like in our own universe.

10.title: I am the knight.

While it is lost in the vast sea of middling superhero fare, The Dark Knight is one of the greatest movies ever made. The somewhat hefty runtime of more than two and a half hours flies by as a captivating and inspired story makes for one of the most enjoyable movie experiences I've ever had. From a technical aspect the movie is just as masterful, notably the cinematography which is eerily beautiful. The effects team pulls out all the stops making both The Joker and Harvey Dent look like they could be real. Heath Ledger's performance may be one of the greatest displays of acting ever put to film. Ledger brings subtlety and nuance to a role that could have come across as a bit too slapstick. The script backs up Ledgers Joker by injecting him with nihilistic motives that make him the most interesting person in the room, even when the other person is dressed like a bat. The writing of the characters is handled with intense care and the climax doesn't fail to disappoint, once again aided by great performances by Christian Bales stoic and graveling Batman and Heath Ledgers unpredictable and haunting Joker. Philosophicaly the movie plays upon themes of nihilism and chaos vs justice. The movie projects it's more sophisticated of messages with no restraint and doesn't talk down to the audience. It breaks the mold of the average superhero movie by portraying similar ideas of hope without the more gratuitous and heavy handed film making of its genre-mates. Overall, The Dark Knight, often penalized for the sins of its species prove that a superhero movie can be this good.

10.title: A deep dive into the Jokers troubled mind
10.content:
"The Dark Knight," directed by Christopher Nolan, presents a compelling interpretation of the Joker, suggesting that he may be a war veteran grappling with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). This unique portrayal adds a layer of complexity to the character, making him more than just a traditional villain.

In this iteration, Christian Bale's Bruce Wayne/Batman remains a captivating force, but it is Heath Ledger's haunting portrayal of the Joker that steals the show. Ledger's performance is mesmerizing as he brings an unpredictable and deeply troubled character to life. The hints and subtle details scattered throughout the film suggest that the Joker's actions and mindset may be influenced by his traumatic experiences as a war veteran.

The screenplay, written by the Nolan brothers, delves into the psychological aspects of the Joker's character. It explores the effects of war and trauma on the human mind, challenging viewers to consider the consequences of neglected mental health. By blurring the line between hero and villain, the film prompts us to question the society's responsibility in caring for those who have served and suffered.

Visually, "The Dark Knight" maintains its stunning aesthetics, with Gotham City serving as a metaphorical battleground for the internal struggles of its characters. The action sequences continue to be expertly choreographed, but it is the moments of vulnerability and introspection that truly shine. By delving into the Joker's troubled past, the film offers a more profound insight into the character's motivations and actions.

Hans Zimmer's score once again enhances the film, creating an atmosphere that mirrors the Joker's chaotic mindset. The music adds an eerie ambiance to the narrative, capturing the internal torment and fractured state of the character.

"The Dark Knight" is not just a superhero movie; it is a psychological exploration that challenges viewers to confront the complexities of the human condition. By introducing the possibility of the Joker being a war veteran with PTSD, the film opens up discussions about the impact of trauma and the importance of mental health awareness.

In conclusion, "The Dark Knight" is a cinematic triumph that pushes the boundaries of the superhero genre. Through its exploration of the Joker's troubled mind and potential war veteran background, the film delves into deeper themes and offers a fresh perspective on a classic character. It is a thought-provoking experience that lingers in the mind long after the credits roll.

10.title: The Dark Knight: A Masterpiece That Redefined Superhero Films

10.title: Best of all time

The Dark Knight is a cinematic masterpiece that it is not just an ordinary superhero movie, but it is the benchmark of all movies in its genre. It is the second installment in The Dark Knight Trilogy and in fact the best among the three.

It tells a gripping tale of moral complexity, grief, chaos, and the relentless battle between good and evil. The iconic and one & only Heath Ledger as the Joker earned him a posthumous Academy Award for the Best Supporting Actor. Heath Ledger's Joker is a force of nature, an agent of chaos who challenges the very essence of justice and morality in Gotham City.

The film's narrative is a tightly woven tapestry of suspense, intrigue, and psychological depth. It explores the consequences of one's choices, the fine line between heroism and vigilantism, and the sacrifices required in the pursuit of a better world. The character of Harvey Dent, masterfully portrayed by Aaron Eckhart, undergoes a harrowing transformation from Gotham's white knight to the tragic Two-Face, adding layers of tragedy and moral ambiguity to the story.

Nolan's direction and storytelling prowess are on full display, as he takes the Batman to a level of sophistication rarely seen in the genre. The film's dark and gritty atmosphere, grounded in a sense of realism, immerses viewers in a Gotham City that feels authentic and lived-in.

It challenges us to confront the chaos within ourselves and the world around us. Ledger's Joker, with his iconic line, "Why so serious?" encapsulates the film's ability to delve into the darkest corners of the human psyche.

In conclusion, it is a film with strong testament to the power of storytelling, this movie continues to captivate and inspire audiences, solidifying its place as one of the greatest films ever made. Whether you're a fan of superheroes or simply a lover of exceptional cinema, the Dark Knight is an absolute must-see that will leave you in awe of its brilliance.

10.title: #MAR#MAKAUT#LOCKDOWN ACTIVITIES
10.content:
We've been subjected to enormous amounts of hype and marketing for the Dark Knight. We've seen Joker scavenger hunts and one of the largest viral campaigns in advertising history and it culminates with the actual release of the movie.

Everything that's been said is pretty much spot on. This is the first time I can remember where a summer blockbuster film far surpasses the hype.

For as much action as there is in this movie, it's the acting that makes it a great piece of work. Between all the punches, explosions and stunt-work is some great dialog work. All the actors have their moments.

Bale's Batman is the definitive Batman because we see everything in this character finally on film. Martial arts skills, cunning, great tactical thinking, forensic application, technological genius to advance or improve Luscious Fox's inventions/technological breakthroughs, intimidating personality, and even a little swashbuckling.

As for Heath, yes he gets credit for his performance as the Joker. But you have to also recognize Jonathan and Chris Nolan for the writing and treatment of the character. It's not just the fact that Ledger makes the Joker so menacing, but the Nolans have given the character this great manifesto that drives its actions. The Joker's stance on chaos, order, anarchy, the morality of the average modern human being make the character so interesting psychologically. The Nolans drafted a complex character and only a perfect performance could've pulled something like this off. That's how difficult of a role this was, and that's why Ledger's performance is so great.

This isn't an action movie. It's a film that explores literary themes of the hero and villain, as well as order and anarchy. Yes, listen to the dialog because it's all in there.

Go see this masterpiece.

10.title: Loved this movie so much.
10.content:
The Dark Knight: A Haunting Exploration of Morality

Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight transcends the superhero genre, delivering a haunting exploration of good and evil. It's not just a comic book movie; it's a crime thriller that delves into the depths of human nature.

**Heath Ledger's Unforgettable Joker**

Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of iconic. His performance is unnerving, unpredictable, and utterly captivating. The Joker is an agent of chaos, a force of nature that throws Gotham City into turmoil. Ledger's embodiment of the character earned him a posthumous Oscar, a testament to the brilliance of his performance.

**A Complex Moral Universe**

The Dark Knight doesn't shy away from complex moral questions. Harvey Dent, Gotham's idealistic white knight, is tragically corrupted by the Joker's schemes. This transformation forces Batman to make difficult choices, blurring the lines between heroism and vigilantism. The film doesn't offer easy answers, instead leaving the audience to grapple with the consequences of violence and the true nature of heroism.

**Gripping Action and Nolan's Vision**

While the film's core lies in its characters and themes, it also delivers exceptional action sequences. The heist sequence at the beginning of the film is a masterclass in suspense, and the final showdown between Batman and the Joker is both thrilling and heartbreaking. Nolan's direction is masterful, creating a Gotham City that is both stylish and gritty, a believable world where outlandish characters like the Joker can exist.

**The Dark Knight's Legacy**

The Dark Knight is a film that stays with you long after the credits roll. It's a powerful and thought-provoking exploration of human nature, disguised as a superhero movie. It's no surprise that it remains one of the most acclaimed superhero films ever made, a true testament to its exceptional filmmaking and enduring themes.

10.title: Heath Ledger steals the show.
10.content: There are several aspects about the Dark Knight that make it stand apart from other superhero films, but the most iconic feature of the movie is Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker. Though not the first to take up the mantle of the Batman's most infamous super-villain, Heath Ledger's take placed the character in a considerably darker and more mature light. The more traditional versions of the Joker offered audiences a dastardly, unpredictable clown with a white paint-plastered face, and while Heath Ledger's Joker is indeed unpredictable, he is definitely no clown. In full costume Ledger stands with a hunched posture in a purple suit, a face covered in white makeup, and an unnerving red smile painted across his lips and cheeks. The overall image is haunting, but what truly sets this act apart is in the monologues of Ledger's Joker. His words are not those of a wise- cracking psychopath, but those of precise and dangerous serial killer. "I'll show you," Ledger tells co-star Christian Bale (the Batman) in one scene. "When the chips are down, these civilized people...they'll eat each other." The Dark Knight may very well be the greatest superhero movie of all time, and it's all because of the talents of Heath Ledger. He's not crazy. He's just ahead of the curve.

10.title: A Masterful Exploration of Chaos, Morality, and the Heroic Struggle
10.content:
The Dark Knight, directed by Christopher Nolan, is a landmark in superhero cinema, seamlessly blending action, drama, and moral complexity. This second installment in Nolan's Batman trilogy features Christian Bale reprising his role as Bruce Wayne/Batman, alongside an unforgettable performance by Heath Ledger as the Joker, whose chaotic philosophy challenges the very foundation of Gotham City.

The film opens with Gotham in turmoil, facing an unprecedented crime wave orchestrated by the Joker. As Batman grapples with his vigilante ethics, he partners with Lieutenant James Gordon (Gary Oldman) and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) in a desperate attempt to restore order. The plot expertly intertwines their stories, exploring themes of heroism, sacrifice, and the fragile line between good and evil.

Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of iconic, infusing the character with a chilling unpredictability that keeps viewers on edge. His performance elevates the film, providing a profound commentary on chaos and morality. The tension between Batman and the Joker culminates in thrilling confrontations, showcasing Nolan's masterful direction and the film's intense pacing.

Visually, The Dark Knight is stunning, with breathtaking action sequences and a haunting score by Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard that heightens the emotional stakes. The film's cinematography captures the gritty essence of Gotham, making it feel like a character in its own right.

While some may find the film's moral dilemmas and darker tones unsettling, The Dark Knight transcends typical superhero fare, offering a complex narrative that resonates on multiple levels. It challenges viewers to consider the cost of justice and the nature of heroism, solidifying its place as a cinematic masterpiece.

Overall, The Dark Knight is a compelling and thought-provoking film that not only redefined the superhero genre but also set a high bar for storytelling in cinema. Its blend of action, drama, and philosophical inquiry makes it a must-watch for both fans of the genre and those seeking a deeper cinematic experience.

10.title: "The Dark Knight" is a masterpiece of superhero cinema

"The Dark Knight" is a 2008 superhero film directed by Christopher Nolan and starring Christian Bale as Batman, Heath Ledger as the Joker, and Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent. The film is widely regarded as one of the greatest superhero movies of all time, and for good reason.

The plot of the movie centers around Batman's attempt to stop the Joker, who is wreaking havoc on the city of Gotham. The Joker is a chaotic force of nature, with no real plan or agenda other than to cause chaos and destruction. Batman is forced to confront the Joker's nihilistic worldview and his own moral code as he tries to save the city.

One of the things that makes "The Dark Knight" so great is its realism. Nolan's vision of Gotham is gritty and dark, and the characters are all complex and multi-layered. The film explores themes of morality, justice, and the nature of heroism in a way that is both thought-provoking and entertaining.

The performances in the movie are all top-notch. Bale's Batman is brooding and intense, and Ledger's Joker is unforgettable. Ledger's performance, in particular, is widely regarded as one of the greatest in cinema history. His Joker is terrifying, unpredictable, and utterly captivating.

Overall, "The Dark Knight" is a masterpiece of superhero cinema. It's a film that transcends the genre and stands on its own as a work of art. It's thrilling, thought-provoking, and emotionally impactful. If you haven't seen it yet, it's definitely worth checking out.

10.title: Gold Standard for Comic book and Crime Drama films
10.content:
The movie is structured as a 4 act thriller.

This movie has the absolute best of the best opening scenes in all of film history. The bank robbery is a masterfully built to show us so much about the joker in barely over 5 minutes. Hes a master-planner who fears nothing, who can keep his identity anonymous and above all off putting body language is able to convey that hes a man to be feared.

The second introduction to the Joker when he crashes the Mob meeting with a pencil trick is gold. He establishes his power over the mob and makes his intent known. Joker puns are always a win.

Batman flying around Hong Kong would have been some of the best visuals ever put onto an IMAX screen in 2008.

Joker's origin story is intentionally kept vague and his changing story every time is so joker like, and agent of chaos, someone who wants to watch the world burn.

The trio of Jim Gordon , Harvey Dent and Batman work so well to epitomize the pure essence of the movie. The interactions they have between the 3 on the Gotham PD rooftop really fleshes out the the characters of Harvey Dent and what he stands for.

The 2nd act with Dent's arrest and the ensuing chase and fight is so well filmed with a mix of practical effects and stunt doubles, win win win.

Joker and Batman's interrogation scene is so good. Heath Ledger's performance, oh man. The way he laughs every time he gets punched. The absolute powerlessness Batman feels dealing with a villain with no weakness, nothing to threaten with.

Harvey's 2 face turn is so well done, the visual effects and the makeup it must have taken to make his half face look so realistic and good is commendable. Criminal that they didn't win the Academy for best makeup.

Batman's sacrifice nails home Harvey's quote " You either die a hero or live long enough to see yourself become the villain." What line, what a character.

Harvey's motivation is entirely believable, he's lost the love of his life because he trust Batman and Gordon to handle the joker and the mob.

James Newton Howard and Hans Zimmer's score for The Dark Knight is the best Film score ever made.

4 S grade performances from Heath Ledger, Christian Bale, Gary Oldman and Aaron Eckhart is way more than we could ask for.

Christopher Nolan's greatest movie, A true masterpiece.

Some people were sceptical when Heath Ledger was given the role, A lot of people didn't think he could possibly pull it off in the wake of Jack Nicholson's zany version and of course the fantastic voice over work done by none other than Mark Hamill in the animated series. I did not let any of this cloud my judgement beforehand, being a die hard Batman fan myself I had huge expectations. Coupled with Ledger's untimely death just before it's release i knew that this film was going to be big in more ways than one. Coming out of the theatre I was thrilled. It was impossible not to love this movie. The Joker that Ledger provided was so dark and disturbing he wasn't even recognizable as the handsome young Australian we all remembered him to be. The Joker was the defining moment of Ledger's career and I am truly saddened that he will never get a chance to try and top such a performance. Ledger's performance aside, the film itself was in my opinion flawless. The building of the story was properly paced, dramatic and exciting where it needed to be without being over the top. I have always been drawn more to the darker, dramatic type filmmaking so I felt this film fit that bill. It was action packed without turning into a Michael Bay explosion fest and the rest of the actors managed to keep up to Ledger respectably enough (although one could argue he outshone them all slightly). This film has stayed with me as one of my all time favourites. I know that I am an easily pleased movie-goer and that not everybody will enjoy this film, and that is understandable because some people just can't be satisfied. Regardless of that, I would urge everybody to see this film!

10.title: The Batman movie that's soooo serious!
10.content:
THE DARK KNIGHT, Christopher Nolan's much anticipated sequel to BATMAN BEGINS, arrived at the multiplexes with great fanfare in July of 2008, but there was tragic baggage attached due to the accidental death of Heath Ledger six months earlier. Prior to his fatal medication overdose, Ledger had completed his work portraying the Joker, and observers on the set of THE DARK KNIGHT felt confident in stating that he accomplished something previously considered impossible: eclipsing Jack Nicholson's 1989 interpretation.

It's an unwritten rule in comic book movies that the villains must always have larger-than-life personalities, that the archenemies be so formidable that ordinary heroes are not enough to combat them, leaving it up to a superhero to deliver us from evil. And every superhero has to have that one special adversary who transcends the usual suspects in the rogue's gallery, one who personifies the antithesis of everything our champion stands for. In the Caped Crusader's case, that supervillain was none other than the Joker, the clown prince of crime, the Moriarty to Batman's Sherlock Holmes.

No one who saw BATMAN BEGINS had any doubt a sequel would follow in two or three years time. Nolan had already hinted at who the villain would be at the conclusion of BEGINS, when Jim Gordon shows the Caped Crusader the criminal's calling card: the playing card of the joker!!! Jack Nicholson's memorably over-the-top performance in the Burton film ensured that future Joker portrayals would be an impossible act for anyone to follow. When plans for THE DARK KNIGHT were made public, the prevailing theory was that only someone with an extroverted personality, such as a Jim Carrey or a Robin Williams, could pull the Joker characterization off.

So when Warner Bros announced that Nolan cast Heath Ledger as the clown prince, my first reaction was "Wait....what???". Ledger had recently received an Oscar nomination for BROKEBACK MOUNTAIN, but I still had a difficult time envisioning him in a role that had previously brought to life by Nicholson {and Cesar Romero before him}. However, being a far better director than Burton, Nolan was never one to allow an actor's marquee value influence his casting choices. In speaking to the media, he told them that Ledger was the only person whom he considered for the part.

THE DARK KNIGHT takes place a year after our titular hero first made his presence known to Gotham City's bad guys. Because Wayne Manor was burned to the ground in BATMAN BEGINS, Bruce now resides in his Gotham penthouse suite, with a huge, segregated underground garage serving as his makeshift Batcave until the new mansion is rebuilt. Officially designated by the police commissioner as a vigilante to be arrested on sight, in actuality Batman enjoys a professional rapport with Lieutenant Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman). The veteran detective has been grateful for the role Batman played in rescuing Gotham from the League Of Shadows, and it is only for this enigmatic ally that Gordon will conveniently look the other way.

By maintaining correspondence through the Batsignal, Gordon and Batman, along with new district attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart), have made major strides towards crippling the organized crime structure that still operates despite Carmine Falcone's incarceration. But the mob will soon become a secondary irritant when another dark presence emerges. A brazen hoodlum known as the Joker and his gang of masked clowns have been robbing the very banks the Mafia uses to launder their ill-gotten booty. Unlike Nicholson's hammy scoundrel, Ledger's Joker is less theatrical, a sort-of Alex De Large decked out in crusty red & white make-up, a purple blazer, and dirty green hair....but without the Nasdat verbiage! He's the walking id, a psychopath whom Alfred accurately diagnoses as a man who "just wants to watch the world burn".

Nolan meticulously explored Batman's roots in the first movie, but in this sequel he avoids explaining the background of his arch nemesis. All we really know about the Joker is that he isn't afraid of anyone....and embraces pain almost as much as he enjoys inflicting it. It's obvious this guy had a dysfunctional childhood; he has two scars, one on each side of his mouth, both pointing upward in the shape of a perennial smile. {The Joker loves to tell differing accounts over how he acquired those scars.} That abnormal upbringing has turned him into a remorseless sociopath to whom human suffering means nothing.

The Joker's audacity is so pronounced that he gatecrashes a secret summit of crime bosses wherein he happens to be one of the items under discussion. With explosives strapped under his jacket {in case any of them get any ideas}, he boldly states to them that neither Harvey Dent nor the police is their biggest problem: it's Batman! Sitting in on the Mafia conclave via teleconference is Lau, a Chinese investment banker, and it's because of his shady fiduciary skills {aka laundering} that the authorities haven't seized all of their funds. The Joker, offering his services to the highest bidder, vows to kill the Caped Crusader once an agreement is in place. He also correctly sizes up Lau as someone who'll make a deal with Dent to save his own skin.

Dent and Gordon are anxious to bring Lau up on criminal charges, but the investor has already fled to Hong Kong....where no extradition treaty exists with the United States. With the help of Lucius Fox (Morgan Freeman) and Alfred, Batman is able to penetrate Lau's skyscraper fortress, capture him, exfiltrate him out of Hong Kong, and drop him off in front of Gotham police headquarters as a gift for Gordon and Dent. With all major Mafia figures now on trial with a grocery list of indictments, they grudgingly accept the inevitable: they've got to do business with the Joker, whether they like it or not.

The Joker wastes no time harnessing his particular brand of anarchy, publicly vowing to kill innocent people every day until Batman reveals his true identity....and then making good on that threat! Displaying a taste for the grandiose, the Joker also earmarks the trial judge, the police commissioner, the mayor, and Dent for assassination {with the first two he is successful}. Citizens who originally praised Batman for putting the fear of God into Gotham's criminals are now condemning him for not coming forward.

But even if Batman does unmask himself, the Joker will never stop the killings, something Alfred and Rachel Dawes (Maggie Gyllenhaal, replacing Katie Holmes) try in vain to convince Bruce of. Luckily, the incorruptible Harvey Dent bails our superhero out of a tight spot by confessing to be the Caped Crusader. Now, of course, everyone who's ever read the DC Comics {or watched BATMAN FOREVER} knows that Harvey will become the villainous Two-Face. {In the comics, a gangster standing trial was responsible for his disfigurement; in this treatment, the Joker is the culprit.}

THE DARK KNIGHT has the distinction of being the only Christopher Nolan picture that has a straightforward narrative minus his nonlinear structures that play tricks with time {not even a flashback!}. The pace moves along quite forcefully from beginning to end, with razor sharp editing and action scenes so stunningly executed that audiences won't realize THE DARK KNIGHT is 2½ hours long. Ledger's {posthumous} Oscar winning performance as the Joker is one of the few times anyone has overshadowed Christian Bale....and this is a movie where every cast member is good!!

Yet THE DARK KNIGHT is not all endless action! Nolan uses his second Batman film to explore the morality of a post 9/11 world where civility goes out the window. The Joker could be seen as a parallel to a modern-day terrorist organization, with Batman echoing a Homeland Security that resorts to cellphone surveillance, the kind which dangerously borders on violating civil liberties, mirroring America's controversial Patriot Act. Must one become a lawbreaker to stop a monster? Do the ends justify the means? This intrusion into people's personal lives horrifies Lucius Fox, who will tender his resignation out of protest once the Joker is apprehended.

THE DARK KNIGHT was deservedly the biggest motion picture of 2008. Critically acclaimed and a commercial juggernaut, it was widely expected {including by yours truly} to become the first superhero blockbuster ever nominated for Best Picture, and there was furious backlash against the Academy when they snubbed it in favor of more "prestigious" nominees. When it was released THE DARK KNIGHT was rightfully considered to be the CITIZEN KANE of comic book movies. Sixteen years later it's still regarded as such, and probably will for the remainder of this century. 🔚

10.title: A masterpiece...
10.content:
Many of us movie-lovers watch a lot of movies. Some times, it turns out to be a disappointing experience. Most of the time, we like the movie, but forget it after a few days. However, there are those rare moments when you watch what is called a masterpiece, and it sticks in your mind for your entire life. This review is about one of these. This review is about Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight.

The Dark Knight is the sequel of the very good Batman Begins, the first movie of The Dark Knight trilogy. It is a masterpiece because I think it will change how movies in general will be made in the future.

Its dark and claustrophobic tone fits perfectly to a Batman movie. The Dark Knight shows that the tone of a movie influences the viewers experience. Throughout the entire movie, we feel that the main character is not totally in control, that it's an all new and different challenge for him and that he doesn't know how to handle it. And that brings me to talk about the Joker. Of course everybody knows the Joker, how he looks, how he is, etc. We even know how he acts because of the great performance Jack Nicholson pulled in Tim Burton's Batman. Actually, everybody had that performance in mind when they started the movie and that is also the reason why Heath Ledger's performance is so astounding. He brings the character to an all new level and in a completely different direction, but still in a very believable and accurate way (in my own opinion, he nailed the character even more then Nicholson did). Ledger made the Joker so crazy but so right about everything at the same time. Even if he is a psychopath, we understand his motives. It is so sad that Ledger died before the film's release and that he couldn't see all the impact his performance had on the film industry (personnaly the greatest performance I have ever seen by an actor). Gary Oldman, Aaron Eckhart, Christian Bale, Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine and Maggie Gyllenhaal also all gave incredible performances. The plot of the movie is also very interesting and refreshing, leaving behind the classic three acts structure. The score of the movie, composed by James Newton Howard and Hans Zimmer, is perfect, very good and very appropriate. The movie itself also looks very good and has a great cinematography. Nolan directed this movie in the best way possibly imaginable.

To conclude, the movie is possibly one of the greatest I have ever seen if not the greatest because of the mind-blowing acting, the great score and the perfect directing. The movie is also great looking. It's the perfect batman movie, with it's most iconic villain and, in my own opinion, couldn't be better.

10.title: Greatest Superhero Movie of All time? Opinions aside it is a must watch for anyone who calls themselves a film fan
10.content:
Overall: If you haven't watched this movie... YOU MUST! It is a fantastic movie and arguably (it is) the greatest superhero movie of all time. There is a reason that, as of today, IMDb ranks it as 4th best movie EVER made.

Good: Stellar performances from EVERYONE especially Heath Ledger who absolutely steals the show with his riveting, groundbreaking portrayal of one of the greatest (fictional) villains ever. Incredible score mixed with incredible cinematography and incredible groundbreaking effects. Great story with mostly great dialogue and, obviously, great characters. A masterpiece.

Bad: The cops are still morons and the Bat-Voice can get annoying.

Best Part: The Joker's interrogation scene

MVP: Heath Ledger as THEJoker

10/10

10.title: A (flat 10). August 18' @AMC
10.content: Ambitious yet necessary. Perfect highs that hit high. No lows. Always engaging and always exciting. Excellent script and dialogue. Strong shots, pacing, editing, direction, and performances. Gold standard.

10.title: Very nice movie
10.content: About as near perfect of a film as you can get for a comic book or action film. The script was brilliant, Heath Ledger's performance was well worth the Oscar he received. Even the intriguing, yet simplistic first scene sets the tone for the entire film. It says something about a film when every other film in its sub-genre tries to emulate it in some shape or form. This really kicked off the style that Marvel is going with now in that the films are first and foremost genre films but with superheroes added to them (this being a crime thriller w superheroes). Definitely one that should be watched by everyone. This film commonly is called the best comic book movie ever and it is hard to argue with people that make that claim.

10.title: The Joker and Batman we needed
10.content: This movie is one of the best portrait of Joker and Batman i have ever seen. It makes you realize how much of a complex deep character Batman is and establishes him as a superhero with human problems and dilemmas . Heath Ledger and his performance of Joker with Nolan guidance makes you understand why The Joker is one of the best villains ever . Twisted , crazy ,genius , this movie allows you to see Jokers insanity at its best plus why a guy with no unique powers whatsoever , in contrast to other superhero movies villains , is so dangerous and so loved by the comic fanbase . This movie delivers it all with epic scenes and impeccable portraits and perfomances.

10.title: The best batman movie to date, without doubt
10.content:
I'm hard pressed ever to give a ten. I don't think a film exists that deserves a ten. That value alone would perhaps mark the downfall of cinema. However grandiose that may seem. The Dark Knight certainly deserves more than a nine. It is quite simply the best batman movie ever.

I have literally just walked out of the cinema. My only criticism is Bale's voice as Batman, which seems a little forced at times. That's about it.

Ledger's Joker steals the movie. IMHO his best role to date, and his last of course. I expected he would get a posthumous Oscar anyway. But in this case he certainly deserves it. His Joker makes Nicholson's look like a joke.

His character has more unexplained depth than any tawdry summoning that occurred before.

The film has subtleties that may allude some viewers looking for a simple comic book action movie.

Many of the comments before mine reveal such intricacies. I shall not bother to repeat them. Anyone that gives this movie a nine or above is pretty much spot on.

Watch the film. Simple is that. Bale's Wayne / Batman are great. Joker is stupendous.

What a shame Ledger isn't around for a sequel or any other movie for that matter.

RIP Mr. Ledger.

And to the Nolan's, thank you for a film which finally does the Batman better than DC.

10.title: Better Second Time Out!!
10.content:
Wowzers, where do you begin with this film? Epic makes it sounds like a long film where your buttocks begin to get numb and you start fidgeting NOT in this film WOW, from the initial opening sequences until the credits roll a whole 152 minutes later you're a gripped to the screen wondering why has it taken so long for this franchise to get all the right ingredients together to make such a kick ass film? At the end of this film I was breathless, the action didn't overwhelm the film the melancholy didn't overwhelm this film; the balance was struck with deft precision. The actors didn't ham it up as in previous instalments (prior to Batman Begins naturally) and you truly feel empathy for the characters, even the Joker! Ledgers character shared his past whilst committing some fiendish crimes, giving an insight as to why his life had gotten him to this point. I suppose there are going to be inevitable comments made as to Ledgers performance in this role due to his untimely death. It would be disingenuous to praise his role out of sympathy, luckily this is not necessary. Ledgers performance in this movie only reminds us of the terrible loss we suffer from him no longer being with us.

Moving swiftly on, Christian Bale continues his solid portrayal of Batman and builds on his previous outing in 'Batman Begins'. The only tiny criticism I have is Bale himself when he gives interviews he is soooo dull, other than that, the role he plays is great (I suppose that is what a good actor does, take note Mark Wahlberg) Michael Cain is, well, Michael Cain, the man is a legend in his own lifetime and following this performance only adds to his kudos. Aaron Eckhart has at last got a role he can get his teeth into; hopefully this will lead to other work. The switch to Maggie Gyllenhaal for the role of Rachel was an inspired choice and pays off. It's a pity her role won't be revived! Lastly we see Gary Oldman reprise his role as James Gordan. The Gordan role second time out is expanded and supports the rest of the film very well. Oldman has been vastly underutilised in recent years, hopefully this will be rectified.

There will be calls to make this into a trilogy and rightly so, however in the rush to make a third instalment I would urge caution to Christopher Nolan not to be rushed to into something to cater to the studio's lust for more profits..

10.title: Truly great, but not without flaws
10.content:
Before seeing the movie, I was ridiculously excited about it. I was hoping my expectations would be met... and in most respects, they were. It's a very enjoyable, well-done movie. But there are things I think need to be different in order for the movie to be perfect.

Comparatively, Batman Begins feels like a more well thought out movie than The Dark Knight. It had a much more focused point to it. The story was more personal and felt more real, I guess you could say. The Dark Knight almost takes on too much.

Action is awesome. The visuals are amazing. Acting is top-notch. The actual production value of this movie is something to be in awe of. The only problems it has are the fault of the script. I think maybe it should have gone through another draft or two.

But, that being said, it's definitely a very good movie. Heath Ledger's performance is as great as we all knew it would be since the moment we first saw the trailers.

*SPOILERS*

My biggest beef with the movie is the fact that there wasn't a huge showdown between Batman and the Joker like it looked like there would be in the trailer. The first theatrical trailer ended with the Joker in the street saying "Hit me!", and then the big low angle shot of Batman sliding past him on the Bat-Pod. I thought this would be the climax. Batman and Joker were gonna have a huge epic showdown in the streets of Gotham. It didn't turn out this way. Those shots were actually part of a scene that comes about mid- way through the movie, and is actually over quite quickly after that. The climax that DOES happen between Batman and Joker is considerably smaller on the edge of a building, and there isn't really anything all that "showdown"-y about it. Perhaps they were saving the showdown for another movie... too bad they didn't know this was the only film they'd get with Ledger as the Joker.

But that bit of disappointment is nothing more than just my misguided expectations, and I can't really blame the film for that.

*END SPOILERS*

So... all in all, I very much like the film. I don't quite love it like I thought I would... yet. Perhaps repeat viewing will get me more comfortable with the movie, and I'll love it. As of this moment, I'm still a little uncomfortable with it.

10.title: heath ledger... love u..
10.content:
The Dark Knight is a 2008 superhero film directed by Christopher Nolan. This film, considered a masterpiece by most critics, offers an experience that impresses the audience with its unique atmosphere, complex story and great acting.

The Joker character played by Heath Ledger has become a legendary character in the history of cinema with his performance. Ledger's naive and subversive acting is considered by many to be one of the best performances seen in the performing arts.

The film is full of psychological tension and action scenes and draws the audience in with its story. Additionally, the philosophical and ethical issues in the film are thought-provoking. The contrast between the internal conflicts of the Batman character and the chaotic thoughts of the Joker provides an experience that deeply affects the audience.

Cinematography and production design can be considered great works. The dark and intense atmosphere of Gotham City makes the film feel not just like a thriller, but also like an epic superhero movie.

In summary, The Dark Knight is a film that offers an unforgettable experience with a compelling and complex story, great acting and impressive visual effects. It has become a classic in cinema history and set a new standard for superhero movies.

10.title: Ledger is Without a Doubt Best 'Joker' There is...
10.content:
I've seen this movie the day after it's release in theaters in the US. I have to say that it's one of the best movie ever. Though like many others would say that it's as good as Godfather. I can't really say since I've never seen that movie and probably never will. But the most thing that caught my attention the most is Heath Ledger's performance as the menacing Joker. I have to admit, Joker is one of my favorite comic book villains of all time, and Ledger nailed it. Sadly he's not here to see how big of a success this became, but I bet he would be appreciable about his accomplishment. Though I came to found out that Ledger was in two other movies that I really like ("10 Things I Hate About You" and "The Brothers Grimm"). I never knew the actor's name in both films until I realize it after seeing "The Dark Knight". Yeah, I felt stupid, but can't help it if I have bad memory sometimes.

Though enough of Ledger's excellent work in this movie. There was other things in this movie that I really loved. Two-Face was awesome. Especially the actor, Aaron Eckhart, was really great for the role. It was like he was born to play as Two-Face (Same for Ledger as the Joker). I actually thought Two-Face would be a cliffhanger to the third movie. I guess not. It was a great ending for the movie to end it as Harvey the hero and Batman on the run from the law for the choice he made (I hope that made sense). Brilliant. Just pure brilliant.

Commissioner Gordon, as always, is my favorite supporting character from the Batman comics. Sir Michael Caine from my favorite movies he starred ("Dirty Rotten Scoundrels", "Austin Powers in Goldmember", "Batman Begins", and of course "The Dark Knight") is a great talent as well. Last but not least, the main character, our favorite Dark Knight caped crusader, BATMAN! He's also known as Christian Bale. All I have to say about what he did for this movie is...well, what can I say? He is the Batman, he was perfect with the role from start to finish.
