10.title: The Dark Knight" is a 2008 superhero film directed by Christopher Nolan and starring Christian Bale as Bruce Wayne/Batman.
10.content:
Storyline: The film picks up where "Batman Begins" left off, with Batman facing a new threat in the form of the Joker, brilliantly portrayed by Heath Ledger in an iconic performance. The Joker's chaos-driven rampage pushes Batman to his limits as he struggles to save Gotham City from descending into anarchy. Alongside the Joker, Batman must also contend with other foes, including the mobster Sal Maroni and the enigmatic Harvey Dent, portrayed by Aaron Eckhart.

Direction and Cinematography: Christopher Nolan's direction is masterful, creating a dark, gritty, and realistic atmosphere that sets "The Dark Knight" apart from traditional superhero films. The film's pacing is intense, with nail-biting action sequences and thought-provoking moments that keep audiences on the edge of their seats. Wally Pfister's cinematography is exceptional, with visually stunning shots and breathtaking visuals that add depth and dimension to the story.

Performances: The cast delivers outstanding performances, with Christian Bale reprising his role as Batman/Bruce Wayne with gravitas and intensity. Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of mesmerizing, earning him a posthumous Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. Aaron Eckhart is also notable as Harvey Dent, providing a complex and tragic portrayal of the character's transformation into Two-Face. The supporting cast, including Michael Caine as Alfred, Gary Oldman as Commissioner Gordon, and Morgan Freeman as Lucius Fox, also deliver exceptional performances, adding depth and richness to the film's characters.

Themes: "The Dark Knight" delves into complex themes of morality, chaos versus order, and the nature of heroism. It explores the blurred lines between good and evil, as well as the psychological toll that vigilantism takes on Batman/Bruce Wayne. The film also delves into the idea of sacrificing one's own morality for the greater good, as well as the consequences of choices made in the pursuit of justice.

Overall Impression: "The Dark Knight" is a groundbreaking superhero film that transcends the genre, offering a compelling, dark, and thought-provoking experience for audiences. Christopher Nolan's direction, along with the exceptional performances of the cast, particularly Heath Ledger's unforgettable portrayal of the Joker, elevates the film to a new level of excellence. With its complex themes, gripping story, and impressive visuals, "The Dark Knight" remains a cinematic masterpiece that has left an indelible mark on the world of superhero films.

10.title: Why so Serious?
10.content:
Why so Serious?

Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight is a critically acclaimed movie that skyrocketed The Batman franchise back into popularity among youth and adults alike. The movie has already been rated as possibly one of the greatest movies of all time; IMDb lists it as number six on their top 250 movies. While many casual movie watchers may think the movie is such a success due to the mysterious mental stability of Christian Bale's Bruce Wayne, more analytical and serious critics recognize that the true reason for The Dark Knight's success was the acting of Heath Ledger as the character known as "The Joker".

Throughout the movie, it is clear that Christopher Nolan was attempting to give the movie a dark composition through both the setting and the character's actions. The fact that all of the fights and action occur at night or in the dark, in addition to the way that Batman speaks when he is in uniform give a subconscious peril to the movie. This allowed Nolan to give The Joker the opportunity to be as sinister and insidious as necessary. Instead of having a serious and always watchful tone, this setting allowed Ledger to give a cynical tone to The Joker. This allowed for a much more intimidating villain. While strong, powerful villains with fortitude are common and depending on the character can instill fear in an audience, a deranged and somewhat psycho enemy is much more frightening. This is because they are willing to do things that other villains would not attempt, such as when The Joker sewed a cellphone into his pawn's stomach. Like the mob boss Salvatore Maroni said to Batman, "You got rules. The Joker, he's got no rules." (The Dark Knight). This shows that even though Batman is powerful, he is limited to what he can do as a vigilante, because he cannot push the limits that The Joker can. This allows for The Joker to gain an advantage on Batman in regards to attempting to destroy Gotham. However, this is not the only reason that The Joker is able to best the Batman multiple times.

The Joker as a villain dominates every opposition he faces not due to his sadistic motives, but rather his psychological supremacy to all others. As a human, The Joker can safely be labeled as borderline psychotic. He clearly has mental instability issues; however this does not draw away from his character. Instead, it allows him to think past opposition and create devious plans that are nearly fool-proof. Included in his mental capabilities are his powers to manipulate people. Almost like a jedi-mind trick, he makes people listen and adhere to exactly what he is saying, not necessarily because it is true, but the way he approaches his point. This is evident multiple times inside the movie. One event that clearly depicts this is The Joker's inaugural scene, where he attempts to convince the mobsters that the only way to secure their money is by killing the Batman. Although they think this idea is ludicrous at first, they see that The Joker operates on a different rule set than they do, in addition to him eliminating any other option to follow by murdering some of their pawns. In addition to this, he also convinces Harvey Dent to turn on then Commissioner Gordon. Harvey Dent was a good-willed man, and had very little bitterness and anger inside of him until the death of Rachel Dawes at the mistake of Batman and Gordon. Realizing this, The Joker manipulates him and drives thoughts into his head that he normally would not have considered. The Joker tells Dent as he is laying in bed, "Introduce a little anarchy. Upset the established order, and everything becomes chaos. I'm an agent of chaos. Oh, and you know the thing about chaos? It's fair!" (The Dark Knight). After this, he gives Dent a gun and turns him mentally inside out, turning him into Two-Face. This effect that The Joker has on people even works on Batman at times, such as when he interrogates him and loses his cool about Dawes. This is all credited not only to Nolan, but the acting capabilities of Ledger.

Unfortunately Heath Ledger died due to a drug overdose shortly after filming, but nonetheless he was brilliant in depicting a psychopath. Examiner.com reviews says that Ledger "was somehow able to embody The Joker in a way that is frightening, maniacal, and even hysterical all at the same time. You will wind up holding your breath and trying not to make a sound every time he comes on screen because you don't want to miss a second of his mesmerizing performance." () Ledger was quoted saying that "I sat around in a hotel room in London for about a month, locked myself away, formed a little diary and experimented with voices."(). This shows that his character was only able to be developed through a nearly psychotic experience that he forced himself through. Even though he may have developed detrimental habits while locked up, he truly established a character that made the dark side of the Batman franchise exponentially prevalent. This character has helped establish this movie as a true success.

10.title: Enthralling and ambitious on both a narrative and directorial scope, The Dark Knight is a stunning spectacle that transcends the comic book genre
10.content:
The Dark Knight marks not just a stunning follow-up to the successful Batman Begins, it is a landmark achievement on the comic book genre as a whole. Visionary filmmaker Christopher Nolan returns to the director's chair with an astounding continuation of the Batman Saga, a story that raises the stakes on the titular cape crusader in more ways than one. In an age when Hollywood has occasionally struggled to adapting superheroes on screen to their faithful roots, the iconic bat hero has never seen an outing for faithful than this one. Raising themes on moral complexity and psychological corruption, this groundbreaking sequel pits Batman in a battle against a threat that is not only more powerful, but much more personal than we have seen in the cinematic realm. And that threat is the iconic clown Joker who is blessed a shocking portrayal by Heath Ledger who was unfortunately unable to see the final results after his death of a drug overdose in January 2008. Set after the events of the first film, this movie follows Bruce Wayne (played by Christian Bale) is set to settle down after eliminating the threat of Gotham that was Scarecrow. Jim Gordon (played by Gary Oldman) is back as a police lieutenant and Harvey Dent (played by Aaron Eckhart) is running as Gotham's district attorney, trying to formulate a plan to ride the city of crime. When a sinister clown only known as the Joker (played by Heath Ledger) arises from the mysterious criminal underworld and begins to wreck havoc on Gotham on a grand scale, Bruce must suit up as Batman and cross the line between hero and vigilante to bring down what maybe the Gotham's greatest threat yet. As the chaos grows deeper, Batman find himself questioning his morals every step of the way.

Christopher Nolan holds no bars when placing the iconic hero on the tension plate. This film is much darker and more poignant than what many fans of the popular source material have experienced in the past. Written by Nolan and his younger brother Jonathan Nolan and David S. Goyer, the story here approaches the cape crusader with complex themes including testing one's morality and battling against inner demons that threaten to destroy you in the process of making sacrifices. The new threat among Gotham is The Joker who is granted with a more sinister portrayal than what we have seen previously in the celluloid. The monstrous clown explodes on screen with an expertise of robbing banks, blowing up building including hospitals into smithereens, and launching a mass rebellion that places the law enforcement in grave danger. And sadly more Gotham, that is just the beginning. His terrifying wave of chaos not only puts Batman's loved ones in danger, but places him in under psychological torture that leaves him questioning if he is even a real hero or not. The question lies within the citizens and law enforcement of Gotham as well, particularly Harvey Dent who sermonizes "You either die a hero or you live long enough to see yourself become a villain." The suspense is high, the atmosphere strikes directly at the heart, and the action, particularly the truck chase sequence, makes for some sweet visual candy; thanks in part to Wally Pfister who captures the action diligently. And you can always count on Hans Zimmer to endorse the grim atmosphere with an arresting score. Congratulations to you Zimmer!

Christian Bale blessed us with a beautiful portrayal of Batman/Bruce Wayne in the predecessor, and now he has returned and is good as ever. Replacing Katie Holmes in the well-acted, but shoddily written role of Rachel Dawes is Maggie Gyllenhaal. The actress excels in a role that is suitably expand upon her previous outing, allowing her with more to work with than what Holmes is given. Her character is nicely explored in a subplot involving a love triangle between Bruce Wayne and Harvey Dent that plays out well rather than hammy. Aaron Eckhart eclipses the role of Harvey Dent, Gotham's district attorney who sees on a dark soul inside Batman and questions his role as a hero. When Batman is force to make an unsettling sacrifice, Dent's lines between good and evil to grow muddy. The actor proves he is know how to strike at the heart in his performance which transcends during a gut-wrenching climax at the end. Gary Oldman and Michael Caine are good as Jim Gordon and Alfred respectively. Morgan Freeman is well, but nothing much to speak of. Without the the shiniest gem in the crowd is, of course, Heath Ledger igniting the role as The Joker. Injecting abundance of ferocity and grit into the darkened iconic villain, Ledger breaths incredible life into the villainous role, one that allows him to expand upon his acting range at shocking proportions. With the nefarious clown burning with insanity and injecting just a small dose of dark humor, if you find yourself giggling just a little bit, chances are it is an uncomfortable giggle. His spellbinding portrayal of The Joker operates the driving force of the film. It is such a shame that Ledger lost his life before being able to see the astonishing gold we left on in his performance.

The Dark Knight is an enthralling, complex, and brutally ambitious rendition of the iconic DC hero that not only boasts the talent of both Christopher Nolan and the cast, but marks an exhilarating game changer on the comic book genre. It transcends the genre in an awarding fashion that results in what could easily be the greatest superhero flick ever to hit theaters. It is not just an exciting experience, it is a powerful one that feels quite personal.

10.title: When chaos is on the boil in Gotham City by an anarchist who bends every rule, a Dark Knight battles with his might and his mind in a bid for redemption.
10.content:
This is my first & probably the last movie review in IMDb. This movie is so good I just had to write my thoughts on it. I would give it 12/10 if it were possible. Christopher Nolan took the momentum from Batman Begins and smashed the ball out of the park in The Dark Knight.

With all the Batman movies that were made in the past, this one left the audience speechless. It took me more than a couple of days to understand that a comic book based superhero movie can be this good. The casting - perfection, Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Aaron Eckhart & Gary Oldman shine in their positive roles. Heath Ledger came right out of left field and delivered a stellar interpretation of a true anarchist with a dark past. His expressions clearly show that the Joker was an obsessive-compulsive introvert with nothing to lose, that made him one of the Batman's most confusing enemies. He puts to the test the flaws of federal department(law & order), and shatters the faith of even the bravest souls of Gotham. While he believes in chaos, his planning of crimes is timed to perfection.

Harvey Dent is a very relatable character in the context of reality. Each of the Gotham's protectors are tested to their limits when the world around them crumbles and each show their flaws while still trying to summon the good in them. The movie also shows that while "money" can buy anything, it cannot buy humanity & to summon humanity in the face of greed/distress is a superhuman trait. Love plays a bigger role in the movie than people think, its just subtle. Ultimately love made and broke the central characters of the movie.

There are no flaws in this movie, from the start to the end. Nolan might just have to live with that fact that while he didn't want to make any more Batman movies, TDK will for a long time remain his masterpiece. The sound, cinematography and action sequences are anything but clichéd. Batman finally is shown to have developed a close contact brawling technique that is far more practical and dangerous than a showy dance-like fight. Lucius Freeman er Fox also gives Batman a new piece of technology that truly makes him just like a..submarine? *wink*

The dialogues are absolutely brilliant with the ending seeming like a poem which resonated in everybody's minds for days. The story itself is entirely based in modern context, it shows the general distrust that people have against the keepers of law, yet the goodness of humanity shines through when others least expect it. The Joker & Batman might have battled physically, but both knew that the real battle going on was of their respective faith on a system.

Christopher Nolan & David Goyer, Thank You.

10.title: MASTER OF MASTERPIECES
10.content:
"The Dark Knight" is a cinematic masterpiece that transcends the boundaries of the superhero genre. Christopher Nolan's visionary direction and the phenomenal performances of the cast make it an unforgettable experience that lingers long after the credits roll.

Led by the late Heath Ledger's breathtaking portrayal of the Joker, "The Dark Knight" delves into the darkest corners of Gotham City, exploring the thin line that separates chaos from order, and the price heroes and citizens alike must pay in the face of true evil. Ledger's performance is a tour de force, delivering a chilling, captivating, and utterly mesmerizing depiction of the iconic villain. His ability to simultaneously exude charisma and menace is unmatched, making the Joker one of the most memorable and iconic characters in cinematic history.

Christian Bale returns as Batman, the tormented hero fighting his own internal demons while tirelessly defending the innocent. Bale's portrayal is captivating, showcasing the complexity of Bruce Wayne and his unwavering determination to protect Gotham City, even at the cost of his own personal happiness. The film explores the psychological toll that being a hero takes on Batman, further deepening the exploration of the character.

The supporting cast delivers exceptional performances, with Aaron Eckhart's portrayal of Harvey Dent, the idealistic district attorney, adding another layer of depth to the narrative. Michael Caine brings warmth and wisdom as Alfred, Bruce Wayne's loyal confidant, and Morgan Freeman shines as Lucius Fox, providing the technological marvels that aid Batman in his fight against crime.

Nolan's direction is nothing short of genius, weaving a complex and intricately layered story that challenges our perception of heroism and morality. The film's gritty atmosphere, coupled with its stunning cinematography and meticulously crafted action sequences, immerses the audience in Gotham's dark underbelly.

Hans Zimmer's score serves as the heartbeat of the film, intensifying the tension and complementing the on-screen drama. The script, penned by Nolan and his brother Jonathan, is intelligent and thought-provoking, filled with compelling dialogue that explores themes of chaos, sacrifice, and the inherent nature of humanity.

"The Dark Knight" is not only a superhero film but a gripping crime saga that explores the fragility of society and the complexities of human nature. It challenges the audience to question the boundaries of heroism, the sacrifices required to maintain order, and the enduring power of hope.

In conclusion, "The Dark Knight" stands as a testament to the power of storytelling in cinema. With its exceptional performances, intricate narrative, and thematic depth, it remains a landmark achievement that has forever left its mark on the genre. A true masterpiece that deserves all the acclaim it has received and more, "The Dark Knight" is a must-watch for film lovers and superhero enthusiasts alike.

10.title: You will become a Die Hard Fan of Joker
10.content:
AWESOME movie that i have ever seen.

"Batman" isn't a comic book anymore. Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" is a haunted film that leaps beyond its origins and becomes an engrossing tragedy. It creates characters we come to care about. That's because of the performances, because of the direction, because of the writing, and because of the superlative technical quality of the entire production. This film, and to a lesser degree "Iron Man," redefine the possibilities of the "comic-book movie."

"The Dark Knight" is not a simplistic tale of good and evil. Batman is good, yes, The Joker is evil, yes. But Batman poses a more complex puzzle than usual: The citizens of Gotham City are in an uproar, calling him a vigilante and blaming him for the deaths of policemen and others. And the Joker is more than a villain. He's a Mephistopheles whose actions are fiendishly designed to pose moral dilemmas for his enemies.

The key performance in the movie is by the late Heath Ledger, as the Joker. Will he become the first posthumous Oscar winner since Peter Finch? His Joker draws power from the actual inspiration of the character in the silent classic "The Man Who Laughs" (1928). His clown's makeup more sloppy than before, his cackle betraying deep wounds, he seeks revenge, he claims, for the horrible punishment his father exacted on him when he was a child. In one diabolical scheme near the end of the film, he invites two ferry-loads of passengers to blow up the other before they are blown up themselves. Throughout the film, he devises ingenious situations that force Batman (Christian Bale), Commissioner Gordon (Gary Oldman) and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) to make impossible ethical decisions. By the end, the whole moral foundation of the Batman legend is threatened.

Because these actors and others are so powerful, and because the movie does not allow its spectacular special effects to upstage the humans, we're surprised how deeply the drama affects us. Eckhart does an especially good job as Harvey Dent, whose character is transformed by a horrible fate into a bitter monster. It is customary in a comic book movie to maintain a certain knowing distance from the action, to view everything through a sophisticated screen. "The Dark Knight" slips around those defenses and engages us.

Yes, the special effects are extraordinary. They focus on the expected explosions and catastrophes, and have some superb, elaborate chase scenes. The movie was shot on location in Chicago, but it avoids such familiar landmarks as Marina City, the Wrigley Building or the skyline. Chicagoans will recognize many places, notably La Salle Street and Lower Wacker Drive, but director Nolan is not making a travelogue. He presents the city as a wilderness of skyscrapers, and a key sequence is set in the still-uncompleted Trump Tower. Through these heights, the Batman moves at the end of strong wires, or sometimes actually flies, using his cape as a parasail.

The plot involves nothing more or less than the Joker's attempts to humiliate the forces for good and expose Batman' secret identity, showing him to be a poser and a fraud. He includes Gordon and Dent on his target list, and contrives cruel tricks to play with the fact that Bruce Wayne once loved, and Harvey Dent now loves, Assistant D.A. Rachel Dawes (Maggie Gyllenhaal). The tricks are more cruel than he realizes, because the Joker doesn't know Batman's identity. Heath Ledger has a good deal of dialogue in the movie, and a lot of it isn't the usual jabs and jests we're familiar with: It's psychologically more complex, outlining the dilemmas he has constructed, and explaining his reasons for them. The screenplay by Christopher Nolan and his brother Jonathan (who first worked together on "Memento") has more depth and poetry than we might have expected.

Two of the supporting characters are crucial to the action, and are played effortlessly by the great actors Morgan Freeman and Michael Caine. Freeman, as the scientific genius Lucius Fox, is in charge of Bruce Wayne's underground headquarters, and makes an ethical objection to a method of eavesdropping on all of the citizens of Gotham City. His stand has current political implications. Caine is the faithful butler Alfred, who understands Wayne better than anybody, and makes a decision about a crucial letter.

Nolan also directed the previous, and excellent, "Batman Begins" (2005), which went into greater detail than ever before about Bruce Wayne's origins and the reasons for his compulsions. Now it is the Joker's turn, although his past is handled entirely with dialogue, not flashbacks. There are no references to Batman's childhood, but we certainly remember it, and we realize that this conflict is between two adults who were twisted by childhood cruelty — one compensating by trying to do good, the other by trying to do evil. Perhaps they instinctively understand that themselves.

Something fundamental seems to be happening in the upper realms of the comic-book movie. "Spider-Man II" (2004) may have defined the high point of the traditional film based on comic-book heroes. A movie like the new "Hellboy II" allows its director free rein for his fantastical visions. But now "Iron Man" and even more so "The Dark Knight" move the genre into deeper waters. They realize, as some comic-book readers instinctively do, that these stories touch on deep fears, traumas, fantasies and hopes. And the Batman legend, with its origins in film noir, is the most fruitful one for exploration.

In his two Batman movies, Nolan has freed the character to be a canvas for a broader scope of human emotion. For Bruce Wayne is a deeply troubled man, let there be no doubt, and if ever in exile from his heroic role, it would not surprise me what he finds himself capable of doing.

Christopher Nolan's Batman trilogy is a masterful reimagining of the iconic superhero that captures the darker, grittier aspects of the character while still remaining true to its comic book roots. With stunning cinematography, exceptional performances, and a well-crafted storyline, Nolan's Batman films stand out as some of the best in the superhero genre.

From the first film, "Batman Begins," Nolan sets the tone for the rest of the trilogy with its dark and brooding atmosphere. Christian Bale's portrayal of Bruce Wayne/Batman is nuanced and complex, with the actor capturing both the character's brooding intensity and his more vulnerable moments with ease. The supporting cast, including Michael Caine as Alfred, Gary Oldman as Jim Gordon, and Morgan Freeman as Lucius Fox, are all exceptional in their roles and bring a level of realism to the films that is often missing from other superhero movies.

The second film in the trilogy, "The Dark Knight," is widely regarded as one of the best superhero movies ever made. Led by a mesmerizing performance by Heath Ledger as the Joker, the film is a tense and thrilling exploration of morality and chaos. The film's stunning action sequences, coupled with its themes of justice, revenge, and the nature of evil, make it a truly unforgettable experience.

The final film in the trilogy, "The Dark Knight Rises," brings the story full circle with a satisfying conclusion that ties up all loose ends. While it may not reach the heights of its predecessor, the film still manages to deliver some memorable moments and a sense of closure to the story that Nolan has been telling over the course of the trilogy.

Overall, Christopher Nolan's Batman films are a shining example of what can be achieved when a talented director, a great cast, and a well-crafted story come together. The trilogy is a must-see for any fan of the Batman character or the superhero genre in general.

10.title: Good

Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" is a cinematic masterpiece that redefines the superhero genre. This thought-provoking film explores the chaotic showdown between Batman (Christian Bale) and the Joker (Heath Ledger), who wreaks havoc on Gotham City.

Key Strengths 1. *Intricate storytelling*: Nolan's narrative is layered, complex, and engaging.

2. *Exceptional direction*: Nolan masterfully explores themes of chaos, anarchy, and heroism.

3. *Outstanding performances*: Ledger's posthumous Oscar win for his iconic Joker portrayal is well-deserved.

4. *Haunting score*: Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard's music enhances the film's atmospheric tension.

5. *Realistic visuals*: The action sequences and stunts are impressively choreographed.

Minor Drawbacks 1. *Lengthy runtime*: The 162-minute duration may test viewers' patience.

2. *Complex conclusion*: The ending requires close attention and interpretation.

Thematic Analysis 1. *Chaos vs. Order*: The Joker's anarchic ideology clashes with Batman's quest for justice.

2. *Heroism*: Batman's sacrifice and determination inspire hope.

3. *Morality*: The film raises questions about moral ambiguity and the nature of evil.

4. *Psychological warfare*: The Joker's cunning tactics push Batman to his limits.

Conclusion "The Dark Knight" is a gripping, thought-provoking cinematic experience. With outstanding performances, direction, and cinematography, this film is essential viewing for fans of superhero dramas and complex storytelling.

Overall, The Dark Knight is a masterpiece that transcends the superhero genre. A film that explores complex issues and human psychology, delivering compelling action and unforgettable performances. This is a testament to the power of cinema and storytelling, and a milestone in the world of cinema.

10.title: Words cannot describe how great this film is!

Ok, before I go into my review I want to say one lil thing. The Dark Knight is the greatest movie ever made!!! Ok, now that that's out of the way, let's get into the review. Now I'm sure most of you have seen this film, and if you haven't, go watch it and your life will finally feel complete! This film for me. Is the gold standard that I think every movie, whether it be a comic book film, a drama, or just any movie, should try to follow and live up to, because this film is freakin perfect! I mean just the opening bank robbery scene is better then Batman Begins, and really shows the audience that the Joker is a smart, calculating, and is indeed, a man with a plan. Now the best part about this film is Heath Ledgers amazing performance which has a screen presence that takes over the movie and captivates the audience. Another thing that makes his character so good, and really shows that he is a formidable foe to Batman, is that he does not kill and steal for the money. But simply because he wants to watch the world burn. The rest of the cast is amazing as well. Christian Bale is great as Bruce Wayne, and really shows the conflict he is having to face within himself. Aaron Eckhart is fantastic as Harvey Dent, and brings character and emotion to the role. Michael Caine and Morgan Freeman are great as supporting characters. Gary Oldman plays Gordon so well it's hard to see anyone else in the role. Maggie Gyllenhaal also gives a great performance as she struggles to choose if she wants to spend her life with Bruce or Harvey. The whole cast is amazing in the roles they play. And each one has their own struggles and parts in the story. Some people ask what it is that makes The Dark Knight the greatest movie of all time. And the answer is. everything! The cast, the story, the performances, even the music, brilliantly composed by the legendary Hans Zimmer. But at the core of all that is the fact that good doesn't always win. And in order to triumph over evil, a hero must sometimes be willing to sacrifice, and be something more. So those are my thoughts on the film. This movie is flawless in my opinion! And is personally one of my favorite movies of all time.

Also R.I.P. Heath Ledger. Your legacy and performance will live on and be remembered forever...

Reviewed by Douglas Mitchell.

The Dark Knight is a gripping, thought-provoking, and visually stunning superhero thriller that sets a new standard for comic book movies. Christopher Nolan's masterful direction weaves a complex narrative that explores the darker aspects of heroism, chaos, and the human condition.

The supporting cast, including Aaron Eckhart's Harvey Dent/Two-Face and Michael Caine's Alfred Pennyworth, deliver solid performances that add to the film's emotional resonance.

Nolan's direction is a work of art, blending action, suspense, and drama into a cohesive whole. The film's themes of morality, sacrifice, and the blurred lines between good and evil are timely and thought-provoking.

The Dark Knight's technical achievements are equally impressive, with Wally Pfister's cinematography, Hans Zimmer's pulsating score, and the innovative action sequences all contributing to a cinematic experience that's both thrilling and unsettling.

Overall, The Dark Knight is a landmark superhero film that transcends the genre, offering a rich, complex, and hauntingly memorable cinematic experience.

10.title: Chaos in a Purple Suit
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight isn't just another superhero flick-it's a true cinematic gem that explores the delicate balance between order and chaos. Christian Bale's intense portrayal of Bruce Wayne brings depth to Batman, but it's Heath Ledger's unforgettable performance as the Joker that truly steals the show, reshaping what it means to be a villain for an entire generation.

Ledger's Joker is a whirlwind of unpredictability, fear, and an odd charm. He doesn't fit the mold of a typical villain; he's not motivated by wealth or revenge-he simply wants to see the world burn. Every moment he's on screen is charged with tension, his dark humor tinged with a sense of danger. From the spine-chilling pencil trick to his philosophical sparring with Batman, the Joker transcends the role of a mere antagonist-he embodies the chaotic pulse of the film.

With Nolan's masterful direction, Hans Zimmer's haunting score, and the film's intricate moral dilemmas, The Dark Knight rises above typical action movies. Yet, it's the Joker who leaves an indelible mark. His presence compels both characters and viewers to grapple with the essence of justice, sanity, and the price of doing what's right.

Ultimately, The Dark Knight goes beyond the classic battle of heroes and villains. It delves into the darkness that resides within us all-and the eerie laughter that echoes from the brink of madness.

10.title: The Dark Knight" remains a monumental achievement in cinema
10.content:
"The Dark Knight" is a groundbreaking superhero film that transcends the boundaries of the genre and stands as a true cinematic masterpiece. Directed by Christopher Nolan and released in 2008, the movie takes audiences on a dark and thrilling journey through the corrupt and chaotic streets of Gotham City.

Led by an exceptional cast, with Christian Bale reprising his role as Batman/Bruce Wayne, and the late Heath Ledger delivering an unforgettable performance as the Joker, "The Dark Knight" immerses viewers in a gritty and realistic portrayal of the Batman universe. The film explores complex themes such as morality, chaos versus order, and the blurred line between hero and villain.

What sets "The Dark Knight" apart is its ability to balance intense action sequences with a profound exploration of character psychology. Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of mesmerizing, capturing the essence of the character's chaos and unpredictability. Ledger's performance earned him a posthumous Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor and solidified the Joker as one of the most iconic and haunting villains in cinematic history.

Christopher Nolan's direction is masterful, creating a dark and atmospheric Gotham City that serves as a character in itself. The film's cinematography, practical effects, and immersive sound design contribute to its gritty realism, heightening the tension and drama.

"The Dark Knight" also benefits from a strong supporting cast, including Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent/Two-Face, Gary Oldman as Commissioner Gordon, and Michael Caine as Alfred Pennyworth. Each actor brings depth and nuance to their respective roles, adding layers of complexity to the narrative.

Beyond its technical and artistic achievements, "The Dark Knight" delves into profound moral dilemmas, challenging the notions of justice and the sacrifices that come with being a hero. It prompts viewers to question their own beliefs and ponder the nature of good and evil in a world plagued by corruption and despair.

10.title: DC can suprise you
10.content:
Absolutely, The Dark Knight is often regarded as a masterpiece, not just in the superhero genre but in cinema as a whole. Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker was hauntingly brilliant and truly immortalised the character. His performance was so layered and intense that it set a new standard for villains in film, earning him a well-deserved posthumous Academy Award. The chilling unpredictability he brought to the Joker was mesmerising, blending chaos, dark humour, and a terrifying sense of danger in every scene he appeared in.

Christian Bale as Batman was equally phenomenal, bringing a perfect blend of grit, complexity, and humanity to the role. His duality as Bruce Wayne and the Dark Knight was executed flawlessly, capturing the internal struggles of a man trying to save his city while battling his personal demons. His chemistry with Ledger was electric, elevating their cat-and-mouse dynamic to legendary status.

Christopher Nolan's vision was revolutionary for the genre. He grounded Gotham City in realism, making it feel like a living, breathing entity. The use of practical effects instead of heavy CGI, especially for action sequences like the truck flip during the Joker's chase scene, added an authentic edge rarely seen in modern blockbusters. Nolan's approach to storytelling was intricate yet captivating, weaving themes of chaos, morality, and heroism into a complex narrative that kept audiences on the edge of their seats.

The supporting cast, including Gary Oldman, Morgan Freeman, and Michael Caine, added depth and gravitas to the film. Hans Zimmer's score amplified the tension and emotion, with the Joker's theme-a rising, nerve-wracking string motif-perfectly capturing his unrelenting menace. Wally Pfister's cinematography, particularly in the IMAX sequences, gave the film a grand, immersive scale that remains awe-inspiring to this day.

The Dark Knight isn't just a superhero film; it's a psychological drama, a crime thriller, and a philosophical exploration of chaos versus order. It transcends its genre, appealing to both comic book fans and general audiences. It's no wonder fans consider it the gold standard of DC films. Truly, it's a cinematic achievement that's difficult to top, redefining what superhero movies could be.

Would you consider it your favourite film, or do you have another close contender in the superhero genre?

10.title: One of the best adaptations of Batman in the television and film medium
10.content: Growing up, I admit I did not read any Batman comics. To this day, the only Batman literary material I have read is Frank Miller's brilliant graphic novel, The Dark Knight Returns. Therefore, I should feel that I do not have a valid opinion on the cinematic portrayal of Batman, right? Not exactly. No, I am not literate in Batman's original medium of comic books, but the inception of my best view of Batman came from the Tim Burton 1989 Batman film and the Animated Series. I did not need to read his comics because that film and that show read them for me and adapted Batman into the film and television art-form perfectly, especially the Animated Series. From the film and the show, I knew who Batman was, I knew what he stood for, therefore allowing me to understand the decisions he would make to seek justice; allowing me to think "Batman would do that." For me, every Batman portrayal from then on were held by the standards set by 1989 Batman and the Animated Series Batman. Those standards were not met by the many Batman's in TV and film of years to come. Not even in Batman Begins. Some of the elements of what I knew and loved of Batman were in Begins, but it was still its own portrayal of Batman, albeit a decent one though. It was not until 2008 when one Batman film was able to transcend those standards I made. The Dark Knight showed me and the world a Batman I had never seen before but one I already knew. His devotion to stopping the perfect personification of chaos known as The Joker was familiar to me and I reveled in it. At the end of this film, Batman does capture the bad guy as I've always seen him do, but this time it was very different. Batman was going to teach my 14 year old self a very important lesson in what a hero truly is, a lesson I was consistently learning in my life at the time. Batman does capture The Joker, but The Joker can still win because of his manipulation of Gotham's former white knight, Harvey Dent, who has now completely transformed into the deadly Two-Face. Batman becomes what Gotham needed him to be and makes the decision to take the blame of all of Two-Face's horrid actions to keep prosperity in Gotham alive. I had always seen Batman as the good guy who just broke the rules evil always used to defend itself. After seeing this film, it allowed me to see Batman in a new light, that he would do anything to save his city, to keep justice alive. From how I knew Batman already, it allowed me to understand and accept his decision and think "Batman would do this." Alfred explained it best when he says "He's not being a hero, he's being something more." The portrayal of Batman in this film showed me what it truly meant for Batman to be a Dark Knight.

10.title: Batman has no limit. But you do, sir.
10.content:
I'm really looking forward to the last film of the "The Dark Knight" trilogy, "The Dark Knight Rises", which will be released in this summer. So I reviewed "Batman Begins" and "The Dark Knight". I was quite impressed by them.

The story of "Batman Begins" is about the reason why Bruce Wayne became Batman, and the story of "The Dark Knight" is about overcoming adversity. But at the same time he lost a lot of things and became "the dark knight".

Alfred, a faithful butler of Bruce Wayne, talked to Bruce, when Bruce returned from his work as a Batman with his injury.

Alfred: Now, your limit, master Wayne. Bruce: Batman has no limit. Alfred: But you do,sir.

At this time, Bruce hadn't realized the fact that even Batman had his limit.

Harvey Dent, a prosecutor believing in justice, and Bruce were fighting against the evil in Gotham City together. Harvey talked to the citizen of Gotham City about hope.

Harvey: The night is darkest just before dawn. I promise you, "Dawn is coming."

They were "heroes", so they were bound by their morality. For example, Batman could never kill anyone.

But their enemy, Joker, was completely free from any rules. He could do anything and drove them into the corner.

Joker: I'm an agent of chaos. Oh, do you know about chaos? It's fear.

Bruce realized his inability and talked to Alfred.

Bruce: What do I have to do? Alfred: Endure, master Wayne.

And then, Batman tried to wiretap all people in Gotham City in order to find where Joker was.

Batman: Beautiful, isn't it? Fox: Beautiful, unethical, dangerous. This is wrong.

In the end, Harvey dropped into his dark side like Darth Vader.

Joker: I took Gotham's white knight and I brought him to our level. It wasn't hard. Madness, as you know, is like gravity. All I take is a little push. Harvey: The world is cruel.

The only morality in the cruel world is chance. Batman dared to suffer the disgrace saving Harvey's honor as Gotham's white knight.

At the end of "The Dark Knight", Batman, as a dark knight, was chased by police.

Gordon: He's a silent guardian, a watchful protector, a dark knight. I'd like to talk a little about myself.

When I was 20's and 30's, I believed that I had no limit. If I had been serious, I could do anything, I thought. But in fact, I was never so serious and I couldn't accomplish anything.

After I have suffered from depression, I realized that I had my own limit. I asked myself what I had to do and just endured my worthlessness. So I can understand how Harvey and Bruce felt.

I myself can come back to our society. I'm looking forward to seeing how Batman, as a dark knight, will get himself back in "The Dark Knight Rises".

10.title: Why so seriously amazing?
10.content:
Serving as my favorite movie of all time, The Dark Knight is the superhero movie we all need. It's dark, it's gritty, it's action-packed, it's well written, it does EVERYTHING a great superhero movie should do. In fact, it's so good, it makes DC look good, even though they still suck. But back onto the movie itself.

What's the story? With the help of allies Lt. Jim Gordon and DA Harvey Dent, Batman has been able to keep a tight lid on crime in Gotham City. But when a vile young criminal calling himself the Joker suddenly throws the town into chaos, the caped Crusader begins to tread a fine line between heroism and vigilantism.

First, let's talk about the greatest aspect of the film: the Joker. Oh my GOD, the Joker in this film is absolutely incredible. Not only does he deliver some of the BEST lines in the movie (such as, "You know how I got these scars?"), but he's a legitimate threat to Batman and he's possibly the best interpretation of the character. I also like how he's far more psychological in this film than the Jack Nicholson Joker. That being said, he TOTALLY blows the Jack Nicholson Joker to the water. Another great thing about this movie is that it has some of the BEST action scenes of any Batman movie, including the car chase scene. And yes, I'm only saying that because there's explosions in it and I love explosions. Yeah, there's a lot of explosions in this movie, and there's even a scene where a couple of little kids are going "pew pew!" and then a building explodes. THAT is just hilarious. My only complaint with this movie is Christian Bale. Don't get me wrong, he's a GREAT Bruce Wayne, but he speaks in some really weird voice when he's Batman. I mean, some could argue that he had throat cancer during filming of this movie, but that actually doesn't apply since he spoke in a perfectly normal voice when he was Bruce Wayne. Not a HUGE complaint, not even enough to lower my star rating for this film, but just a tiny little detail that I wanted to go over. Other than that, the movie is fantastic.

In conclusion, The Dark Knight is not just Christopher Nolan and Batman movies at their best, but it's superhero movies at its best: awesome action, great effects, compelling characters, a serious tone, and a fantastic Joker. If you're a Batman fan or even a movie fan in general, you'll fall in love with The Dark Knight. And the best quote in the entire Batman franchise is from this very movie, spoken by Batman himself: "You either die a hero, or live long enough to see yourself become the villain."

10.title: The best Batman movie that was ever made. Nolan at his best.
10.content:
"Batman" isn't a comic book anymore. Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" is a haunted film that leaps beyond its origins and becomes an engrossing tragedy. It creates characters we come to care about. That's because of the performances, because of the direction, because of the writing, and because of the superlative technical quality of the entire production. This film, and to a lesser degree "Iron Man," redefine the possibilities of the "comic-book movie."

"The Dark Knight" is not a simplistic tale of good and evil. Batman is good, yes, The Joker is evil, yes. But Batman poses a more complex puzzle than usual: The citizens of Gotham City are in an uproar, calling him a vigilante and blaming him for the deaths of policemen and others. And the Joker is more than a villain. He's a Mephistopheles whose actions are fiendishly designed to pose moral dilemmas for his enemies.

The key performance in the movie is by the late Heath Ledger, as the Joker. Will he become the first posthumous Oscar winner since Peter Finch? His Joker draws power from the actual inspiration of the character in the silent classic "The Man Who Laughs" (1928). His clown's makeup more sloppy than before, his cackle betraying deep wounds, he seeks revenge, he claims, for the horrible punishment his father exacted on him when he was a child. In one diabolical scheme near the end of the film, he invites two ferry-loads of passengers to blow up the other before they are blown up themselves. Throughout the film, he devises ingenious situations that force Batman (Christian Bale), Commissioner Gordon (Gary Oldman) and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) to make impossible ethical decisions. By the end, the whole moral foundation of the Batman legend is threatened.

10.title: The ultimate Batman story
10.content:
Though this film deserves a very long review, as I have so much to say about it, what more needs to be said than has already been mentioned by the nation's critics, who have contributed to The Dark Knight's whopping 94% rating on Rotten Tomatoes? Some are saying it's better than Batman Begins, director Chris Nolan's first film in this new Batman series. I disagree, but only because I think that film is a lot better than some critics remember it. I do think, however, that The Dark Knight is just as masterful, and since I consider both to be nearly flawless enough to give them each five stars, it's high enough praise to say this new film is the rare sequel that lives up to the original.

Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker? Everything you've heard, all of the praise and hype? All true. His is a riveting, terrifying, and darkly hilarious portrayal of the ultimate villain, and it's a completely original take on the character. Everyone will be talking about his performance, as well they should be, but I hope they won't lose sight of how terrific the acting is across the board. Christian Bale continues to impress as the best Batman/Bruce Wayne ever. Since he was so well established last time, he's given slightly less screen time here, but he's equally compelling as a man pushed to his limits.

Michael Cain and Morgan Freeman have less to do, but every second they're on screen, they're terrific. Gary Oldman continues to show that he's just as compelling playing good guys as bad ones; his Commissioner Gordon is a pillar of virtue. Maggie Gyllenhall (Stranger Than Fiction) steps in for Katie Holmes as Rachel Dawes. While I'm one of the apparently few people who didn't mind Mrs. Cruise in the first film, Gyllenhall adds a bit more life to the character. Finally Aaron Eckhart gives a subtle and layered performance as Gotham D.A. Harvey Dent. If Ledger wasn't stealing the show, it'd be Eckhart's acting everyone would be talking about.

The action: terrific (a mid-movie chase scene stands out in my mind). The screenplay: just like Begins, it's full of fantastic moral investigations, fleshed-out characters, and plenty of surprises which I wouldn't dare reveal here. Like the first film, this is dark and scary, but with a lining of humanity and just a touch of humor. The direction is even better this time (thank you, Mr. Nolan, for allowing us to actually see the fights). Don't believe those reviews which say they don't know how this slipped by with a PG-13 rating; it is intense, and the Joker is brutal and horrific, but just like a great Hitchcock movie, the actual gruesome stuff occurs in your imagination, not on-screen. There's not any blood that I can remember, though there are some freaky images vis- a-vis the villains' physical appearance and the sight of some corpses.

That being said, this is not a movie to take kids to. Just because you don't see a lot of gore, doesn't mean it isn't terrifying. If you're afraid of clowns, buckle up. Pushed to his limits, Batman gets mean. I mean Jack Bauer mean! At any rate, this is a terrific film; a crime/morality drama first, an action thriller second, and a comic book movie third. It isn't flawless, but the minor complaints are so nit-picky that I've no need to mention them here. Sorry Wall- E, but you're gonna have to pass the crown of year's best film over. The Dark Knight is king, and his jester is chilling. ***** (out of five).

10.title: best film ever
10.content:
one of the best movies I have ever seen In my life. Heads up: a thunderbolt is about to rip into the blanket of bland we call summer movies. The Dark Knight, director Christopher Nolan's absolute stunner of a follow-up to 2005's Batman Begins, is a potent provocation decked out as a comic-book movie. Feverish action? Check. Dazzling spectacle? Check. Devilish fun? Check. But Nolan is just warming up. There's something raw and elemental at work in this artfully imagined universe. Striking out from his Batman origin story, Nolan cuts through to a deeper dimension. Huh? Wha? How can a conflicted guy in a bat suit and a villain with a cracked, painted- on clown smile speak to the essentials of the human condition? Just hang on for a shock to the system. The Dark Knight creates a place where good and evil — expected to do battle — decide instead to get it on and dance. 10.title: Exceeds Expectations

When you go to a movie surrounded by hype, it's easy to be let down. I'm not a die hard comic book movie fan by any stretch so I wasn't prepared for the spectacle that is by far one of the top 3 films of the 2000s, if not #1.

How this film wasn't nominated for Academy Awards is beyond me, but it likely had something to do with the comic book genre.

Well, this film transcends all comic book film expectations and is one of the best crime thrillers I ever saw. The entertainment value is so good it's shocking. It has everything you can ask for in a summer blockbuster, and boy does it deliver.

Heath Ledger gives the performance of a lifetime as his psychotic Joker, which is deeper and unlike any Joker we've seen to date. Gary Oldman is absolutely shining in his reprising role, and Christian Bale is perfect as his sympathized Bruce Wayne.

With unexpected plot twists, incredible character introductions, and philosophical undertones, this dark, disturbing psychological study of psychosis and narcissism, combined with its' high level drama, suspense and riveting performances will leave you thoroughly satisfied.

From the thrilling opening sequence, the pacing never let's up, and it feels like there isn't a single frame of wasted film. The only minor nitpick is that since it's not a fun & cheerful movie, and incredibly dense, it loses some rewatchability.

From the tiny details of burning the accoutnat alive or the pencil murder, Heath Ledger's performance really sells this. He really did deserve that posthumous Oscar, creating an engaging and unnerving Joker. His death especially tragic here since he was clearly a franchise villian; better than any I've seen (Homelander is on his level, but that's about it). The entire cast was fantastic, but the practical effects & very sparing use of CGI Nolan insisted on also help keep with the incredible immersion.

I didn't know CBMs could be that good.

A++, 10/10.

O'Donnell.

We see Wayne's all-important training period (previously ignored), and his connection to the Tibetan shadow-ninja clan led by Ra's Al Ghul. Gary Oldman looks just like a young Commissioner Gordon (and doesn't dominate), Morgan Freeman and Rutger Hauer give solid heavyweight support to the boardroom machinations at Wayne Enterprizes. I love Michael Gough(?) but Michael Caine is great as Alfred. It's only Katie Holmes who didn't ring true for me - not because of her performance, but simply because she looks all of 15 years old (sorry Katie). Christopher Nolan's The Dark Knight is a masterclass in storytelling, a film that transcends the superhero genre to become a gripping exploration of chaos, morality, and the human condition. From the very first frame to its haunting conclusion, the film grips you with relentless momentum. The pacing is flawless, balancing heart-pounding action with intimate character moments that linger long after the credits roll. At its core is Heath Ledger's legendary performance as the Joker, a villain so terrifyingly unpredictable and philosophically unhinged that he redefines what it means to be a cinematic antagonist. Ledger's Joker isn't just a criminal-he's an anarchic force of nature, challenging Batman's ideals and Gotham's fragile sense of order with every chilling monologue and meticulously orchestrated act of terror.

But the brilliance of The Dark Knight doesn't stop there. Christian Bale delivers a nuanced portrayal of Bruce Wayne, torn between his duty as a protector and the moral compromises that come with wearing the cowl. The supporting cast shines equally: Gary Oldman's grounded, compassionate Jim Gordon anchors the chaos, while Aaron Eckhart's tragic arc as Harvey Dent-the 'White Knight' whose fall from grace mirrors Gotham's own descent-adds layers of tragedy to the narrative.

Nolan's direction is razor-sharp, weaving complex themes of sacrifice, duality, and societal decay into a tightly plotted thriller. The film's technical achievements-from Wally Pfister's stark, immersive cinematography to Hans Zimmer's pulse-pounding score-elevate every scene into something visceral and unforgettable. The practical effects, including the jaw-dropping truck-flip sequence, ground the spectacle in tangible realism.

The Dark Knight isn't just a comic-book movie; it's a Shakespearean drama dressed in Gotham's shadows, a film that asks whether heroism can survive in a world drawn to madness. Over a decade later, its relevance endures, cementing it as not just a genre classic, but one of the greatest films of the 21st century. A must-watch-and a must-feel-for anyone who craves cinema that challenges as much as it entertains.

10.title: Batman is good
10.content:
"Batman" isn't a comic book anymore. Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" is a haunted film that leaps beyond its origins and becomes an engrossing tragedy. It creates characters we come to care about. That's because of the performances, because of the direction, because of the writing, and because of the superlative technical quality of the entire production. This film, and to a lesser degree "Iron Man," redefine the possibilities of the "comic-book movie."

"The Dark Knight" is not a simplistic tale of good and evil. Batman is good, yes, The Joker is evil, yes. But Batman poses a more complex puzzle than usual: The citizens of Gotham City are in an uproar, calling him a vigilante and blaming him for the deaths of policemen and others. And the Joker is more than a villain. He's a Mephistopheles whose actions are fiendishly designed to pose moral dilemmas for his enemies

10.title: "If you're good at something," the Joker wheezes, "you never do it for free."
10.content:
For a while, it seemed as though life in Gotham City was looking up. Gotham's finest, led by straight-arrow Lt. Gordon, was squeezing the city's crime syndicates. Harvey Dent, a new and fearless district attorney, stalked the courtrooms. Batman prowled the city's darkest alleys. Mob bosses stopped meeting at night, afraid they'd be pinched.

What? A city where crime kingpins are afraid of the dark?

Then-like the flu, like a hailstorm, like a crowbar to the side of the head-comes the Joker. No baggage. No backstory. No greedy motive. Just a leering, cackling demon of chaos. He crashes a high-level mob meeting and offers his services as the city's very own bat exterminator. What does he want? Nothing. Everything. What does he ask for? Half the mob's money.

"If you're good at something," the Joker wheezes, "you never do it for free."

So begins perhaps the deepest, bleakest summer blockbuster ever, an explosion-riddled saga about order and anarchy, about good and evil, and about the line we draw between the two.

"Batman: The Dark Knight" is a cinematic masterpiece that redefines the superhero genre. Directed by Christopher Nolan, this epic conclusion to the Dark Knight trilogy delivers a thrilling and emotionally resonant experience from start to finish.

Christian Bale delivers a riveting performance as Bruce Wayne/Batman, grappling with his inner demons and facing his greatest challenges yet. Bale's portrayal brings depth and complexity to the character, making Batman both relatable and inspiring.

Nolan's direction is masterful, seamlessly weaving together action, drama, and suspense. The film's set pieces are breathtaking, from the heart-stopping aerial sequences to the pulse-pounding showdowns between Batman and his adversaries.

What truly sets "The Dark Knight" apart, however, is its thematic depth. Exploring themes of sacrifice, redemption, and the nature of heroism, the film offers a thought-provoking meditation on the human condition. It challenges the audience to consider what it truly means to be a hero and to confront the darkness within ourselves.

Visually stunning and emotionally powerful, "The Dark Knight" is a fitting conclusion to Nolan's Batman trilogy. It's a film that not only entertains but also resonates on a profound level, leaving a lasting impression long after the credits roll. For fans of the superhero genre and cinephiles alike, "The Dark Knight" is an absolute must-see.

10.title: Dark Knight Review
10.content:
The Dark Knight is a superhero movie with a darker twist making it more interesting and thrilling than the other Batman movies in the past. Christopher Nolan's trilogy set a new premise for the comic book tale. The characters her created were more realistic and less cartoonish. The theme of Dark Knight is good vs. evil. We have several characters such as Aaron Eckharts, Harvey Dent and Maggie Gyllenhaal's, Rachel who are fighting the evil doers of Gotham. While they are fighting through the law to clean up Gotham we have Chriatian Bale's character Bruce Wayne/Batman who is working as a vigilante to clean up Gotham as well.

One of the most captivating characters of the movie is Heath Ledger's Joker. In all the movies before we have never seen the Joker played as such a psychotic, manic as Ledger portrayed him. The casting of this character was perfectly done and the execution was flawless. Even though he was the villain he was captivating and drew you in from the first scene of him standing on that street corner with his back toward you. He always kept you guessing and you never knew what he might do next.

Since the theme of the film was darker the scenes are darker as well. Even during the day time scenes are overcast and dark. There never seems to be any light in the city of Gotham. The creators of the film used this specifically to emphasis the darkness that plagues the city and what the heroes are constantly facing. As the movie progresses we see that even the evil starts to have its effects on the good guys. The Joker captures Harvey and Rachel and is playing the Batman against the police force as to who should be saved. Batman wants to save Rachel because he loves her, the police want to save Harvey because he is one of their own. Batman however ends up with Harvey and saves him while Rachel gets blown. When the scenario goes wrong and Harvey spills the oil barrel he is drenched in gas when the explosion occurs as they are escaping. With Harvey losing Rachel and getting burned he turns from good to evil and seeks his own revenge for what has happened to those he loved. Harvey becomes Two Face. The transition of Harvey from good to evil is one of Gotham's greatest secrets and we see that it's carried on into The Dark Knight Rises.

Overall, this movie is very well done and sets a precedents for superhero movies. We can see that no matter how old you are you can always renew your love for good vs evil depending on how it's done. Introducing the darker aspect to the beloved comic was a great accomplishment for Christopher Nolan and his complex vision brilliantly displayed by the actors on the screen.

10.title: The most frequently posted film ever? (#3223)
10.content:
As I just checked the number of comments that have been written and accepted for IMDb, I see there are 3222 for "The Dark Knight". Typing this at 12:44 am (EST), I wonder who will read this umpteenth musing on what is the monster hit movie of our era?

What makes this flick so awesome? I went to it the first time at an IMAX screening and was pleasantly shocked at how effective the full screen shots were (I counted at least 35 separate ones in the film overall). Seeing the collective jaws drop over this made me wish the whole thing had been shot in this format, but that would have made it criminally expensive. Is charging thirty dollars a ticket an acceptable way of getting another "Batman" sequel IMAXed?

I saw it a second time at the same theatre a few months later when it was brought back for a limited return engagement. This time there weren't any other people in the front section I prefer to sit in and the absence of a huge crowd helped me focus on the entire film. I liked it much more the second time, when it's relentless hype machine was finally taking a break.

The role of this superhero has been played by so many different men over the years, I have come to the conclusion I don't want to see anyone else in the part other than Christian Bale. He fits this part like the tight suit he runs around Gotham in fits him. It gets rather silly when the casting of such a world wide franchise is being shuffled like a deck of cards. Stick with one dependable person and be done with the games already! (Some folks think Michael Keaton almost had the kibosh put on his career when he didn't want to play this a third time. I don't know if that's true, but hope it isn't. He's a great talent and shouldn't be limited to something he doesn't have his heart in anymore.)

The role of the Joker is another matter entirely. I'm beyond angry Heath Ledger died such a stupid and preventable death. A little girl lost her father, a family lost their son/brother and we as his fans don't get to share in his unique gift anymore.

I got sick of all the pre-release publicity and then disgusted by the tabloid fest his demise became. Let the family and friends grieve in peace. Only now, after all the smoke clears, can I truly view his amazing performance and take it in as the brilliant acting it was. Not just the vehicle for awards driven advertising, but a sincere relationship between a star, their art and his audience.

If there's another "Batman" down the line, it'll have a hard time topping this. Too bad the price one pays for success is having to compete with their own legacy.

10.title: In an attempt to take down organized crime in Gotham, Batman goes to odds with the Joker
10.content:
The oldest story in existence is that of good vs evil. Audiences to the story identify with the force of good which is only natural; the narrative practically always follows the "good guy" and people prefer to think of themselves as being inherently good. "The Dark Knight" (2008) explores the dichotomy of good and evil by keeping the traditional narrative, but challenging the way in which audiences identify with certain themes.

For as long as Batman and the Joker have been at odds, Batman has always represented truth, justice, and the force of good while the Joker has been an advocate for chaos and self-indulgent depravity. The two characters' motivations for their respective behaviors had always been overlooked by audiences until the release of "Batman: The Killing Joke" in 1988. In The Killing Joke, the Joker's origin story is revealed and he divulges that he commits atrocities to prove that deep down, everyone (even Batman) is just as immoral as he is, proclaiming that "all it takes is one bad day."

In The Dark Knight, the Joker sets out to prove that very same argument, which culminates with his plan involving the two ferries. Before the Joker's plan fails to come to fruition, audiences assume that Batman intends to prove that people are inherently good, but as the film nears its end, it becomes apparent that the true moral of the story is that people choose whether to be good or evil, something the Joker had anticipated and abused. The Joker takes advantage of Harvey Dent's grievous situation as his "ace in the hole," with hopes that the people of Gotham will become disheartened after seeing the most noble of people turned evil. In the end, to keep the Joker from winning over the minds of the people, Batman ascribes Dent's misdeeds to his own reputation to save Dent's, giving the people of Gotham an idol to rally behind.

Overall, the film's production, acting, and effects work in perfect rapport with its themes and narrative to achieve a perfect 10 in my opinion.

10.title: Who would've thought a Batman movie could be so...Perfect?

The Dark Knight is a revelation in film making-both comic book and regular. Usually I give comic book movies slack, since the actors aren't meant to be brilliant, he plot is not meant to be mind-bending and meaningful, and the theme is supposed to be something along the lines of, "Heroes will always be there to save the day!". However, if I give Christopher Nolan's masterpiece "The Dark Knight" slack, I would be driving myself insane to put an infinity out of ten for the rating. The Dark Knight needs no slack put on it, it is a GREAT film. Starting off with the acting (I'll end with The Joker), Alfred (Michael Caine), Bruce Wayne/Batman (Christian Bale), Lucius Fox (Morgan Freeman), and Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) pull off the (second) best part of the film, the acting is...Beautiful. Yes, these actors are beyond good, however, the "main attraction" is Heath Ledger's version of The Joker. You feel as if Ledger is actually as insane as The Joker and his acting is beyond brilliant and beautiful to the thousandth power (RIP).

However, that is only the acting, the plot is GREAT and the theme is something we should all remember. I won't spoil anything, though, you deserve to watch this movie for yourself.

Or, better yet, IT deserves for you to watch it.

OVERALL: The Dark Knight is quite possibly the best movie I have ever seen, the acting, plot, theme, directing-I could go on-is just magnificent. If you haven't seen it simply because it's a "Batman movie" you are truly missing out. Nolan's work of art is so brilliant and good that The Dark Knight isn't even a Batman movie anymore. If you haven't seen it, you are truly missing out on something extraordinary.

10.title: Amazing
10.content:
The Dark Knight is a movie that I can't recommend enough. It's one of the best superhero movies ever made, and it's also one of the best movies of the 21st century. It's a movie that manages to be both thrilling and thought-provoking, and it's a movie that will stick with you long after you've seen it.

The movie is directed by Christopher Nolan, who is one of the most talented directors working today. Nolan is known for his ability to create complex, layered movies that are both entertaining and intellectually stimulating, and The Dark Knight is no exception. The movie is a sequel to Batman Begins, which Nolan also directed, and it continues the story of Bruce Wayne, who is also known as Batman.

The Dark Knight picks up where Batman Begins left off. Gotham City is still a dangerous place, and Batman is still fighting to keep the city safe. However, a new villain has emerged, and he is unlike anything Batman has ever faced before. The Joker, played by the late Heath Ledger, is a psychotic criminal who is determined to bring chaos to Gotham City. He is a mastermind who is always one step ahead of Batman, and he is a villain who is impossible to predict.

The movie is a study of good and evil, and it's a movie that asks some tough questions. Is it possible for good people to do bad things? Is it possible for bad people to do good things? These are the questions that The Dark Knight asks, and it doesn't provide easy answers. The movie is a meditation on morality, and it's a movie that will make you think.

One of the things that makes The Dark Knight so great is the performances. Christian Bale is excellent as Batman, and he brings a brooding intensity to the role. He's a hero who is struggling with his own demons, and Bale captures this perfectly. However, the real standout performance is Heath Ledger as the Joker. Ledger's performance is nothing short of incredible. He's a villain who is terrifying, but he's also a villain who is funny. He's a character who is impossible to look away from, and Ledger's performance is the reason why.

The movie is also visually stunning. Nolan is a master of visual storytelling, and he uses the camera to great effect in The Dark Knight. The movie is shot in a gritty, realistic style, and it's a movie that feels grounded in reality. The action scenes are thrilling, and they're shot in a way that makes you feel like you're right in.

The Dark Knight is a wonderfully made film and is one of the best comic-book movies ever created. The story centers on the conflict between Batman/Bruce Wayne, played by Christen Bale, and The Joker played by the late Heath Ledger. The Joker tests Batman throughout the movie by killing people and going through with some elaborate schemes. The Joker wants Batman to step forward and reveal his true identity. The movie also involves Bruce Wayne's old love interest Rachel, played by Maggie Gyllenhaal, and her boyfriend at the moment district attorney Harvey Dent, played by Aaron Eckhart.

The main theme of the film in my opinion is that sometimes the truth is better off being hidden if it helps the greater good. Batman in the film represents good and The Joker represents evil. The Joker tries to turn Batman into something more sinister throughout the movie, but is unsuccessful. The Joker does succeed in turning Harvey Dent into an evil character named Two Face. If the city of Gotham found out that Harvey Dent had turned into a monster, it would destroy their faith because he is the one person that is looked up to.

There is two main scenes that demonstrate the theme of the film. The first scene is where the housekeeper Alfred, played by Michael Caine, receives a letter from Rachel. Rachel tells Alfred to give the letter to Bruce and for Alfred not to read it. Alfred reads it anyway and it says in the letter that she is done waiting for Bruce and that she is going to marry Harvey Dent. Alfred never gives Bruce the letter because he knew that it would crush Bruce. Bruce was better off not knowing.

The other scene that demonstrates the theme is the end scene. Harvey Dent is holding Commissioner Gordon's, played by Gary Oldman, family hostage. Batman shows up and accidentally kills Harvey Dent. If they tell the truth about all the bad things Harvey was doing, it would devastate Gotham. So instead, they place the blame on Batman and say that he killed an innocent Harvey Dent, so that he can become a symbol of hope for Gotham.

The main technique that got the theme out was the dialogue in the film. The acting was excellent throughout and the dialogue was spot on in most scenes. Also, the editing of the film was very well done to make the theme very clear. They threw in montages when necessary and the pace of the film was very well done. This movie shares a common theme that is demonstrated in many other comic-book films such as Spiderman and The Avengers.

The Dark Knight is a film that needs to be seen by everyone, even the people that dislike comic-book characters.

10.title: Christopher Nolan's Master Piece
10.content:
This isn't the first time Christopher Nolan directs a good movie. This time, with The Dark Night, we have a very different example. And why is it? Well, this isn't simply a good movie: this is, with no doubt, his best work until now, and a movie that is out-rightly perfect.

We can perfectly resume the script as sublime. There are many elements from the comics that are mixed in this film and taken into a "reality level" that I haven't seen before. In the other hand, we have a lot of characters who are introduced as very deep and human, and this is even harder to do. Of course, Bale, Eckhart and Ledger's acting are delirious in the best sense there could be, and they alongside Nolan make three incredible main characters. Nevertheless, secondary characters are also impressive.

Nolan has done a perfect movie, 150 minutes long and seems to be an hour and a half. There is no plot hole: everything is perfectly connected and tied. Yes, ladies and gentlemen, every single second of this film has a reason to be, has sense, and this makes of it an amazing job that not many have done before Nolan. Of course, "The Dark Night" is not the best movie ever made, but it doesn't even try to be.

I have read a lot of reviews saying that this film has faults, and these faults mentioned don't exist. For example, Dent's progression as a character. Many people criticize that there is no progression for Dent, that he becomes "Two Faces" from a second to the other, and there is no way to say such a thing. After Gordon's Death, Harvey gets mad and steals a vehicle. We can already see there what kind of change will he suffer. As well, after Rachael's stuff and death, Harvey lets his rage out in the hospital and the mighty Joker (before Ledger's Joker, I have seen actors being dresses AS Joker; Ledger, by the way, IS Joker) takes this opportunity to manipulate him. We can then conclude that Harvey starts his madness with Gordon and his police men, and he tries to pay it with him.

Another example would be the sequence with the boats: "the prisoners have no feelings". What Nolan is trying to show here is simple that in the worst situations, humanity is the most important thing. As the police are armed, it is logical that the prisoners do not try anything. As the ones in the other boat "mess around", we even find an allusion to Two Faces: one side who does something and the other one that does not, but in the end, we see that nobody has the courage to explode themselves or the others, and this is where Nolan is showing this "humanity".

Of course, there will always be people arguing against everything and saying that movies like "Spider-man 3" are much more deep. I always tell this people that "The Dark Night" denies it with its perfect ending. And that is everything to be said.
