10.title: It is still the movie we both need and deserve
10.content:
It was a welcome surprise for some that there was even ever a sequel to Batman Begins. Nolan's first outing into Gotham, while well reviewed, had a modest opening weekend. Not even clearing $50 million for its three day total, box office predictors immediately wrote off the dark crusader's reboot as one and done. But then a miraculous thing happened. It turns out that if you make a good movie, audiences will show up. Begins had small drops for the rest of summer 2005 and eventually earned over $200 million domestically. It went on to make a killing on DVD and Warner Bros. was off to the races.

The ending of the original left little question of who the villain in a Batman sequel would be. During its final seconds, a newly promoted Lt. Jim Gordon is meeting the Batman atop a precinct roof and hands the masked man a playing card from a crime scene. When Batman turns it over, it is an ominously foreboding Joker. Batman promises to look into it, as did Nolan and screenwriter David S. Goyer. The two correctly sensed there was a way to do the villain more menacingly than anything that had come before. Nolan did not just want to make another vigilante and clown actioner like the 1989 film. He wanted to open it up in an epic way and turn Gotham into more than a setting. He wanted his visualization of this age-old comic battle to be an ideological fight for the soul of Gotham and all those who reside therein. In short, he wanted to make a movie that had no rules, superhero or otherwise.

The most unlikely thing ever is occurring in Gotham....Things are getting better. Since Batman (Christian Bale) took out Carmine Falcone, the multiple factions of the mob are running scared. Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman) is heading his own task force that is taking it to organized crime and new District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) is a voice of hope and change for the city as he puts away criminals just as effectively as the Batman. Everyone from Crime Boss Salvatore Maroni (Eric Roberts) to the lowliest of drug dealers is thinking twice before they go out at night. It is in this moment of urban optimism that all Hell breaks loose. And the face of that Hell is a Joker.

A methodical psychopath, the Joker (Heath Ledger) has big plans for Gotham City. He will systematically break every institution in the city until there is only chaos. The city's political leadership, law enforcement, media and organized crime are all in need of being taken down a peg. Their only hopes are crusading DA Harvey Dent and the Dark Knight. But how can Batman stop the Joker, when his mere existence may be a response to Batman's presence?

Okay, let's get it out of the way. Heath Ledger's stunning performance as the Joker in this film is insanely iconic. It holds the distinction of being the first time an actor's work in a superhero movie was recognized by the Academy Awards when he won the Oscar for Best Supporting Actor. Yet sadly, it will also be forever remembered as the actor's final complete role. Shortly after production wrapped on The Dark Knight, the troubled star died from an accidental sleeping pill overdose. The hype for the movie became nearly hysterical after the idiotic myth that the character drove Ledger to his grave went viral. Cynics write off his posthumous awards and perhaps the whole movie as nothing more than a fatalistic culture obsessing over trite...and they are incredibly wrong. Anyone with common sense can see that there is much more to his last performance and the movie as a whole than this tragedy.

Ledger succeeded at creating a new type of monster that struck a chord with audiences in 2008 and is just as potent now. If Nolan and Goyer wet their ankles in the idea of post-9/11 terrorism with begin, they loudly screamed, "CANNONBALL!" when they dove into it with The Dark Knight. In the first film, Ra's Al Ghul is a bearded religious zealot hiding in distant mountains with dreams of laying waste to American cities. Liam Neeson was as much Osama bin Laden as he was the Denny O'Neal character in that movie. Still, his plan was very comic book friendly and felt safely impossible.

The Joker is something else. In the years following 2001, the horror of foreign non-state actors gripped the minds of many Americans, including Hollywood filmmakers, but there is a much older and more insidious fear; the fear of pure anarchy. All societies are bound by a sense of order. Whether these social constructs are a natural extension of the human condition or an artifice constructed by people to protect (or control) one another is irrelevant to this movie. The point is society works because there are rules and there are those who enforce the rules. The poster boy for enforced order and harmony is the Batman. Then there are those who do not like following rules or being ruled. As Michael Caine's Alfred says in the movie, "There are those who just want to watch the world burn." Nolan and Ledger's Joker is the marriage of the greatest terrors for Westerners in the early 21st century. He is a man who wants to inflict chaos, death and wanton suffering on an entire culture for no other reason than he can and he will do so using the tactics of a terrorist. The Joker has no ideological cause for his madness, other than the belief in an absence of ideology and does not behave like a normal criminal or enemy. He is both everywhere and nowhere and he is causing a society to turn on its own self-righteous principals just to stop the lone gunman from killing again.

That is the real strength of the movie. It is more than just the Joker. It is a movie about how Gotham, a parallel for American culture, reacts to an existential threat. Early in the film, the triumvirate of Batman, Gordon and Dent deliver a series of crippling blows to the mafia. Gotham's salvation seems within grasp, but a few political assassinations later, the media is calling for Dent and Batman's heads. Harvey is supposed to be the city's White Knight who does things by the book and upholds their ideals. But when the Joker threatens his lover, Rachel Dawes (now Maggie Gyllenhaal), Harvey shows signs of sliding into the muck to protect her. Meanwhile, Batman's methods, often used in the comics without much thought, are given real world context. His interrogations of mobsters and eventually the Joker himself seem less like grisly crime procedure and are instead ethically blurry scenes of torture. What does it say of "the one good cop," Gordon, when he allows a masked vigilante to beat his prisoners? Batman even wiretaps every Gothamite's cell phone in the film's Third Act to find the clown terrorist.

As we watch the city begin to tear itself apart when the Joker morbidly threatens to blow up a hospital unless an accountant is murdered by fellow citizens or see him force young families to play an explosive game of prisoner's dilemma with a boatful of convicts, we are more disturbed than amused. This is not a traditional superhero movie about stopping a villain. This is an ensemble piece about how far a society will bend its own rules to stop someone who only wants to break them. It is clearly influenced by several comic stories. The Long Halloween by Jeph Loeb and Tim Sale, is about Batman, Gordon and Dent taking down the mob and how it tragically cost the DA his soul. Alan Moore and Brian Bolland's The Killing Joke is a character study of the green haired supervillain and his desire to mentally break Jim Gordon, thereby proving that everyone is as nutty and cruel as he is. Nolan and his scribe brother Jonathan Nolan seamlessly weave these concepts into the final film. However, this Gotham does not feel like the noir-ish nightmare of the page. It looks like our world being set on fire.

If this picture were an overblown popcorn movie, as its critics still insist, it would have ended during a confrontation between Batman and Joker with the hero being victorious. Indeed, that scene is in the movie...only it is a fleeting victory. The Joker laughs in an exhausted and pained Batman's face, "Do you really think I would risk the battle for Gotham's soul on a fist fight with you?" His real goal was to break the system. The true climax is Batman being faced with saving a friend's child by breaking his one rule (THOU SHALT NOT KILL) or letting another lost friend take the boy's life. The second villain of the film isn't even a villain, but a tragic hero who could not handle the moral ambiguity of modern society. He lost everything and forces our remaining heroes into a conspiracy and a political cover-up. Hardly the stuff of reassuring popcorn.

The Dark Knight is a stunning achievement of taking old comic book tropes and reinventing them in a terrifying way for today. It is both the most comic-faithful Batman movie to date and also the most removed from that world. Batman, Joker and everything in between is still absurdly impossible, but this movie made it feel all too real. It is that rare blockbuster movie that transcends its genre and commercial interests to become something more. To call it the best superhero movie ever made is an understatement. It struck the cultural zeitgeist in 2008 like lightning and is still the movie we both need and deserve.

10.title: Absolutely the best movie i have ever seen
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight," the second installment in his Batman trilogy, is often cited as one of the most significant superhero films to ever grace the big screen-a statement that, upon closer examination, proves to be more than just hyperbole. Released in 2008, it expertly combines elements of psychological thriller, action-packed cinema, and philosophical inquiry, evolving the superhero genre into a realm that poses heavy ethical dilemmas and moral questions about justice and chaos.

From the outset, Nolan-who co-wrote the screenplay with his brother Jonathan-presents a Gotham City immersed in darkness. The film picks up where "Batman Begins" left off, with Batman (Christian Bale) and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) working in tandem to eradicate crime. The groundwork Nolan lays here is meticulously crafted, establishing a moral landscape that begs the audience to confront their interpretations of justice and heroism.

At the heart of the film lies the unparalleled performance of Heath Ledger as the Joker. Ledger's portrayal transcends traditional villainy, redefining what it means to be an antagonist in modern cinema. The Joker is not merely a foil to Batman; he represents chaos incarnate, an anarchistic force intent on exposing the fragility of societal order. Ledger captures the character's erratic nature with brilliance-his laugh is disconcerting, his mannerisms disturbingly captivating. The Joker's philosophy, articulated through twisted humor and psychopathic reasoning, presents a chilling argument that challenges the very fabric of what the audience perceives as heroism.

Nolan masterfully stitches together a narrative filled with tension and unpredictability. The film opens with a meticulously choreographed bank heist, showcasing the Joker's cunning and strategic ruthlessness. This sequence sets the tone for the ensuing chaos and establishes the Joker as a formidable opponent to Batman, highlighting their philosophical divergences. While Batman is bound by a moral code, the Joker revels in the chaos, aiming to dismantle the facade of order in Gotham.

Christian Bale offers a nuanced portrayal of Batman, grappling with his dual identity throughout the film. Bale's performance captures Bruce Wayne's internal conflict-the weight of his role as protector of Gotham, juxtaposed against the rising tide of chaos that the Joker brings. The film delves into the psychological toll that the duality of his character imposes, especially as he witnesses the moral decline of those around him, particularly Harvey Dent.

Aaron Eckhart's portrayal of Harvey Dent is equally compelling. Initially depicted as Gotham's white knight, Dent undergoes a catastrophic transformation into Two-Face, illustrating the film's exploration of morality and the fragility of heroism. His descent into vengeance and nihilism serves as a stark counterpoint to Batman's unwavering commitment to justice. Eckhart masterfully navigates Dent's trajectory, from a beacon of hope to a tragic figure driven by loss, further emphasizing the film's grim message about the thin line between good and evil.

Nolan's approach to cinematography, led by director of photography Wally Pfister, creates a visually striking experience. The stark contrast between light and shadow metaphorically underscores the film's deeper themes. Iconic set pieces, such as the Joker's fiery assault on Gotham's mob bosses and the climactic showdown that culminates in the construction of the fate that befalls Harvey Dent, are nothing short of masterclass in both direction and visual storytelling. The action sequences are executed with meticulous precision, utilizing practical effects that create an authenticity often absent in the computer-generated landscapes of contemporary cinema.

Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard's score heightens the film's tension, punctuating moments of suspense and emotional gravitas. The haunting musical themes serve as an auditory reflection of the characters' struggles and the overarching conflict between order and chaos. Particularly effective is the discordant motif introduced with the Joker, which reinforces the psychological warfare he wages against Gotham, amplifying the stakes of the narrative.

"The Dark Knight" also compels the viewer to confront the societal implications of its narrative. Subtle social commentary woven throughout the film raises questions about civil liberties, the ethics of vigilantism, and the psychological wear of confronting evil head-on. The moral ambiguity depicted within the story resonates strongly, encouraging audiences to critically evaluate the concept of 'the greater good' and to reflect on the consequences of one's choices in the pursuit of justice.

Ultimately, "The Dark Knight" transcends its classification as a superhero film to become a complex exploration of the human condition, illuminated through the lens of Gotham's chaotic landscape. It poses a bold challenge: Can one truly uphold justice without succumbing to the very darkness they seek to combat?

In conclusion, Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" is an indelible work that successfully marries thrilling entertainment with deep philosophical inquiry. Its remarkable performances, particularly those of Heath Ledger and Aaron Eckhart, combined with a gripping narrative and visual storytelling, secure its place not only as a standout in the superhero genre but as one of the greatest films of the 21st century. Still as relevant today as it was upon release, "The Dark Knight" is a stark reminder that in the fight against chaos, heroes must continually confront their own shadows.

****This review may contain spoilers****

First off I want to say that the director, Christopher Nolan's choice in actors and actresses is amazing, I do not believe anyone else could have fulfilled these roles any better than the actors themselves. Christian Bale as Bruce Wayne aka the Batman, Health Ledger as the Joker, Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent, Gary Oldman as Gordon, Morgan Freeman as Lucius Fox and Maggie Gyllenhaal as Rachel are some of the main characters in this movie. The Dark Knight (2008) was produced by Warner Bros., and is set in Gotham City.

In this sequel from Batman Begins (2005), it is placed about a year after the Batman has started to make his mark in Gotham. With the help of Lieutenant Gordon and newly appointed District Attorney Harvey Dent, they are making a war on crime and cleaning up the streets of Gotham in a hurry. As they seem to be making progress a new insane enemy known as the Joker makes his mark and makes sure that no one will forget it. With this new enemy, the one rule that Batman holds true to himself to separate him from the criminals will be tested in more ways than one. The Joker is out to bring chaos and try to prove that no man is incorruptible. A love triangle is formed between Bruce, Harvey and Rachel, where Rachel makes her choice. Once Batman was able to finally reel in the Joker in the construction building, Wally was able to have that insane type sound to go with the Jokers laugh and remarks towards Batman on how he couldn't kill him. During that time the Joker was upside down and the camera slowly started to rotate with the spot lights on him and the darkness to Batman's back. It helped the audience to know that this wasn't the end of the Joker and that they had become arch enemies to each other. This sequel really helped the audience understand who the Batman was and wither or not he was a hero or just a vigilante. The Joker is an enemy that the Batman will face for years to come along with new ones down the road. Gotham is safe for the time being but how long can Batman go for? There is not one thing that comes to mind in changing any aspect of this movie. Great acting and directing really help to mold the theme and keep the audience in tuned.

10.title: Nolan at his best
10.content:
Gritty reboots have taken over the world! Batman Begins wasn't the first movie to do it, but it was the first to do it right. After the utter failure of Batman & Robin in 1997, fans were reluctant to return to the franchise. But the awesomeness known as Christopher Nolan managed to not only get people interested again, but also got us to take the character serious for once. Instead of making a typical superhero movie where the first half is the origin story and the second half is the character finally using that power, Batman Begins is an entire origin story. We get it over with in one movie.

By the time the sequel, The Dark Knight, starts, the story is already established. We don't need an introduction of the characters, because we already know them. We get an introduction of Joker, but it's not an origin story for him. We're introduced to him as he's robbing a mob bank. We get right away that he's psychotic. We do get a bit of a back story on him later on, but even later on we find out that was just a lie, because he tells a different version. I guess this is one of those cases where the less you know, the more creepy it is. We don't need to know Joker's story to get why we're supposed to be scared of him. The Dark Knight is by far the best entry in the Dark Knight trilogy. Its dark, well-written storyline keeps you hooked until the credits roll, the music fits perfectly with the epic feel of the story, and the characters are complex and believable. When this movie came out, it was Batman at his most vulnerable (until The Dark Knight Rises came out and we saw Bruce Wayne walking with a cane). The now-famous image of Batman standing over the wreckage of a building is as haunting in context as it is out of context.

The Dark Knight Rises infamously disappointed fans, myself included. I went to go see it in theaters when it came out. But it would have been very difficult to outdo The Dark Knight, which in my opinion is the best superhero movie.

10.title: A Modern Masterpiece

Christopher Nolan's sequel to 2005's "Batman Begins" is one of those rare films that transcends the boundaries and preconceptions of its genre and becomes something much, much more. From the very opening shot, you know you're in for something different - something special.

Batman is not alone in his fight to rid Gotham of organized crime and poverty-driven violence, teaming up with a hotshot district attorney and his ever faithful friend in the police department, Jim Gordon. But none of them see what's really coming - a dark, malevolent force of nature called Joker. This isn't your father's goofy, wise-cracking clown...this Joker (played iconically by the late Heath Ledger), is a maniacal, anarchic, nihilistic beast hell-bent on the dismantling of civilization; a man who cannot be bought, bullied, or reasoned with.

This is a dark, gritty film that will have you on the edge of your seat, filled with shocking twists, raw emotion, and ideas about sociology and character archetypes far beyond what anyone could imagine a comic-book movie could grapple with; able to function as both a fan-serving superhero epic and a gripping crime thriller.

The stakes are ever higher, the themes never more resonant, and Nolan's masterful stroke in orchestrating this now labeled "Godfather" of comic-book movies has set the bar so high that all in-genre movies that follow it will inevitably be compared and come up short.

"The Dark Knight" is a modern masterpiece.

You clearly see the inspirations from the graphic novels like, "The Long Halloween," "Dark Victory," and of course, "The Killing Joke." The irony of Gotham's true hero, Harvey Dent, lived long enough to see himself become the villain. The joker, he pushed everyone to their limits, he wanted to make everyone have just "one bad day" like the Joker in the graphic novel, "The Killing Joke." It is a story of Shakespearean proportion. To those who rate this movie a criminally underrated 1-7, are just joking yourself and clearly trying to die down the hype. Take a rain check, nine years later this movie still best the super hero genre, and it's simply because it is more complex than the genre itself. That is why it belongs as one of the best films ever made. Also, if you're still confused, and argue that Iron Man is better than the Dark Knight because they both have 94% on rotten tomatoes, look more closely. It's average rating is a 7.7/10, while The Dark Knight's average rating of 8.6/10 on rotten tomatoes. Not even The Avengers came close to besting, "The Dark Knight." Deny it all you want, to this day, "The Dark Knight" is a film that is in a league of its own.

10.title: The Dark Knight: A Mesmerizing Triumph of Darkness and Heroism
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" defies the boundaries of the superhero genre, elevating it to new heights of cinematic artistry. This brooding and exhilarating masterpiece stands as a testament to the creative genius of Nolan and the transcendent performances that breathe life into the iconic characters of Gotham City.

Led by the late Heath Ledger in an unforgettable tour-de-force, "The Dark Knight" showcases a mesmerizing portrayal of the Joker that transcends any previous interpretation. Ledger's haunting and unpredictable performance is a revelation, leaving an indelible mark on the landscape of cinema. With every twisted mannerism and chilling line of dialogue, he immerses us in the chaotic depths of the Joker's psyche, captivating and terrifying us in equal measure.

Christian Bale's portrayal of Batman is equally remarkable, as he effortlessly embodies the duality of Bruce Wayne's tortured soul. His physicality and emotional depth bring a profound authenticity to the Caped Crusader, delivering a performance that transcends the confines of the superhero archetype. Bale's on-screen presence is magnetic, drawing us into the morally ambiguous world of Gotham's Dark Knight.

Nolan's direction is a masterclass in storytelling, expertly balancing intense action sequences with introspective character development. The film's taut narrative explores themes of morality, chaos, and the blurred lines between heroism and villainy. The dark and gritty visual palette of the film mirrors the psychological journey of its characters, immersing us in a world rife with corruption and moral dilemmas.

"The Dark Knight" boasts a rich ensemble cast that further elevates the film's brilliance. Gary Oldman's Commissioner Gordon exudes quiet strength, while Aaron Eckhart's nuanced portrayal of Harvey Dent showcases the tragic descent from idealism to darkness. Michael Caine and Morgan Freeman deliver stellar performances as Alfred and Lucius Fox, respectively, grounding the film with wisdom and compassion.

Hans Zimmer's haunting score intensifies the film's gripping atmosphere, perfectly complementing the emotional depth and escalating tension. The relentless pace and intricate plotting keep audiences on the edge of their seats, while the film's philosophical undertones provoke thought long after the credits roll.

Beyond its technical prowess, "The Dark Knight" transcends the superhero genre by exploring profound themes that resonate with the human condition. It questions the nature of heroism, the existence of true justice, and the masks we wear in society. Nolan's expertly crafted screenplay challenges our preconceptions and forces us to confront our own darkness, ultimately leaving us with a profound sense of introspection.

"The Dark Knight" stands as a cinematic triumph, a powerful and thought-provoking experience that redefines what a superhero film can be. Christopher Nolan's vision, combined with mesmerizing performances and a relentless exploration of the human psyche, has set a new standard for the genre.

Prepare to be engulfed by darkness, to witness the birth of legends, and to question the very nature of heroism. "The Dark Knight" is an extraordinary journey that will linger in your mind and leave an indelible mark on your soul.

10.title: The Dark Knight: A Cinematic Masterpiece (10/10)
10.content:
The Dark Knight (2008) is not just a superhero movie-it's a genre-defining masterpiece that transcends its comic book origins to deliver a compelling, thought-provoking, and emotionally intense experience. Directed by Christopher Nolan, this film is the pinnacle of storytelling, character development, and technical brilliance. Every element, from its gripping narrative to its iconic performances, comes together to create a perfect 10/10 film that remains unparalleled in the superhero genre.

A Gripping Story The plot of The Dark Knight is razor-sharp, expertly balancing multiple narrative threads without ever losing focus. The story delves into the moral complexities of justice, chaos, and heroism, challenging the very idea of what it means to be a hero. Gotham City is under siege, not just by criminals but by the Joker-a force of nature whose goal isn't power or money but pure anarchy.

The film's pacing is flawless, keeping the audience on edge from start to finish. Every scene, every line of dialogue, and every action set piece serves a purpose, pushing the narrative forward while exploring the characters' moral dilemmas. It's more than just good versus evil; it's a battle of ideologies, making every confrontation between Batman and the Joker electrifying.

Iconic Performances Heath Ledger's Joker is nothing short of legendary. His performance redefined the character, transforming the Joker from a cartoonish villain into an unsettling, unpredictable, and deeply terrifying antagonist. Ledger's portrayal is magnetic, with every scene he's in commanding attention. His lines-"Why so serious?" and "You either die a hero or live long enough to see yourself become the villain"-have become ingrained in pop culture, and his physicality and voice work make him unforgettable.

Christian Bale continues to deliver as Bruce Wayne/Batman, capturing the duality of the character with ease. His struggles-both as Gotham's protector and a man trying to hold onto his humanity-are palpable and deeply relatable.

Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent/Two-Face brings a tragic dimension to the film. Dent's arc, from Gotham's "White Knight" to a man consumed by vengeance, is executed flawlessly, adding emotional weight to the story. Supporting performances from Michael Caine, Gary Oldman, and Morgan Freeman further elevate the film, providing heart, gravitas, and wisdom.

Themes and Depth The movie's exploration of chaos versus order is profound and thought-provoking. The Joker isn't just a villain; he's an agent of chaos, challenging Batman's principles and forcing him to confront the darker side of his mission. The film dives into the grey areas of morality, showing how far one can go to achieve justice without losing their soul.

Harvey Dent's transformation into Two-Face embodies the film's central theme: how easily even the noblest of individuals can be corrupted when pushed to their limits. These philosophical underpinnings give The Dark Knight a weight and depth rarely seen in blockbuster films.

Action and Cinematography Nolan's direction is impeccable, blending practical effects with intense action sequences that feel raw and real. From the jaw-dropping opening bank heist to the gripping chase through Gotham's streets, every moment is meticulously crafted. The IMAX cinematography by Wally Pfister is breathtaking, giving the film an epic scope while maintaining an intimate focus on its characters.

The Score Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard's score is iconic. The pulsating, tension-filled strings that accompany the Joker's presence perfectly encapsulate his chaotic nature, while the soaring themes for Batman evoke a sense of hope and determination. The music is as much a character in the film as any of the actors.

Cultural Impact The Dark Knight redefined what a superhero movie could be, proving that these films can be as sophisticated and impactful as any Oscar-winning drama. Its influence on the genre is immeasurable, raising the bar for storytelling, character development, and thematic depth in blockbusters.

Conclusion The Dark Knight is a flawless achievement, blending gripping storytelling, unforgettable performances, and technical brilliance into a movie that is both thrilling and deeply resonant. It's not just a superhero film-it's a masterpiece of modern cinema that continues to inspire and captivate audiences years later.

A perfect 10/10, The Dark Knight is a rare gem that only gets better with each viewing. It's a film that will stand the test of time as one of the greatest movies ever made.

10.title: The Dark Knight (2008) - A Masterpiece of Modern Cinema
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's *The Dark Knight* is a cinematic triumph that transcends the superhero genre, delivering a gripping, thought-provoking experience that resonates long after the credits roll. From its groundbreaking direction to its unforgettable performances, the film is a tour de force in filmmaking.

Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of legendary. His performance is chilling, unpredictable, and magnetic, completely redefining the character as a force of chaos and destruction. Ledger's Joker is a mesmerizing antagonist whose anarchistic worldview challenges Batman, Gotham, and the audience in ways never before seen in a superhero film. His performance, arguably one of the greatest in cinema history, elevates *The Dark Knight* to an entirely new level.

Christian Bale, as Bruce Wayne/Batman, brings the character to life with depth and complexity. Bale's internal struggle between his duty as Gotham's protector and his own moral compass forms the emotional core of the film. The way he navigates the delicate balance between heroism and vengeance is portrayed masterfully, making Batman not just a symbol, but a deeply human figure.

The supporting cast, including Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent, Maggie Gyllenhaal as Rachel, and Michael Caine, Gary Oldman, and Morgan Freeman as the loyal allies of Batman, add strong layers to the story. Each character brings something vital to the film, making Gotham feel alive and its conflicts personal.

Nolan's direction is meticulous, creating a tense and immersive atmosphere that heightens the stakes of every scene. The film's pacing is perfect, with each sequence building towards the next in a relentless, pulse-pounding manner. The practical effects, the stunning IMAX sequences, and the iconic Batmobile chase through the streets of Gotham are visually exhilarating and ground the film in a gritty realism.

Hans Zimmer's and James Newton Howard's score is another key element of the film's success. The music, particularly the eerie, escalating notes tied to the Joker, creates an unsettling atmosphere that adds to the tension and unpredictability of the narrative.

*The Dark Knight* isn't just a superhero movie-it's a deep exploration of morality, justice, and the fine line between hero and villain. It asks tough questions about the cost of heroism and the nature of good and evil, all while delivering action sequences that are both thrilling and thought-provoking. It remains one of the finest examples of filmmaking in the 21st century, a film that not only shaped the future of comic book movies but also left an indelible mark on cinema as a whole.

In short, *The Dark Knight* is a masterpiece that continues to stand the test of time, offering both heart-pounding action and intellectual depth in equal measure.

10.title: Personal Favourite due to Heath Ledger
10.content:
A very well done and a personal thank-you to Christopher Nolan for making in my opinion, the greatest superhero movie of all time. The Dark Knight is hands down the best film of 2008 and is a personal favourite of mine. Everything about this masterpiece amazed me; from the engaging script to the incredible award-winning performances. It has every element you'd want from a movie, which captures you with such allure.

It had me at that fantastic moment where the bus reversed into the bank. This exposition was one of the finest; instantly roping me in with the amazing use of camera angles in the first moment and the mystery of the story and characters within these opening minutes. The film is highly script and character driven. Christopher Nolan and his brother Jonathon have written a highly complex and solid script with sharp dialogue to accompany the brilliant performances. The action and drama are perfectly balanced and is the centre of the conflict during the movie.

Although it is a follow-up from Nolan's first Batman movie: Batman Begins (2005), which is also a very good movie, this is most certainly the best Batman movie to date. But in this flick, Gotham is a place of good versus evil. There is a new villain in town and he's not playing by the rules. The Joker, played by the greatly missed legend, Heath Ledger is hands down the best thing about this movie. He wants to take over as Gotham's leader, which causes Lieutenant Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman), Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) and Batman (Christian Bale) must come together to stop this wicked clown before he causes a time of social unrest for their city.

As for the performances, Nolan couldn't have casted better talent. Bale takes on the dual role of the Batman and industrialist Bruce Wayne. Bale proves himself in this movie and is much better than the previous actors playing the Batman role. He was a great choice of actor; being a natural and already blowing everyone out of the water in Batman Begins, he continues to bring the character to life. Although Bruce Wayne is covered beneath a mask for a lot of the time, he is still able to convey everything he needed to with just half of his face.

Eckhart plays and nails the character of DA Harvey Dent, a district attorney who wants justice and to bring down all the criminals of Gotham City. He makes Dent his own and is very admirable as a good guy. After the Joker has had his way with him, Eckhart makes us feel Dent's anger and pain through his performance as Two Face. Dent and Wayne's love interest, Rachel Dawes is played by the lovely Maggie Gyllenhaal, who takes over and gives a much stronger and better show than Katie Holmes previously. Gyllenhaal gives depth and has substance, making the audience build a rapport with her character and manipulates us emotionally into caring for her.

Leaving the best till last is the amazing and terrific Heath Ledger. Ledger gives the most outstanding Oscar nominated performance and completely steals the show. Giving me constant thrills, chills and goose bumps, his performance as the psychotic Joker is highly disturbing yet simply astounding. He created certain mannerisms (licking his lips) to define his psycho character. His voice and way of speaking was perfect for the maniac who gets kicks out of inflicting pain on others. With his lunatic laugh and malicious wicked manner, he successfully sets the tone for this dark movie about a world that has gone nuts. Ledger is a daring and extraordinary actor who perfects his character and I don't think I'll have any disagreements when I say I cannot picture any other actor who could have done a better job; the act is master class and most definitely his best throughout his career. It is completely mesmerising.

Putting the amazing cast and performances aside, this is a big movie. There are thrilling and intense action scenes such as the heist in the exposition and the high-speed car chases. I'm not a massive fan of action movies but these scenes kept me on the edge of my seat, completely indulged in each minute of the brilliant and exhilarating action visuals that shouldn't be missed under any circumstance. Although these scenes are captivating, even the quieter moments in the movie are equally as engaging.

The main theme in the movie, aside of good versus evil, is sacrifice and justice. Sacrifice is shown through Batman and Dent's characters where they both make self-sacrifices for the city. Batman is willing to sacrifice his good name in order to protect the people. All Dent wants is justice, and to take down the criminals of Gotham City.

I could speak and write about The Dark Knight all night. It will certainly take a lot of work to make a film that will knock this off the top spot for me; it will stand out for a very long time. It is a brilliant and chilling masterpiece that would be criminal not to watch.

10.title: Nolan's Knight Captures Everything I Love About the Batman Mythos
10.content: The picture-perfect Batman movie; dark and gritty and tragic but ultimately optimistic and meaningful, with an armful of colorful characters tossed in for seasoning. Of course, it's impossible to discuss the film without first touching on Heath Ledger, whose magnificent turn as the Joker unconscionably steals the show from the very moment he appears on the screen. Magical moments, memories and faces routinely come and go on the silver screen, but a role this iconic only comes around once or twice a generation, and the power of his appearance has been amplified over the years. Ledger deserves every bit of the credit he reaped for the part, even if his untimely demise may have heightened the hype to superhuman levels. The things his character gets to do, say, and imply are downright remarkable, and really elevate this from a very good superhero movie into a brilliant social commentary that just so happens to revolve around a man with a cape, cowl and vast personal armory. As in Batman Begins, the supporting cast is heavily peppered with brilliant performances from Hollywood's heavy-hitters, with particularly excellent showings from Michael Caine, Morgan Freeman and Aaron Eckhart, and once again Christian Bale masterfully inhabits the dual roles of Bruce Wayne and Batman. It's a great action movie, detective story, political thriller, superhero flick and moral tragedy, never feels half as long as its 152 minute run time lets on, and sticks the landing in every single important scene. One for the ages.

10.content:
"The Dark Knight" is a 2008 superhero film directed by Christopher Nolan, starring Christian Bale as Batman and Heath Ledger as the Joker. The film is a sequel to "Batman Begins" and is considered one of the best superhero films ever made.

The film's story follows Batman and Lieutenant Jim Gordon as they try to take down the Joker, a psychopathic criminal mastermind who wreaks havoc on Gotham City. The Joker's actions force Batman to confront his own morality and push the limits of what he is willing to do to protect his city.

One of the most remarkable aspects of the film is Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker, which is often considered one of the best performances in cinema history. He brings an unsettling and unpredictable energy to the character, making him both terrifying and captivating to watch.

The film's themes of chaos and morality are explored in a thought-provoking way, and the action sequences are thrilling and well-executed. The cinematography and score are also highlights of the film, adding to the overall tension and atmosphere.

Overall, "The Dark Knight" is a masterpiece of the superhero genre, with a compelling story, great performances, and excellent technical aspects. It's a must-watch for any fan of Batman or superhero films in general.

10.title: The Dark Knight is Brilliant
10.content: The Dark Knight is a brilliant follow-up to Batman Begins and the definitive Batman movie to date, which makes you wonder if Christopher Nolan will be able to accomplish like this again. The Dark Knight takes place in a world where the line between good and evil is drawn in pencil. With The Joker's lunatic smile and gleefully malicious manner setting the tone for a wild romp through a world gone mad. Batman's universe is teetering on the edge and the conflicted superhero is trying to unravel the puzzle of how best to protect Gotham City while believing he's not the savior his city deserves. 2005's Batman Begins introduced Christian Bale in the dual roles of Bruce Wayne and Batman, and The Dark Knight serves to cement the fact he is the perfect casting choice to shoulder the lead in the Batman film franchise. Gotham City's falling to pieces and Batman is both the problem and the solution. The caped crusader has taken down a king-sized helping of bad guys, although he's not working on his own. Ordinary citizens have taken up his cause, donning their own Batman costumes and patrolling the streets. And now the mobsters left in town have joined forces in order to keep the real Batman at bay. No disrespect meant to Jack Nicholson but this is the performance of The Joker everyone will remember. Nicholson's Joker in Tim Burton's 1989 Batman fit perfectly with the tone of that movie. In The Dark Knight, it's Ledger's Joker the rest of the cast needs to keep step with. This Joker is nasty-scary, a greasy, grotesque creature lifted straight from the nightmares of coulrophobics. Even those not given to fearing clowns are going to recoil in fright from Ledger's mesmerizing performance. The Dark Knight's action sequences are controlled chaos with cars and motorcycles and Mack trucks careening down city streets, and the film's quieter moments are equally as engaging. There's just so much to say about The Dark Knight, so much I want to analyze and discuss, but expanding on a review of the plot would lay out potential spoilers and it's best to go into the film without any knowledge of the story line other than the bare minimum. Nolan and company have surpassed what they accomplished the first time out, and The Dark Knight is everything you'd want from a superhero movie and much, much more.

10.title: Perfection

Heath Ledger gives us the best live action Joker. Ledge and Nolan created a realistic version of the iconic comic book villain. Ledger not only brought the comic book to life, but also expanded on the characters by creating little mannerisms.

Aaron Eckhart plays Harvey Dent. Eckhart portrays Harvey as a man who is trying to clean up the streets of Gotham.

Michael Caine and Morgan Freeman reprise their roles as Alfred Pennyworth and Lucius Fox. Both actors continue to build off from where their characters left off from Batman Begins.

Maggie Gyllenhaal plays Rachel in this movie. Maggie takes over the role after Katie Holmes didn't want to reprise the role.

Christopher Nolan returns to produce, write, and direct the sequel to Batman Begins. Nolan makes some very great choices for this film. There are two scenes where he could easily use CGI, but he decides to actually pull these stunts off.

The Dark Knight is the best comic book movie ever, and according to IMDb is in the top 5 of all movies. The fact this movie wasn't nominated for Best Picture would've been an insult, if Heath Ledger didn't win Best Supporting Actor. This movie is personally my favorite movie ever.

10.title: Proof that a sequel can be as good, if not sometimes better than its predecessor

Special mention must be given to the late Heath Ledger, who delivers one of the most disturbing turns of a comic book villain ever seen on the big screen. His mere presence permeates the whole of the movie and the unpredictable nature of his character makes for some really surprising story's twists and turns. That's the nature of the whole movie. The audience is constantly kept on their toes and there is no safe ground on which to rest. This incarnation of The Joker, more than any other, really gives Batman a run for his movie. A solid script, with very well written characters and a definite improvement in the way the action set pieces are handled, makes this,one of the best Superhero sequels ever made and a water mark for future ones. Not much else can be said about this marvel. Good performances throughout and remarkable production values, this one takes the action up a notch with the inclusion of a bunch of sequences shot with IMAX cameras. If given the chance, watch it this way. I did, and it was a terrific experience.

10.title: The Dark Knight: A Dark, Gritty, and Flawless Comic Book Adaptation
10.content:
The Dark Knight is a stunning achievement in comic book filmmaking that raised the bar for the entire genre. Directed by Christopher Nolan and starring Christian Bale as Batman, the film is a dark and gritty exploration of heroism, villainy, and the blurred line between them. Heath Ledger's unforgettable performance as the Joker is nothing short of legendary, with his chaotic and unpredictable presence dominating every scene he's in.

But the film is not just a showcase for Ledger's talents. The entire cast delivers, with Aaron Eckhart's portrayal of Harvey Dent and Gary Oldman's turn as Commissioner Gordon adding layers of complexity and depth to the story. The action sequences are expertly choreographed and filmed, and the film's pacing never lags despite its lengthy runtime.

What sets The Dark Knight apart from other comic book adaptations is its commitment to realism and grounded storytelling. The film eschews flashy superheroics in favor of a more grounded approach that emphasizes character and themes. The Dark Knight is a film that asks tough questions about justice, morality, and the nature of heroism, and it does so with nuance and intelligence.

Overall, The Dark Knight is a flawless comic book adaptation that sets the standard for what the genre can achieve. Christopher Nolan's direction is masterful, and the performances are top-notch across the board. The film's impact on popular culture cannot be overstated, with its influence still felt in superhero movies today. The Dark Knight is a triumph of filmmaking that will continue to be revered for years to come.

10.title: Why So Serious
10.content:
Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" (2008), sequel to Christopher Nolan's other Batman film "Batman Begins," (2005) left its viewers on the edge of their seats. The characterization of the film is just spectacular. When Batman's (Christian Bale) archenemy, the Joker (Heath Ledger), first appears in the beginning of the movie, he shows us just how psychotic he really is. His plans and schemes are so elaborate, yet unpredictable, that he leaves the audience guessing and wondering how one man could be so sick in the head to put such plans together.

Batman/Bruce Wayne has made dramatic changes to the city of Gotham. The crime rate is down and what's left of the organized crime is too afraid to come out at night. Also hell bent on making Gotham a better place is Gotham's new District Attorney, Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart). Batman knows that he will not be able to protect Gotham for the rest of his life. Dent may be the one to replace him as someone the public can look up to. A hero that's not hidden behind a mask. However, for every good, there is evil. In an attempt to rise back to the top, Gotham's underground mob turned to a man whom no one could begin to understand. The Joker gives them a simple yet effective plan: "kill the Batman." Of course, throughout the movie we learn that that is the opposite of what the Joker is trying to do. "I don't want to kill you. What would I do without you, go back to ripping off mob bosses," Joker says as him and Batman have a one on one discussion in a police interrogation room. In this scene the Joker makes a very valid point that the people of Gotham love Batman know, but once they don't need him anymore, they will turn on him. This seems to be true since the people have already asked for Batman to turn himself into the local authorities.

Batman knows better. He can't turn himself in because he protects Gotham, but he's only a hero to those who know it. That's why he's not a hero. He's whatever Gotham needs him to be. He still protects the people, but they need someone to look up to, like Harvey. They need public officials who are uncorrupted and can be viewed upon as a white knight. That's why Batman can take the hit, because he's not a hero. He's a dark knight.

10.title: A Heart-Stopping Ride Through Chaos and Redemption
10.content:
As I walked out of the theater in July of 2008 with my best friend Ray, my mind was racing, and my heart pounding. The Dark Knight was not just another superhero movie; it was a rollercoaster of emotions, darkness, and chaos that gripped me from the very beginning.

Christian Bale's Batman may not have undergone much growth in this film, but his portrayal of the tormented and determined hero is still a sight to behold. What really steals the show, though, is Heath Ledger's Joker. This isn't just a villain - he's a force of nature, a demon unleashed upon Gotham, and his chaotic actions challenge the very core of Batman's existence.

The supporting cast is nothing short of phenomenal. Michael Caine's Alfred provides a compassionate, wise anchor amidst the madness, while Aaron Eckhart's Harvey Dent is the tragic fallen hero. Their performances truly tug at the heartstrings, making us feel deeply for these characters caught in the Joker's twisted web.

Christopher Nolan's storytelling is a masterclass in suspense, as he brings us along on a breathtaking journey filled with unforgettable moments. The opening bank heist, the Joker's horrific pencil trick, and the nail-biting highway fight had me on the edge of my seat. But it's the climactic boat scene, where the people of Gotham prove that they won't be corrupted by the Joker's schemes, that restores hope in humanity and leaves a lasting impact on our hearts.

The atmosphere of The Dark Knight is undeniably dark and gritty, yet it's punctuated by moments of triumph that remind us of the resilience of the human spirit. This film shows us the ugliness of the world, but also the beauty that can emerge from it.

Hans Zimmer's score is the beating heart of the film, setting the pulse for every scene and wrapping us in a cocoon of emotion. I've lost count of how many times I've listened to the soundtrack, and it still gives me goosebumps every time.

In the end, The Dark Knight is a movie that shakes you to your core, leaving an indelible mark on your soul. It's not just a film, but an experience that will stay with you long after the credits have rolled. This is the kind of movie that reminds us why we love cinema - for its power to move us, to challenge us, and to make us feel deeply. Don't miss out on The Dark Knight; it's a journey you won't soon forget.

10.title: Do you wanna know why this film is a masterpiece?
10.content:
Superhero flicks are too lackluster these days. It's all about the fast action, the cheesy albeit funny dialogue, the either super serious or super corny tones, and the dramatic action scenes. Now that's not necessarily bad, but this movie goes above and beyond every superhero film with only a few others rivaling it. The Dark Knight proves that it's possible to make a great film first, before making a good Superhero film. Many have said that this trilogy is the best trilogy of the 2000's. Now this may or may not be wrong, but Christopher Nolan definitely aces it with this masterpiece.

The first thing he does is make memorable characters that fully embody what they should be. Each character has extreme effort put into them, and each one is characterized by a phenomenal cast. Heath Ledger, may he rest in peace, did a phenomenal job as the Joker, and there will be moments in his performance that will trump anything that Jared Leto throws your way. That being said, Christian Bale is a superb Batman who pays homage to the Batman universe while also giving an amazing performance. Then there's Michael Caine as Alfred, Gary Oldman as James Gordon, Morgan Freeman as Lucius Fox, and Aaron Eackhart as Harvey Dent. They all carry the movie and make it even more of a masterpiece. There are more to list but this film is so well cast that when I say that any of them could have won Oscar's, I'm dead serious.

Additionally, the realism of this film shines through. As people reflect on all the "praised films" of our generation, they will probably realize that many of these films are mediocre crime dramas. However, this film will not be one of them. It really is a a highly intense thriller that just happens to take place in a DC comic book universe. Everything from the vehicles, to the corruption caused by a mob, to the themes involved totally embody realism to the point where you could believe that such a scenario presented in the movie could occur in real life, for the most part.

This is a movie worth watching, even if you don't like superhero movies. It's gripping, intense, powerful, and enthralling. You will be on the edge of your seat the entire way and will look back on this as one of the best films you had the pleasure of watching. If you're a movie fan, it's a highly recommended film, for DC and Superhero fans, it's a must.

Overall, The Dark Knight is an exceptional movie that transcends its genre, displaying impressive filmmaking, stunning performances, and an engaging narrative that establishes it as one of the best superhero movies ever made.

10.title: A Review for the Pretentious and Overprotective Fanatics of The Dark Knight
10.content:
Let me start by this: I love The Dark Knight. I saw it for the first time when I was eight and have watched it two more times ever since. And it has always held up. It's special. Heath Ledger's perfromance is my favourite thing about this movie and I also love Hans Zimmer's score,Nolan's world building and the themes. You know,everyone always talk about the positives of TDK. Audience and critics alike praise this movie. It's pretty much considered a sin to criticize this movie. Some of the...less tolerable fans of TDK get insecure and triggered when a new action movie is out and gets more higher ratings than TDK even for a short time. It's rather pathetic and hilarious how hard these particular fans try so hard to degrade the new movies as if their precious TDK was perfect. There I said it! The Dark Knight is a flawed movie. Is it a 10/10 movie? For me,yes. I can overlook the flaws because I can overlook those flaws bit that doesn't mean they aren't there.

Let's take a look: The story is convoluted with many cases of ' plot convenience'. The story goes out of its way to be in favour of Joker and his schemes so many times and it's apparent from the very beginning. Nobody absolutely noticed Joker's school bus. Joker can easily enter the building in which a meeting between the most dangerous mob bosses of Gotham is held which means he can pass their security team. How conveniently incompetent the guards are. How did these fools take control of Gotham in the first place? Joker can easily enter an important building,bringing a corpse of an adult male with him and hang him there. Nobody noticed. Joker can easily get close to the mayor of Gotham in a public event despite his gruesome scars. Joker's henchmen are more organized and more precise than the entire police force and mob bosses combined. The plot is heavily in his favour. And it's contrived. Joker's insane capability makes the ending of the movie odd and quite frankly,stupid. Batman decides it's better if he takes the blame for Dent's death. Because it's so hard to put the blame on Joker,right? Yes,Joker was apprehended at the time but come on,you easily could have put the blame on his henchmen. This guy blew up a Judge,poisoned the police commisicommissioner at the same time! Nobody would have questioned it if the blame of Dent's death had been put on him. It actually would have made sense since it would have made Dent am even bigger martyr. But I guess that wouldn't have been melodramatic enough?

Then there is the creepy romance between Christian Bale and Maggie Gyllenhaal. Are we supposed to believe these two were childhood sweetheart? Gyllenhaal looks so much older than Bale. The whole thing comes off as creepy and forced.

Also,Mr.Bale's Batman voice sounds too stupid and almost ruins the atmosphere of the movie. HISHE best describes it a the sound of someone who is gargling marbles.

This review was written for all the pretentious,insecure,overprotective fanatics of The Dark Knight who who like to keep telling themselves that other movie can't be better than muh TDK! The Dark Knight is great but it's not perfect.

10.title: Great Film
10.content:
Following Batman Begins, Director Christopher Nolan continues the story of Batman and Gotham City's war on crime in the 2008 The Dark Knight. Batman/Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale), along with Lieutenant Gordon (Gary Oldman) and new District Attorney, Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) are eager to destroy Gotham's organized crime gangland. Their attempts are quickly halted, however, when they cross the mastermind and commander of the criminal world, The Joker (Heath Ledger). After being outwitted by The Joker, anarchy hits Gotham, Batman full force.

As if there were not enough chaos in Bruce Wayne's life, there was also the motif of the love triangle between Batman, Harvey Dent, and Rachel (Maggie Gylienhaal), Bruce Wayne's long time love and childhood friend. While Bruce Wayne continues being Batman and fighting crime, there is no future for Rachel and himself. While waiting for Bruce to come back to her, she finds herself falling in love with Harvey Dent, who can provide her with the future that she desires. The love triangle between the three characters adds to the plot of the movie.

Another technique relevant to the theme of the movie is the use of the camera. During a few scenes with The Joker, the camera is used remarkably to intimidate viewers. In a particular scene where The Joker is threatening Rachel's life by holding a knife to her head, the camera focuses on them by blurring the other characters in the background. The result of this technique encouraged viewers to feel the same feeling of fear that Rachel felt in that moment. Throughout the movie, the camera also shoots scenes that add to Batman's character of being fearless and gallant. For example, there is a shot of the tall building and the long drop that Rachel is about to face. When she drops out of the window, Batman swoops out after her. The camera shot reflects how courageous Batman is by showing the audience the risk he took.

Although maybe not quite as memorable as The Dark Knight, Batman Begins continued the theme of good VS evil. The 2005 film was necessary in order to lead into The Dark Knight. And at the end of The Dark Knight, Nolan left viewers with questions to be answered and the need for a sequel.

My personal review notes the many unexpected twists and surprises that keep viewers on the edge of their seats.the scenes are vivid and picturesque.and the shots are impressive and breathtaking from the beginning till the end. Truly a movie made for high definition and for the big screen.

10.title: NOLAN did it again
10.content: Christopher Nolan's second bundle of joy "The Dark Knight" EXCEEDED all of my expectations!!! With the success of 2005's reboot of the Batman franchise, they took what was already established and expanded it, amped it up, and gave a deeper, darker and brooding story that is more gripping and the suspense is likely to catch you of guard several times throughout. Christian Bale delves more deeper into Batman, sworn to fight evil and injustice, though also quite reluctant and uncertain if his crusade can ever end and cleanse his inner turmoil from his fractured soul due to the murder of his beloved parents. But with the help of his trusted butler/ally Alfred (played superbly by Michael Cane) grounds him, gives him moral support, and keeps him in check. But the real star of the show is Heath Ledger as Batman's most deadly enemy, The Joker. I can HONESTLY tell you that: as good as Jack Nicholson was in Batman'89 he is CHILD'S PLAY compared to this Joker. He is sadistic, psychotic, and downright SCARIER and PSYCHOLOGICALLY disturbing than the previous incarnation of The Clown Prince of Crime and Ledger gives it his all to do him justice. Along with the original cast comes some fresh faces such as Aaron Eckhart, Maggie Gyllenhaal and more. I must say though I liked Katie Holmes, Gyllenhaal gives a much better performance and is a far cry from the "damsel-in-distress" stereotype (though there's a little of it, THANKFULLY) that's common in films. Bale and Gyllenhall have MUCH better chemistry this time around more so than Holmes. Even better, the fight sequences are vastly improved and feature more brutal and bone crushing combat than "Begins" in addition to new technology at Batman's disposal. Also worth mentioning is screenwriter Jonathan Nolan, who gives the film an added frosting to an already delicious cake. Simply put, The Dark Knight is totally more bad ass than "Begins." The action is great, and the plot is more deeper and engrossing. I applaud Christopher Nolan, Christian Bale, and especially Heath Ledger (who sadly passed away earlier this year) and all those aboard for believing in Mr. Nolan's talents for this second installment. Although some may feel a bit of melancholy over Ledger's death, but as a final note I will say this sincerely from my heart: Remember Heath Ledger and honor him in your minds and hearts not only for his performances, but as a human being and father to his daughter Matilda Ledger. May we issue him best wishes for his family and friends and his daughter for years to come. Remember . . . Honor him not only for this role and past roles, but as an incredible individual and talented actor. Rest in peace. Heath Ledger: 4/4/1979-1/22/2008.

10.content:
The Dark Knight (2008)

Cast: Christian Bale, Heath Ledger, Maggie Gyllenhall, and Aaron Eckhart

Director: Christopher Nolan

Produced by: Syncopy

Music: Hans Zimmer

Christopher Nolan's amazing "Dark Knight" trilogy has hit heights no other movie has in superhero franchise history financially and quality wise. The "Dark Knight" is one sign that Chris Nolan is going to continue hitting home runs with his fantastic movies. The "Dark Knight" stars Christian Bale as Batman and Heath Ledger as the maniacal fame "Joker". This movie is simply amazing in the way of craft, performances, tone, and graphics. I guess the 180,000,000 million dollar budget was really worth it.

With the help of Commissioner Gordon, and new district law attorney Harevy Dent, Batman tries to eradicate all the mobs and gangs that fill the streets at night. The Joker, is the biggest one of those mob leaders, and has become a new major target in Gotham after robbing Gotham's bank. Rachel loves Harvey, and Bruce( Batman) loves her. The rest of the plot forms on how he eradicates the mob and confronts the Joker.

This movie starts off with a spectacularly shot robbery scene. The description, tone, and dialogue give you a strong liking for the movie immediately and never lets you down. The lead in this story is simply amazing. From the first scene, it hints at a bigger meaning and intent that is imposed throughout the rest of the story. Shortly, the "Joker", played by "Heath Ledger" is introduced. All of the villains and characters are introduced very uniquely, brought up with unique dialogue and meaning. This character is played spectacularly and could not have been better, and his intent, tone, dialogue, and craziness help in giving great justice to the character. Even though you might feel he is being overplayed at some time with too much screen time, this movie handles the character very nicely. Heath's Joker doesn't really look menacing until he laughs or reacts to a conversation, unlike Nicholson's Joker which was truly menacing and frantic. Batman, played by Bale is normal, but definitely proves that he is a worthy foe for such a character like Joker. Heath definitely deserved an Oscar for his role, and made a worthy and sad send-off.

The place that this movie flies high in the colors are in the plot and storytelling. Chris has crafted such a story that involves and drags you in. He has written such a story that wouldn't make you feel like watching a Batman movie, but more like a Crime Drama, and that, he has achieved splendidly. The set pieces are simply superb, and thoroughly explain the menacing place named Gotham and how it's being directly affected. The characters are given enough time to explain themselves and how they are all placed in a pivotal place in the story. This movie is high on dialogue more than action, and that's fine mainly because the action is explained in dialogue. Yes, at some points the story does take a bit too long to explain themselves, but when the ideas are fully developed, it really does work. This movie is high on emotion and bonding, and no unwanted subplots. Ultimately, this movie has deep, heavy, and dark storytelling that most movies don't accomplish doing.

The pace of this movie is very fast compared to most other superhero DC movies, and has a lot to offer. Christopher Nolan has simply made an amazing movie. This is definitely a different kind of superhero movie that conveys heavy meaning and intent without making it boring. Most superhero dwells on superpowers and overpowered villains, while this movie doesn't as much. Well I guess that what makes DC, "DC".

Now, this movie's score is simply spectacular and out of this world. It drags you off the edge of your seat, and makes it more nail biting and dark. Hans has done it yet again with his heavy usage of strings, flutes, and trumpets, while abandoning the new- generation of electronic. That's what probably makes Hans Zimmer one of the most genuine artists in the industry.

Overall, his movie is very well done and shouldn't be a miss. I admit, this movie is a bit overrated and shouldn't be the fourth best movie of all time, but it still hits a mark that no other movie in the superhero industry ever has. Chris has given us the unique Batman that shouldn't be a miss for all audiences.

10.title: The Dark Knight review
10.content:
Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of legendary, earning him a posthumous Academy Award. Ledger's Joker is a terrifying embodiment of anarchy, with his chilling laughter, unpredictable behavior, and philosophical musings about the fragility of societal order. His performance is both magnetic and unsettling, making the Joker one of the most memorable villains in film history.

Christian Bale delivers a strong performance as Batman, capturing the duality of his character - the masked vigilante and the tormented billionaire. His internal struggle and moral dilemmas are central to the film, particularly as he faces an adversary who challenges his fundamental beliefs about justice and order.

Nolan's direction is meticulous, balancing high-octane action with thought-provoking themes. The film's pacing is tight, maintaining tension and suspense throughout its lengthy runtime. The screenplay, co-written by Nolan and his brother Jonathan, weaves together multiple narrative threads, exploring themes of heroism, sacrifice, and the fine line between order and chaos.

10.title: The film also focuses on Gotham's ongoing economic crisis
10.content:
The comics show Batman in various interpretations: a martyr as Jesus taking away society's sins, a modern-day knight in the form of the early feudal era when the peasants throw what they can at their protector and he successfully fights for them in war.

Batman: The Beginning plays on several semantic fields at once. In one, the hero is the protector of the city who cares for him like a father cares for his child. In another, Batman is Bruce Wayne's subconscious. More than once the film mentions Jung and his psychoanalysis. It is no coincidence that the hero goes precisely to the cave, faces his fears and tames them - these are all symbols from the classification of the unconscious.

The film also focuses on Gotham's ongoing economic crisis. Because of it, the mobsters gain power in the city, constantly finding new recruits. This crisis is somehow unsolvable. As a possible outcome, it is proposed to tear everything down and start all over again. Together with the people. Panic becomes an instrument of destruction. It only needs to be provoked. But Batman comes to the people's defense, eliminates the result of the hallucinogens, prevents panic, but does not solve the crisis.

He wants to become everyone's idea of individual responsibility for what is happening. To become a symbol, as yet anonymous, but courageous in the face of injustice.

Thus director Christopher Nolan has added new meanings to the character through this film.

10.title: Excellent Action Film that is a Must See
10.content:
Spoiler Alert!!! The Dark Night movie review starring Christian Bale as Batman (Bruce Wayne), Gary Oldman as Lt. Jim Gordon, Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent (Two-Face) and Heath Ledger as the Joker. This is a Christopher Nolan film who has also directed The Dark Night Rises, Interstellar and Inception.

The Dark Night tells the story of Gotham City and the intense crimes being committed. The Joker wants to run the town and is challenging all the local gangs so that he can become the top dog. The opening scenes of the movie is a bank robbery about to happen and the Joker is part of the team. The mental games begin by the Joker as he one by one either picks off or has the team killing each other until he is the last one of the team. He escapes by a school bus being backed into the bank loading the cash in the back and blending in with the law enforcement being non the wiser. As Batman tries to clean up the streets he at times utilizes the help of Lt Jim Gordon. Lt Gordon is stuck between Batman and District Attorney Harvey Dent as Dent feels that the Batman is taking matters into his own hands and not following the law.

With an ironic twist Dent and Batman are in love with the same girl Rachel. As the Joker has set up a plot for Batman to either save Rachel or Dent, Batman fails and saves Dent when he thought he was going after Rachel. There is an explosion almost killing Dent but leaves him terribly scarred and he becomes Two-Face.

The movie ends with Batman saving the day and the Joker behind bars. This movie has excellent music scores with some strong one liners that will be forever stuck in your memory. Batman holding Joker up by the neck and yelling, "Where is she!" in his awesome masculine voice. The chase scenes are intense and well put together. The fighting action is very believable and excellently executed. There are some dark spots in the film but does not take away from the film or pull you out of the movie experience. This is a thrill ride from the very beginning and leaves you wanting more at the end.

Excellent movie a total must see. Two Thumbs Up.

10.title: The Dark Knight "Batman"
10.content: *The Dark Knight* (2008), directed by Christopher Nolan, is a standout in the superhero genre, celebrated for its complex narrative and exceptional performances. The film's portrayal of moral ambiguity and its examination of chaos versus order are both thought-provoking and gripping. Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker is particularly noteworthy, bringing a depth and intensity that significantly enhances the film's impact. The movie's high-octane action sequences, combined with a tightly woven plot and Hans Zimmer's evocative score, create a memorable cinematic experience. *The Dark Knight* stands as a powerful exploration of heroism and villainy, cementing its status as a modern classic.

10.title: One of the greatest films I have ever seen
10.content:
If I had to use one word to describe The Dark Knight it would be one of the following: astounding, incredible, unforgettable, mesmerising, awe-inspiring, masterpiece, unmissable, amazing, gripping, inconceivable, captivating, dizzying, enthralling... And the list of superlatives could go on and on, and these words will probably featuring too much in my review. It's amazing to think that I've been missing out on this hype for about four years, having only just watched it last night (or should I say Knight), it took me a while to sink my teeth into Batman Begins because I thought it was going to be just another naff superhero film, but I actually ended up loving it! After I couldn't wait any longer I snapped The Dark Knight up for the incredible price of £6.00 on blu-ray (that's about $10 I think) and prepared myself to watch it. Although, I was scared that it wasn't going to live up to the hype, it did.

The Dark Knight makes Batman Begins look like kids stuff. It can proudly sit amongst Christopher Nolan's other 5 star masterpieces (Memento, The Prestige, Inception) and make friends with every single one of them. Because Christopher Nolan hasn't created a superhero film, but a straight-up adult crime thriller. It's much more mature than Batman Begins and I was surprised and Begins' maturity, because a superhero film suggests that a hint of slight comic violence or caper is going to be involved (even Begins had the comic idea of crazy gas being poured into the city's drain pipes) but there isn't a single camp feature in The Dark Knight thanks to it being so cemented in reality its unreal!

The Dark Knight is only rated a 12A because of the merchandising that appeals to young children, but I would not let anyone under 12 watch this. Although no blood is seen, the violence is still pretty horrific with an absolutely frightening and truly psychotic villain which children aren't going to take too lightly. The first hour or so is also incredibly intricate and showcases Nolan brothers outstanding writing skills, which kids are not going to understand in the slightest. Even I found it hard to follow and I'm 17 going on 18! So remember parents, just because its got Batman in, doesn't mean its the hyper-camp 60's TV show that you used to watch! This is an adult Batman (and I don't mean that in a weird porn way) it's incredibly dark. The hefty running time of two and a half hours will also make kids restless, however this film suits being an epic and I didn't want it to end!

The action is absolutely mesmerising with some truly unforgettable set-pieces that had my jaw on the floor (The lorry chase sequence was one of the highlights for me) these are heart-pounding action sequences that have an incredible intensity about them because they just feel so real and directed with style! Not only does it make the film unbelievably entertaining to watch, but it makes it utterly captivating and involving, just willing you not to take your eyes off the incredible action that's unfolding. But of course, this isn't just about astounding action sequences (although they do thankfully have a major part) there is also an equally involving and very human story underneath that has you cheering for Batman and cowering from the Joker.

Which brings me on to that little chestnut. Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker is just as legendary as everyone says it is. You might dismiss and think "well they're only saying that because he's dead" but even if he was alive, he wouldn't lose an ounce of respect. He is absolutely terrifying and a captivating character. Most villains have an objective or motive, but the Joker just wants to cause absolute chaos. And he succeeds. He's like a one-man version of 'Project Chaos' from Fight Club, which makes him one of the most compelling and captivating villains of all time. He leaves Batman in the shade, which is fine because he had his time to shine in Batman Begins! The rest of the cast is superb too. Christian Bale again makes a very suitable Batman, Michale Caine and Morgan Freeman are of course as amazing as ever and the character of Rachel is also made much more interesting and deeper, perhaps down to the wonderful Maggie Gyllenhal (is that how you spell it?) who plays her. I also thought that Harvey Dent would be quite a dull character (probably because of his profession) but he actually turned out to be an incredibly emotional character, played with brilliant humanity by Aaron Eckhart (of Conversations With Other Women fame). Dent's transition is brilliant and his make-up is Oscar-winning stuff (you'll see what I mean).

I also have to comment on the incredible music throughout. The score is mesmerising and especially the Joker's theme which really increases the tension and intensity. The music lifts the film straight off the ground just to reaffirm its classic status.

The Dark Knight is just pure escapism. By the end of it you feel as if you've stepped into Gotham City and had a deliciously dark tour of a place that feels too real to be true. It's incredibly entertaining and the dynamic relationship between Batman and the Joker is absolutely enthralling. It's jam-packed with breath-taking and intense action sequences and Christopher Nolan has definitely matured in directing. His direction is jaw-dropping at times and the Ariel shots of the city literally made me gasp in awe. There is also some wonderful moments of smouldering tension as well as iconic scene after iconic scene. Throw in a beautifully intricate script, amazing performances and an ending to die for and you have one truly amazing film. You know a film is good when an ending gives you chills and this one did, and that doesn't happen too often. I can't wait to see The Dark Knight Rises! (hopefully soon!)
