9.title: Puts the "Dark" in Dark Knight
9.content:
In a summer of comic book movies, deciding which one was the best is a hard task. So far we have been treated to film adaptations of Iron Man, The Incredible Hulk and a Hellboy sequel, all of which were very good. The Dark Knight makes the decision even harder.

Christopher Nolan's sequel to the already excellent Batman Begins is better than the original, better than all four Burton/Schumaker films combined, and better than other comic book films such as every Superman movie ever made. Christian Bale returns as the Caped Crusader, reprising the role that made him a star. Bale once again blows us all away as he makes Michael Keaton look like George Clooney in the Batsuit. However, there is a reason the word "Batman" is not in the title: This movie belongs to not Batman, but the Joker. The late Heath Ledger makes his presence felt in his final film. Compared to Ledger's Joker, Jack Nicholson's portrayal of the Clown Prince of Crime in Tim Burton's 1989 version of Batman is the equivalent of the disaster that was Arnold Schwarzenegger as Mr Freeze in Batman and Robin.

The film picks up a few months after "Begins". Gotham City (a thinly disguised Chicago) is becoming safer thanks to the efforts of Batman, good cop Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman), and new Gotham DA Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart). The real Batman, Bruce Wayne, is facing some problems in social life, much like Peter Parker in Spider Man 2. Dent is currently dating Bruce's childhood sweetheart Rachel Dawes (Maggie Gyllhanall who replaces Katie Holmes). Gotham is suddenly threatened by The Joker, a sadistic killer who wears clown makeup and gets a kick out of torture. When Nicholson did the role, he went for laughs. Ledger does the same. The only difference is when Jack tried to be funny, he did silly things like point a gun with an outrageously long barrel. When Heath tries to be funny he does magic. He makes a pencil disappear! Wanna know how he does it, kids? He puts the pencil on the table, then throws a guy head-on into the pencil! Sir Michael Caine and Morgan Freeman reprise their respective roles as Alfred and Lucius Fox. Both are a couple of the greatest actors we have ever seen, and are not afraid to demonstrate. They both are the voice of reason in Bruce Wayne's crazy brain, and crack out the funny one liners to lighten the mood of this dark film.

Speaking of the film's darkness, it's not a great idea to bring the kiddies to this one. This is darker than all of the previous five and even some adults may be affected by Ledger's death when viewing this film. It's impossible not to think of Heath's passing when he is on screen, and some images seem a bit disturbing due to his death. For example, there is one scene where The Joker hides in a body bag to avoid some rival gangsters.

Ledger, once again, makes this film. Fans, like myself, will love his memorable quotes such as "Why so SERIOUS?" or "Let's put a smile on that face!". However, sometimes Ledger makes his presence felt by not saying a word at all. For example, a scene where The Joker, dressed in as a nurse, blows up a hospital, is made funny in a sick way. Heath simply walks through the crumbling building as explosions go off behind him. After a while they stop. Ledger, makes a few funny faces, messes around with a controller, then casually walks away as the building explodes.

Ledger couldn't have done it without a little help, though. Oldman's Gordon is given a much bigger role in the film, much to the viewer's delight. While everybody loved Oldman is "Begins", "TDK" establishes Gordon as the greatest hero in Gotham not named Batman. Eckhart is great as Dent, and even better as the villainous Two-Face, who Dent becomes when his face is horribly scarred by The Joker. Eckhart makes fans forget about Batman Forever, where Tommy Lee Jones completely butchered the part.

Sadly, though, the film is not without its few flaws. Gyllanhall has no chemistry on screen with anyone, not even Bale. Katie Holmes is, surprisingly, missed. Caine is very good, but his role is made smaller in this film. And finally, one of the things that made "Begins" so good was Cillian Murphy's Scarecrow. Sadly, Scarecrow makes only a quick appearance that has almost nothing to do with the plot. He is, however, spared, leaving Scarecrow fans, like myself, hopeful.

Overall, The Dark Knight makes us love the comic book film even more. It also gives us a tragic reminder...we are Definitely going to miss Heath Ledger.

9.title: Greatest movie of 2008 but certainly not the greatest movie ever.
9.content:
This comes from the logical side of my brain-the one which tells me that despite all the excitement and how great this movie is, it should not have replaced The Godfather on IMDb's list.

Godfather is iconic, I don't think comparisons should even be made with Godfather and The Dark Knight. I think The Dark Knight is a stand out movie for it's genre and Heath Ledger's performance was brilliant but the movie was not perfect. Everyone else held their own in the movie but that was it.

The movie wasn't perfect-Two face was poorly developed. His transition from "white knight" to an evil guy was just too sudden for me. And I hated how everyone kept stating their intentions in the movie verbally over and over again-that includes The Joker too. 9.title: A Great Epic
9.content:
What I still like after seeing it a couple of times at home is that Christopher Nolan created in cinema what comic fans appreciate in the drawn medium : a sense of continuity. Wayne Manor is still under reconstruction, the Dark Knight has already profoundly left his mark on Gotham, Lieutenant Gordon slowly ascends to Commissioner. But please, give me your light on this : how come he has not confronted the Joker face to face in the one year interval separating the end scenes with the Joker card in Batman Begins from the beginning of TDK ? Given his determination to eradicate crime, such a long wait seems strange. Fans already told everything on TDK so I would just like to express a personal interpretation of what makes such a rare quality in the superhero films genre. The secret resides in Christopher Nolan's pertinent treatment of redundant themes in the Batman's myth.

1) Batman's influence. "You have changed things", says the Joker. There is no coming back, the mantle of the bat has already inspired a large bunch of copycats and given hope to many citizens, he is already an essential part of the city. His legend is firmly installed. But the influence of Batman also brings the egg and chicken question : does Batman exist to stop the criminal element or is it because of his work that criminals as imposing and theatrical as he arise ? The Burmese story of Alfred gives as an echo to the intrigue an interesting point of view on the Joker. He embodies in evil what Batman embodies in good, his pleasure and criminal energy feed on destruction rather than material possessions. A super terrorist, "agent of chaos" as he defines himself. This confrontation breeds doubt in Batman : is it right to burn the whole forest to get rid of one single malignant element ?

2) Batman's ambivalence. He bends the law a little to pursue his quest for justice until one small problem comes : what if he had to break his whole code of morality in the face of madness ? The Joker's interrogation and the violation of privacy through phones show Batman resorting to a certain dose of fascism, that is why fans like him, because he is human and sometimes gets reactionary. He does not always remain the boyscout Superman or friendly neighborhood Spiderman. The story of Two-Face appears in a somewhat shorter version compared to that of the comics, nevertheless with ingenuity. Dent could have been the true hero, "the White Knight", he became instead what Batman could have become if desperation had taken over after his parent's murder : a criminal. Everyone ends in frustration, morally stained with a load of mental tortures in their heads. This is the Batman spirit.

The general critical appreciation largely complete the commercial and deserved success of the film. With the present Batman Begins and Dark Knight diptych, Nolan achieved what Burton didn't, and probably didn't want to : a solid base for a movie serial. Let's hope he will keep his writing and directing quality for the further installments.

9.title: Stunning.
9.content:
I awarded this film 9/10 because I just can't endorse this film being the #1 film of all time.

However, it's one of the most satisfying theatrical experiences i've ever undergone. It's actually incredible what Nolan's achieved with this film. Batman Begins was terrific, and i'd insist on seeing that before The Dark Knight as it repositions the Batman character from a campy one-dimensional characateur to a complex, fascinating, credible and multi-dimensional subject. Having established the core elements of this character with BB, the Dark Knight is a terrific bit of character exposition bound up in one of the best action movies i've ever seen.

The Joker was apparently always intended to be the anti-Batman. Nolan really explores that in this film. Harvey Dent and Gotham City serve as metaphors and Litmus tests for the 'Good/Evil' dichotomy that are central. The grotesque nature of all the characters is handled so superbly, that you forget this is an adaptation of a comic and almost suggests the comics themselves should be revisited as serious pieces of literature. This film surpasses the comic book ethic and becomes more like a modern Shakespearean Tragedy. The genius of it is that it works as a comic book adaptation (with satisfying sincerity to the subject matter) but also works as an independent study. Realistically, there are better character studies out there, but those tend to be those that focus all energy on that study, at the expense of satisfying the other other requirements of film.

This contains some of the best action, effects, set-pieces that i've seen in a film. Some of the heist scenes and chase scenes beat anything i've seen elsewhere. Most heist movies fall into the trap of being contrived, smug and pseudo-unpredictable (e.g. Ocean's 11). This one feels like something conceived of a reckless mind. The film's sequences really feel the product of an impulsive and reckless psychopath and adeptly cultivates the feeling of impotence of the hero. Brilliant. The Joker genuinely feels like an invulnerable nemesis. As an action movie this is really outstanding. There is some terrific violent scenes and stunts that will delight any thrill junkie, and there was no overdependance on CGI.

The script was impeccable and i'm sure will work with all levels of viewer without being patronising. The performances were terrific. Bale and Ledger steal the show, though the latter really is brilliant. Watching this you get a real sense of shame that you won't ever see him reprise the role. Ledger is absolutely magnetic. Hilarious, terrifying, menacing but also tragic. He really does blow Jack Nicholson out of the water and the third time you see him on screen you'll feel nostalgic about his loss. The supporting cast are exemplary (I was impressed by Eckhart too, having previously written him off), and you get the same quality performance from the likes of Oldman, Freeman etc. as you'd expect.

The cinematography is superb. I saw this on the IMAX (do so if you can) and it was stunning, the relevance of the film aided by the portrayal of a real Gotham. The pace and plot are terrific and keep you gripped for the duration. There is also a healthy dose of humour and social commentary that is all impressively appropriate. Even the soundtrack is absolutely on point.

I can't hail this as the best film i've ever seen, but it so so good and if the next can improve on this, then that may well have a justified claim. It's a true shame that Ledger as Joker won't be involved.

9.title: Almost Perfect
9.content:
Heath Ledger's greatest performance is also his last. What a terrible shame. He stole this movie away from the powerhouse Christian Bale - who never shone brighter than he did in Batman Begins - and the tremendous understated Gary Oldman. Aaron Eckhardt is also a great talent and was a surprising treat as Harvey Dent. There was almost nothing wrong with this film.

But I think it was too long. At least, I'm pretty sure it was.

I honestly thought the show was over when the Joker was apprehended the first time and was very satisfied with that ending. But it was only half way finished.

Don't get me wrong, there was nothing wrong with the 2nd half, either. It was good storytelling, deeply thoughtful psychodrama, and filled with amazing action. So, why not make two movies out of it? Then we could have savored the legacy of the late Heath Ledger that much more.

9.title: Stunning
9.content:
In my opinion, the best Batman movie and the best comic-book adaptation ever. Mature, engaging and complex. Shades of Frank Miller's work and nods to Batman's darker origins as envisaged by Bob Kane.

I love the character contrasts in this movie. Alfred is a great foil for Bruce Wayne. Gordon is a great foil for Harvey Dent.

The movie has its roots in comics, so I can forgive the occasional lapse in realism - the 'skyhook' rescue - and it all looks spectacular and I never expected realism in the first place.

Performance wise, the movie is hard to fault. From 'Zeus' as one of the prisoners - surprisingly good, to Eric Roberts - again, surprisingly good, through to the leads. A million other people will comment on Heath Ledger, so I won't go on too much about him, but he is stunningly brilliant. A twitching, clicking, off the wall performance. My favourite scene? The Joker leaning out the cop car window and all you hear is the wind rushing past him. Absolutely captures the Joker's anarchic world.

Christian Bale captures the struggle of Batman's dark side and his faith in humanity wonderfully. Tortured but ultimately good.

Christopher Nolan wisely chooses not to overplay the gore. There is plenty of violence but not much blood. Sometimes things are best left 'suggested' rather than graphically displayed. This may have been done for rating purposes, but for me, it works.

A superb piece of cinema.

9.title: Did Ledger Deserve All The Accolades? Oh yes!
9.content:
Batman is back. And so is director Christoperh Nolan who directed the amazing BATMAN BEGINS. As someone who thoroughly enjoyed Nolan's previous Batman film, I felt confident he'd never be able to surpass it. I was horribly wrong.

The dark sets. The amazing acting (with one exception). The wonderful dialogue. It was a sheer joy to watch. And the fact that it was 152 minutes long didn't bother me in the slightest. The action was practically nonstop with enough plot twists, explosions, and funny lines to make one cringe and laugh at the same time.

The big question, though, on many people's minds (including my own before I watched it) was "Is Heath Ledger's performance that good or are the critics just being nice after Ledger's unfortunate death?" Hollywood has a history of doing this where they honor someone for an achievement that really wasn't deserved, but they felt sorry for the performer's family, etc. and decided to throw them a bone by overly-praising a performance or a life that wasn't particularly notable. I was concerned that this might be the case for Ledger's Joker. But my worries were immediately stripped away as soon as The Joker made his appearance. Creepy. Funny. Line delivery that'll blow your mind ("See, I'm not a monster...I'm just ahead of the curve."). Ledger's performance put all others in his shadow (yes that includes Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Aaron Eckhart and Gary Oldman).

Christian Bale (3:10 TO YUMA) has now become synonymous with what Batman means to movie-goers and comic book fans alike. He plays the cocky, rich, and uncompromising Bruce Wayne with the perfect amount of grace and toughness the role deserves. The only downside is his heavily whispered Batman voice that grates on the nerves after a short while.

Michael Caine (CHILDREN OF MEN) and Gary Oldman (HARRY POTTER) reprise their roles and do so with the talent we've all come to expect from these two fine actors. Morgan Freeman (GONE BABY GONE) returns as Lucius Fox, Batman's weapons designer and conscious. Although not particularly riveting, his performance did help move the plot along.

An addition to the cast was introduced with the arrival of Harvey Dent/Two-Face (Aaron Eckhart, CONVERSATIONS WITH OTHER WOMEN). Exquisitely incorporated into the story, the uncovering of Two-Face's origins is masterfully pulled into the story and given ample screen time.

The only less-than-stellar performance came from Maggie Gyllenhaal (STRANGER THAN FICITON) who replaced Katie Holmes (FIRST DAUGHTER) in the role of Rachel Dawes, Bruce Wayne's love interest. Although no fan of Katie Holmes, I found Gyllenhaal's performance to be relatively unmoving in comparison to the rest of the cast. That's probably not a knock against Gyllenhaal considering the entire production held some of the strongest roles I've seen this year. But no one came close to Ledger and his wonderful performance, least of all Gyllenhaal.

If you're looking for the action film of the year with one of the best performances by an actor that is no longer with us, The Dark Knight is the ticket. No Jokin'.

9.title: A dark vision almost perfect
9.content:
While I write this I'm still immensely impressed with the forcefulness of this film, there are really few action or adventure movies that will create what "The Dark Knight" gets in just a few minutes, and that is to bring the climax of emotions with a script that is strengthened in each of its lines and with an edition that frame after frame doesn't exist any wastage. Anything that we had heard about this film before its premiere, all these positive comments that the criticism launched after having seen it, all the positive references are true, very true.

To begin with, the action sequences are a visual choreography, in each one's emotions are as much as possible, because not only are loaded by a perfect use of special effects, explosions and an audio editing forceful, but also because Bale, and Heath Ledger above all, build two characters who represent two sides of the coin and their clashes are so catastrophic that makes everything a witness from the edge of the seat.

And is that really the performances are at the level of what anyone could expect, but definitely this is the film of The Joker. Either that, including me, thought that no one could deprive the best interpretation of this murderer to Jack Nicholson, really we have our mouths open to the strength, vitality and terror that manages to combine Ledger villain in this, I confess at times was too crazy up to me, and that is what succeeds, it succeeds really that you think that this man is a man without any kind of moral questioning, everything for him is a macabre game.

So Joker works well because it also has a dramatic, dark and vertiginous screenplay that unfolds quickly to each of the characters and at the same time, for that speed with which everything happens, forcing the viewer to be attentive to each of the sequences, each of the planes, and the richness of this script is that even if it is full of action is also an ode about a moral antihero, that make you think about the various faces of good and evil, and leads to comic character to a much more psychological level, reflected whenever Joker and Batman exchange lines, and which culminates with a hopeful end even when circumstances suggest quite the opposite and balance between the two sides of the coin has been broken. That's because the script is really something worthwhile, for all Batman, The Joker, Harvey Dent and James Gordon mean and represent.

The film is not an idealistic and beautiful portrait of a hero, is a dark film about a man who loads a weight of being a hero that nobody wants, is the battle of a man in front of the chaos, is the fascination of anarchy and violence and hope that lies even after the cataclysm. Yes, it has its errors of continuity, some holes in the plot, but not all opaque this marvelous film. This is a great film in a genre in which there seemed no room for maturity, for the visual beauty that has made the best Batman film.

9.title: The Dark Knight review
9.content:
I have looked forward to this movie for about a year, and with it being my most anticipated movie ever, i was expecting a roller coaster ride of emotion, chaos and anarchy... I got it all and more.

Heath Ledger's performance is nothing short of brilliant. When he's on screen, hes amazing, and when he's off screen, you want him back. Thats how good he is in the film. I did however, think they could have had The Joker in the film a bit more.

Christian Bale is very good as Batman, but tries a bit too hard on the Bruce Wayne character. Maggie gyllenhaul is better than Katie Holmes period, although she wasn't as involved in the crime fighting as Katie Holmes' was.

Aaron Eckhart was a perfect choice for Harvey Dent, and you could tell throughout the film that he had a dark side, especially when he had a few angry outbursts at Gordon and Batman.

In conclusion, I've never seen a film travel so fast, considering its a 2.5 hour movie. It fells like 1.5 hours!! It is very well written with many memorable quotes..

The highlights for me in the film were: The Joker's meeting with the mob bosses, and for that split second when Gamble calls him crazy - Joker's reply is priceless!! The Bat Pod chase to the Joker was amazing, along with the hospital scene with a bit of dark comedy..

Ledger carried this film, and without him, i wouldn't have the satisfaction i have now for this great film, SEE THIS FILM NOW!!

9.title: "The Dark Knight" - A Masterpiece of Modern Cinema
9.content: This film is more than just a superhero story; it's a complex, dark, and thought-provoking exploration of the human psyche and the consequences of choices. Heath Ledger's unforgettable portrayal of the Joker alone makes this film worth watching. The film's plot is brilliantly constructed, offering a gritty and realistic take on Gotham City, plagued by crime and corruption. Batman, played by Christian Bale, is at the center of the conflict, grappling with the moral dilemmas that come with his vigilante persona. The late Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of iconic. Ledger's performance is chilling, and his unpredictable, anarchic character is a perfect foil to Batman's moral code.

9.title: An exceptional super hero film that defines it genre and is praiseworthy as a film in general.

9.title: The Dark Knight is a must-watch.
9.content:
The Dark Knight (2008), directed by Christopher Nolan, is a masterful superhero film that redefined the genre. The movie follows Bruce Wayne (Christian Bale) as Batman, battling the chaos unleashed by the anarchic Joker, brilliantly portrayed by Heath Ledger. The film explores themes of morality, justice, and the fine line between heroism and vigilantism.

With a gripping plot, stunning cinematography, and an unforgettable performance by Ledger, who won a posthumous Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor, The Dark Knight delivers intense action and emotional depth. It remains a landmark in cinematic storytelling, praised for its complex characters and thought-provoking narrative.

9.title: The first Dark Superhero I ever watch.
9.content:
A thunderbolt is going to blast through the blanket of mediocrity known as summer movies. The Dark Knight, Christopher Nolan's stunning follow-up to 2005's Batman Begins, is a forceful provocation disguised as a comic-book film. Check. Fierce action. Check. Awe-inspiring spectacle? Check. Devilish amusement? Check. But Nolan is just getting started. In this imaginative cosmos, there's something raw and primordial at work.

Nolan departs from his Batman origin narrative to explore a deeper level. Huh? Wha? How can a troubled man in a bat costume and a villain with a cracked, painted-on clown smile speak to the core of the human condition? Just brace yourself for a jolt to the system. The Dark Knight creates a place where good and evil, instead of fighting, opt to get it on and dance. "I don't want to kill you," the crazed Joker, played by Heath Ledger, tells Christian Bale's sturdy Batman. "You complete me." Don't fall for the ruse. He truly believes it.

The problem is that Batman, a.k.a. Playboy Bruce Wayne, has had it with playing the knight in shining armour up to this point. He's furious that the public perceives him as a vigilante. He'll leave the heroics to district attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) and prevent the DA from pursuing Rachel Dawes (feisty Maggie Gyllenhaal, filling in for lovely Katie Holmes), Batman's sole hope for a normal life.

Bale plays the Joker as a fallible human crusader at war with his own conscience. Cinematic finesse rivals Michael Mann's Heat for action that rivals Heat.

I can only speak in superlatives about Ledger's performance as the Joker, who is insanely great. In contrast to Jack Nicholson's generally amusing portrayal of the character in Tim Burton's 1989 Batman, Ledger takes the part into the shadows, where even the comedic is rarely a respite. Ledger's face is caked with rotten makeup, highlighting the crimson scar of a grin, the scruffy hair, and the decaying teeth of a dog straight from hell. A knife, rather than a gun, is preferred by the clown prince of crime, who prefers to "savor the moment."

Batman vs Joker, Yin vs Yang, silent fury vs uncontrolled chaos, the Dark Knight vs the unorganised mastermind.

The precedence and merit of this film, beyond the brilliant screenplay and excellent acting, can be further shown by the insane marketing that was surrounding this film. With such passionate marketing, we form a more personal and interesting bond with the trilogy and the franchise overall.

Christian Bale, despite being on the front cover of the film, merely occupies the protagonist role all throughout the film. So much so we aren't even conditioned to fully applaud and commend his performance as legendary compared to another performer... Bale's Batman is good and does a great job in swapping dualities Bruce Wayne and Batman through tonality, personality and mannerisms. Though despite all that, he is overshadowed by Heath Ledger's Joker.

Earlier before, Ledger is the performer I was referring to that played the antagonist and main character of this film. 9.title: Amazing and Compelling
9.content:
Theatres are finally back open again! To celebrate I had a lot of choices. But I decided I should go back to a film I hadn't liked as much as the general public the first time I saw it. I had seen the opening scene on YouTube a few weeks ago and I wanted to see it on the big screen and well... yeah it didn't disappoint. A lot of the times for me a movie either has enough action for me to forget about the characters or enough character depth for me to care about everyone. This is one of the rare and I truly do mean rare occasions where neither of those things happens because they both blend together so well. The depth behind Bruce Wayne in this film is amazing. Because while in Batman Begins he has to fight against his own morals and such in this movie he has a lot more resting on his shoulders. He has the entire city of Gotham looking up to him as Batman and he still has his own feelings about Rachel that he is fighting against.

The score and camera work in this movie are both done well. Knowing the outcome of certain characters and watching it again really helps you to appreciate it more, pay attention to what the film shows you and you will appreciate it. It all does pay off. The score of the film really surprised me. While on the first watch I was focussing on the action on this watch I was focused on character interactions. The chemistry between Christian Bale and Michael Caine is phenomenal. I also like how in this movie they show off parts of Bruce Waynes intelligence and his problem-solving.

My problems with this movie are few but sadly they are enough to keep it from that 10/10 rating I was hoping to give it. There are a few spots where the CGI and sound design are off. It's not consistently enough to ruin the movie or anything like that but I did personally notice it. I also feel like the rising action in the middle of the film was better than the ending. While the ending does leave you with more of a philosophical thing I did think that the action in the middle wasn't topped by anything else in the film. There are also a few tiny plausibility errors here and there but it is after all still a superhero movie so it's not like I'm going to be screaming my head off about it. Overall I liked it a slight bit more on a secondary watch, happy that theatres are open again

9.title: "Some men just want to watch the world burn!"
9.content:
The Dark Knight (2008)-

As with 'Batman Begins' the first ten minutes hooks you in properly and with far more effect than the "Other" four. And it's hard not to compare these newer incarnations with those first films, because they were just so bad and these new ones aren't at all.

It's a shame that with 'Batman Vs Superman' (2016) and 'Justice League' (2017) it looks as if they're going back to a more cartoon like style.

We will have to see what Robert Pattinson's portrayal offers in 2022, but I don't expect much.

And it's odd to think that I didn't bother with the Christopher Nolan three when they were released, because of my distaste for Mr Bale. However, he surprised me so much, but then I do wonder whether the films would have been just as successful with another actor, as long as the production and direction was the same. I don't wish to take anything away from him, because I really do rate these films and his version of the "Knight", but my mind likes to ponder things sometimes. Who else could have done the stories the same justice or more?

What's also good about this film, as well as it's predecessor, is how they were actually about Batman, where the previous films didn't really achieve that and yet that focus still didn't diminish the inclusion of The Joker and the story of Harvey Dent, who both appeared.

The series so far has been cleverly conceived, because they established the title character properly in 'Batman Begins' (2005), so this second film was able to show him at his best, having learned his lessons. It pitted him against The Joker, who was shown effectively and appropriately, in a new, but ideal style.

The origin of Harvey Dent was also thoughtfully portrayed too. You can really see how he changed and why, unlike that God awful representation of him in 'Batman Forever' (1995). Aaron Eckhart probably doesn't get enough praise for his performance, so overshadowed as he was by the films main villain and the subsequent publicity of their real life demise, but he does do justice to his role as well.

The fact that The Joker was played superbly by Heath Ledger can never be in question. He really brought something fantastic to the role and proved that some people just get their kicks causing trouble for no reason but their own amusement. He was perfect in the role as far as I'm concerned. A tad Jack Nicholson and a bit of Cesar Romero, but with that darkness that the "Nolan" Batman films all have. And I think that is what makes them more believable, yet still comic book in their own way.

It's such a shame that Heath died, as he could really have gone far, not only with this character, but in films in general. He certainly left on a high!

I do like Fox too. Played by the super cool Morgan Freeman. He was a new character for me and may have appeared in the comics, but I don't know. Either way, I think that he was a good addition to the films and in this one he came in to it a bit more. His characters presence seemed to answer some of the questions about the gadgets in use, done in a "Q" from 'James Bond' kind of way. It's bits like this that improve a film. I hate it when the hero can just knock up a quick weapon all of a sudden, but Fox's resources and skills add to the films and the gadgets credibility.

The replacement of Katie Holmes with Maggie Gyllenhall was a good choice too, as they are so similar I barely noticed. They also didn't get too hung up on the romance and make things unnecessarily soppy. Knowing that he has something to fight for is enough.

I also like the fact that they addressed the mobility issues with the suit, again it added to the credibility. It's like they listened to the fans and critics and adjusted, to fix what might have been wrong before, although he still seemed to struggle to speak when wearing the head piece.

There are only a couple of elements that didn't work for me. At the end of the party for instance, it was left a bit open as to what happened, which was untidy. There was another bit too, but I've forgotten it, which means that it can't have been that important and I'm just nit picking.

This series as a whole was made to be so much darker and scarier, which I believe was the right choice. It's actually really tense too and had me rapt with attention. The only thing that I would criticise properly is that this one was a bit long, but I'm really not sure where it could have been cut?

It's such a clever story, but maybe there were a few too many good ideas and some could have been saved for another film, although they're all delivered well and appropriately to the story and again I wouldn't know which one to cut out, because they did all work so well.

It's just that a lot of things happen in just one film. If I'd watched it at the cinema, I might have missed the end, because I wouldn't have been able to sit for that long without a wee.

A lot of people would favour this one over "Begins", but although the Joker is iconic here and brilliantly mad, I think the origin story of Batman himself just wins as the best of this trilogy. This one is not far behind and still scores highly though.

900.55/1000.

9.title: A Complex and Intelligent Movie that is not so much a Superhero Movie as it is a Noir-Thriller
9.content:
Many hold this in regard as the best superhero-movie of all time, and has given other movies in this genre the biggest shoes ever to fill. I myself believe that to be kind of unfair, since this is not what I would immediately classify as a superhero-movie, simply because it has Batman in it. Because Nolan is such a master at mixing intelligent themes and high-quality entertainment together, he took one of the most iconic superheroes in history and made him a human being in a realistic world, where nothing really is to over the top: no doomsday-devices or superpowers, just a masked vigilante who needs to combat organized crime and the anarchy within the very people he fights for to protect them. He and David S Goyer wrote a complex and layered script with deep characters, and made one of the darkest and well-made crime-noir movies I have ever seen(and I don't even like that genre)

Acting:

Christian Bale continues to prove that he is a fantastic actor, with a subtle and laid-back performance as Bruce Wayne and a harsh and brutal portrayal of a struggling Caped Crusader. This is not his best role, not by a long shot, but I can imagine that Ben Affleck was pretty nervous to replace this man.

Heath Ledger, what more can we say about his real that hasn't already been said? In his final role, he delivered one of the most impressive method-acting roles you will ever encounter, with all odd mannerisms, a creepy voice and laugh, and an enigmatic character that steals every scene. Oscar was well deserved.

Aaron Eckhart was the absolute surprise of this movie. Given how few good movies the guy has actually been in, it is a relief and a shame at the same time that he will only be remembered for this role. He gives a down-to-earth, sassy and yet intense performance as a white knight who falls into the abyss of insanity. I believed Bruce Wayne when he said that with a man like Aaron's character, his Batman would no longer be needed.

Gary Oldman's role as Jim Gordon gets expanded in this sequel, showing a grim and hard-working commissioner who suffers just as much from the consequenses of underestimating the Joker as the other protagonists. The man gives a great performance.

Maggie Gyllenhaal as Rachel is a slight improvement over Katie Holmes, who wasn't very interesting in Batman Begins, but still her character feels like little more than the damsel in distress, and the few words of wisdom and advice that she gives are not nearly enough to compensate for her lack of likability.

Veteran Actors like Morgan Freeman and Michael Caine play their part, and they do it well. I can't help but miss the emotional core that was much more present in Batman Begins with these two characters. The sound of their soothing deep voices is enough though to appreciate every scene that they are in.

Direction: Christopher Nolan always has a very clear vision and approach to his movies, and this firm grip is visible throughout the entire movie. The tension and weight is felt in every scene, and even the more lighthearted moments are handled very well.

Cinematography: Wally Pfister, who has worked with Nolan on multiple occasions, has switched drastically in style when compared to Batman Begins. The muddy, brown aesthetic of Gotham in that movie has been replaced with a moody grey, while still maintaining the dark shadowy feel that is associated with Batman. The dialogue scenes in particular are shot very well on steady-cam, and draw your attention immediately. Overall, this is great work.

Music: Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard collaborate for a second time for a Batman Movie, and Hans brought a harsher and more electronical element into the score. The old themes from Batman Begins are still there, but more expanded, and with a harrowing theme for the Joker that sets you on edge the more you hear it pop up. As a score to listen to without the movie, it isn't that solid, but it is essential to the atmosphere of this picture and Zimmer and Howard should receive high praise for this.

Plot: David S Goyer and Nolan wrote a complex and dark movie that can become confusing if not careful. That being said, the execution is brilliantly done, with many twists and turns, and surprisingly relevant questions are brought to light.

Editing: This ties directly into the plot, and is the main reason why this movie succeeds so well in its execution: because of the complex structure, good editing is necessary, and Lee Smith absolutely delivered in that department. Particulary the scene transitions after powerful emotional moments are exceptionally well done.

Sound: The old sounds from Batman Begins are back, including Batmobile and gadgets, and now also including the high-speed humm of the Batpod and the unique-sounding explosions that you don't really come across in other movies. It is not outstanding, but very pleasant for your ears.

Production Design: Even though the setting of this movie appears quite normal, Nathan Crowley spend an extraordinary amount of detail on the sets and props, making them all feel realistic and Gotham like a real city.

Costumes&Make-up: Batman's dark suit is the best version yet, picturing Batman as a frightening and looming presence without the need to move a muscle. The Joker is exactly what you'd imagine he would look like. So, perfect.

VFX: Nolan uses cgi as little as possible, which is a rarity nowadays, and the major exception is Two-Face. Like Inception, Nolan aims for the perfect blend of digital and the real thing, and when you look at the horrifying imagery, it is really hard to believe that it is not real. Chapeau!

Tone: The darkest Batman movie thus far, largely in thanks to the Joker and his schemes, which have such gruesome consequences that the desperation and fear easily carries over from the screen to the audience. The tension is masterfully handled throughout scenes, and a scene in an interrogation room particulary transcends it to a whole new level.

Overall Concensus:

While not all characters and actors are as charismatic as they should be, Heath Ledger and the complex script, together with masterful editing and direction, elevate Nolan as one of the best filmmakers working today.

As an adaptation it's not accurate one but as a movie it's stand above everything .

The Dark Knight is a 2008 superhero film directed by Christopher Nolan from a screenplay he co-wrote with his brother Jonathan. The film is based on the DC Comics superhero Batman, is the sequel to Batman Begins (2005) and the second installment in The Dark Knight Trilogy. The plot follows vigilante Batman, police lieutenant James Gordon, and district attorney Harvey Dent who form an alliance to dismantle organized crime in Gotham City. Their efforts are derailed by Joker, an anarchistic mastermind who seeks to test how far Batman will go to save the city from complete chaos. The ensemble cast includes Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Heath Ledger, Gary Oldman, Aaron Eckhart, Maggie Gyllenhaal, and Morgan Freeman.

Warner Bros. Pictures prioritized a sequel following the successful reinvention of the Batman film series with Batman Begins. Nolan and Batman Begins co-writer David S. Goyer developed the story elements, making Dent the central protagonist and tragic hero who is caught up in the battle between Batman and Joker. In writing the screenplay, the Nolans were influenced by 1980s Batman comics and crime-drama films, and sought to continue Batman Begins' heightened reality tone. From April to November 2007, filming took place with a $185 million budget in Chicago and Hong Kong, and on sets in England. The Dark Knight was the first major motion picture to be filmed with high-resolution IMAX cameras. Nolan avoided using computer-generated imagery unless necessary, insisting on practical stunts including the flipping of an 18-wheel truck and the blowing-up of a factory.

9.title: "The Dark Knight" (2008), directed by Christopher Nolan, stands as a monumental achievement in the superhero genre and transcends its comic book origins to become a cinematic
9.content:
The film is a thrilling and complex exploration of the thin line between justice and chaos, anchored by an outstanding performance from Heath Ledger as the iconic Joker.

Nolan's vision is evident from the opening sequence, a bank heist masterfully orchestrated by the Joker. The film immediately establishes a tone of tension and unpredictability that persists throughout. Gotham City is depicted as a gritty and corrupt metropolis on the brink, plagued by organized crime and a desperate need for a savior.

Christian Bale reprises his role as Bruce Wayne/Batman, embodying the character with a brooding intensity. The film delves deeper into the psychological toll of being a masked vigilante, exploring the internal struggles of Wayne as he grapples with the consequences of his actions. Bale's performance adds a layer of vulnerability to Batman, making him more relatable and human.

Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of legendary. Ledger's commitment to the role, coupled with his chillingly charismatic delivery, elevates the character to new heights. The Joker's anarchic philosophy and sadistic sense of humor make him one of the most compelling and memorable villains in cinematic history. Ledger posthumously received an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor, a testament to the impact of his performance.

The film's moral complexity is exemplified through the character of Harvey Dent, portrayed by Aaron Eckhart. The transformation of the charismatic district attorney into the vengeful and disfigured Two-Face is a tragic and thought-provoking narrative arc. It challenges the notion of heroism and explores the corrupting influence of chaos on even the noblest intentions.

Nolan's direction is masterful, utilizing practical effects and immersive cinematography to create a visually stunning experience. The action sequences, including the now-iconic chase scenes, are choreographed with precision and intensity. The film's score, composed by Hans Zimmer, further enhances the atmosphere, contributing to the overall immersive experience.

"The Dark Knight" is not merely a superhero film; it's a crime drama and a character study that delves into the complexities of human nature. It raises philosophical questions about morality, justice, and the consequences of one's choices. The film's impact on the genre is undeniable, influencing subsequent superhero films to aspire to greater depth and sophistication.

In conclusion, "The Dark Knight" is a cinematic triumph that transcends its genre. With a compelling narrative, exceptional performances, and groundbreaking direction, it remains a benchmark for superhero films. Christopher Nolan's vision, coupled with Ledger's unforgettable performance, cements "The Dark Knight" as a timeless classic that continues to captivate audiences and shape the landscape of modern cinema.

9.title: DARK KNIGHT

The Joker, however, has a deadly plan that will bring tragic consequences for Harvey Dent, Batman aka Bruce Wayne and Rachel, the love of Bruce Wayne's life who has fallen for Harvey Dent.

Because of this and other problems, the movie's last 20 minutes are tedious. Also, the Joker character does not change, so it becomes monotonous watching him on the screen. 9.title: NOLAS IS A GENIUS!

"Batman: The Dark Knight" is an absolute masterpiece that transcends the superhero genre and stands as one of the greatest cinematic achievements of all time.

One of the most remarkable aspects of this film is Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker. Ledger's portrayal of the iconic villain is nothing short of mesmerizing. He completely disappears into the character, delivering a chilling and unforgettable performance. Ledger's Joker is chaotic, unpredictable, and utterly compelling. His every scene is a masterclass in acting, and it's no surprise that he posthumously won an Academy Award for his role.

Christian Bale continues to excel as Bruce Wayne/Batman. His brooding intensity and unwavering commitment to the role make him one of the most compelling Batman interpretations to date. Bale's dedication to his craft is evident in every scene, and he brings a complex depth to the character.

Aaron Eckhart's portrayal of Harvey Dent/Two-Face is another standout performance. His transformation from a principled district attorney to a vengeful and disfigured villain is handled with nuance and skill. It's a tragic arc that adds emotional weight to the film.

The film's screenplay, penned by Christopher Nolan and his brother Jonathan Nolan, is a triumph of storytelling. It weaves together multiple plot threads, themes of morality, chaos, and the nature of heroism, and keeps the audience on the edge of their seats from start to finish. The dialogue is sharp and thought-provoking, and the pacing is impeccable.

Visually, "The Dark Knight" is a treat for the eyes. Wally Pfister's cinematography captures the dark and gritty atmosphere of Gotham City perfectly. The action sequences are thrilling, and the practical effects add a level of authenticity that is often missing in contemporary blockbusters.

Hans Zimmer's score is another standout element of the film. The haunting and iconic theme for the Joker perfectly complements the character's chaos and unpredictability. Zimmer's music elevates the tension and emotion of the film to another level.

In addition to its technical and artistic achievements, "The Dark Knight" explores deep philosophical and moral questions. It challenges the audience to consider the blurred lines between hero and villain, the nature of human morality, and the consequences of one's actions.

In conclusion, "Batman: The Dark Knight" is a cinematic masterpiece that transcends the superhero genre. Ledger's performance as the Joker is legendary, and the film's storytelling, acting, and technical elements are top-notch. It's a thought-provoking and exhilarating experience that continues to captivate audiences years after its release. Christopher Nolan's contribution to the Batman mythos is nothing short of extraordinary, and "The Dark Knight" remains a timeless classic.

9.title: A Dark and Riveting Masterpiece
9.content:
Uilding upon the foundations laid in Batman Begins, Nolan takes the Batman mythos to new heights in The Dark Knight. The film centers around the battle between the masked vigilante, Batman (Christian Bale), and the anarchic and enigmatic Joker (Heath Ledger). Their clash of ideologies and relentless pursuit of their goals drives the film's tension and propels the story forward.

Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of mesmerizing. His performance is a haunting and immersive tour de force that earned him a posthumous Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. Ledger's Joker is a chaotic force of nature, embodying anarchy and unpredictability, leaving an indelible mark on the audience's psyche.

Christian Bale delivers a brooding and introspective performance as Batman, grappling with the moral complexities of his dual identity. Bale's portrayal captures Batman's inner turmoil and his unwavering dedication to justice, even in the face of immense personal sacrifice.

Nolan's direction is impeccable, crafting a visually stunning and emotionally charged Gotham City. The film's gritty realism is enhanced by the use of practical effects and Nolan's signature style of grounded storytelling. The action sequences are expertly choreographed and provide a visceral experience that keeps viewers on the edge of their seats.

The Dark Knight's screenplay, written by Christopher Nolan and his brother Jonathan Nolan, is a testament to intelligent and thought-provoking storytelling. The narrative is multilayered, exploring complex themes such as the nature of heroism, the consequences of choice, and the blurred lines between good and evil. These themes are woven seamlessly into the story, elevating the film beyond a mere superhero spectacle.

The film's supporting cast, including Gary Oldman as Commissioner Gordon, Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent/Two-Face, and Michael Caine as Alfred, deliver exceptional performances that enrich the narrative and add depth to the characters. The ensemble cast brings a level of authenticity and emotional weight that further immerses the audience in the film's gripping story.

The Dark Knight is not just a superhero film; it is a psychological thriller that challenges conventions and explores the darkest aspects of the human psyche. It raises profound questions about the nature of heroism and the choices we make when faced with impossible moral dilemmas.

9.title: The struggle between Light and Shadow
9.content: "The Dark Knight" by Christopher Nolan leaves an indelible impression on the cinematic landscape. Guided by Nolan's visionary genius, viewers are transported into a dark and grandiose world, where the battle between good and evil reaches new heights of complexity and drama. The film opens with a spectacular bank heist, serving as a prelude to the epic confrontation between Batman and his most formidable adversary, the Joker, memorably portrayed by Heath Ledger. Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is simply extraordinary. His character is characterized by a sinister madness and a magnetic presence that dominates every scene he appears in. Ledger brings to life a cruel and unpredictable Joker, who embodies chaos and destruction with chilling naturalness. It's hard to look away from this iconic figure of evil, boldly juxtaposed against Batman, portrayed with the usual intensity by Christian Bale. Nolan skillfully blends action and drama, providing an engaging narrative rich in tension. The film offers a profound insight into the psychology of the characters, exploring complex themes such as justice, morality, and ethics in the fight against crime. The presence of characters like Harvey Dent, portrayed by Aaron Eckhart, adds further depth to the plot, highlighting the thin line between good and evil. The action sequences are spectacular, particularly those shot in Imax, which captivate the audience and take them to the edge of their seats. However, Nolan avoids excessive spectacle, always keeping the focus on the characters and their relationships. The nighttime settings of Gotham City, combined with the dark cinematography and evocative soundtrack, contribute to creating a bleak and immersive atmosphere that permeates every scene of the film. Despite its length and excessive media hype, "The Dark Knight" stands out for its ability to entertain and engage the audience. Nolan once again demonstrates his mastery of the genre, offering the audience a captivating and unforgettable cinematic experience. "The Dark Knight" is undoubtedly an extraordinary film that transcends mere entertainment. With its extraordinary performances, compelling plot, and dark, evocative atmosphere, the film stands out as a masterpiece in the superhero film genre. While Ledger's dominant presence may have slightly overshadowed Batman's prominence, the film remains a landmark in contemporary cinema.

9.title: This is how you set a high standard in movies nowadays 9/10
9.content:
Aside of this film being a cult classic, the kind of movies you watch once in your lifetime, enjoy it, and later on watch it 5 more times and love it more and more with every re-watch. The Dark Knight is a movie that in my opinion has set a high standard to movies nowadays and how they should be made.

Either it's Heath Ledger's ultimate performance of a antagonistic, or the structure of the story that plays well, The Dark Knight is the kind of movie I can't find one bad thing to say about it (same case of movies such as The Big Labowski, Back to the Future and A New Hope).

I want to direct you to a YouTube channel called "Lessons From the Screenplay" by Michael Tucker, his channel made a great video analysis on The Dark Knight and its craft of the ultimate antagonistic: how he needs to be powerful, good at attacking the opponent's greatest weakness, compete and fight to achieve the same goal as the hero and so on.

With all that being said, the movie has genuinely shown us what needs to be in a villain to be compelling.

Every other feature in this film is made in such a careful way to perform the best way possible: The composing and soundtrack by Hans Zimmer.

The cinematography in every single shot.

"The Nolan Crosscut" in the third act of the film.

The rest of the cast's performance in this film.

And so on, etc.

Every time I watch this film (and Michael Tucker's analysis). I get goosebumps, I'm thrilled and get excited with every re-watch. It's the kind of movies that have also set a high standard as I mentioned earlier. This movie gives a huge slap in the face to every other mediocre superhero film, and puts in the center subjects much smaller and significant, and grows them to be center elements of a story: character's choices and true colors, chaos vs. Order, sacrifice and endurance, etc.

These elements are so significant and get to be the center of the story, any other movie should embrace this method of taking small things and expanding them.

In conclusion, this is by far the best film in the "superhero" category. But it's not a superhero movie, it's something much more realistic and compelling than having a CGI figure walk through the scene.

If anyone wants to make movies and set themselves a high standard, they should look at The Dark Knight as an example.

9.title: Amazing Movie
9.content:
The Dark Knight, directed by Christopher Nolan, is a masterclass in superhero cinema that transcends its genre to explore complex themes of morality, chaos, and justice. Released in 2008, the film is the second installment in Nolan's Batman trilogy and stands as a landmark achievement in modern filmmaking.

The story picks up after Batman Begins, as Gotham City faces an unprecedented threat from the Joker, portrayed brilliantly by Heath Ledger. Ledger's performance is nothing short of iconic; he embodies chaos itself, delivering a haunting portrayal that blurs the line between madness and genius. His unpredictable antics challenge Batman, played by Christian Bale, forcing the Dark Knight to confront his own ethics and the consequences of his vigilantism.

Nolan's direction is tightly woven, creating a tension that grips the audience from start to finish. The film's pacing is expertly managed, balancing intense action sequences with deeper philosophical inquiries. The cinematography by Wally Pfister captures Gotham's gritty atmosphere, enhancing the film's dark tone while the score by Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard amplifies the emotional stakes.

Supporting performances from Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent and Maggie Gyllenhaal as Rachel Dawes add layers to the narrative. Dent's transformation into Two-Face serves as a poignant commentary on the fragility of morality, and Gyllenhaal's portrayal provides a strong emotional anchor for Bruce Wayne.

What sets The Dark Knight apart is its willingness to engage with challenging questions about justice and the impact of fear. The Joker's anarchistic worldview serves as a catalyst for exploring these themes, making the film not just a superhero story, but a compelling psychological thriller.

In conclusion, The Dark Knight is more than a film; it's a cultural phenomenon that redefined the superhero genre. With stellar performances, a gripping narrative, and profound thematic depth, it remains a benchmark for all future films in the genre. A must-watch for both comic book fans and cinephiles alike, it solidifies its place as a modern classic.

9.title: A Cinematic Masterpiece That Redefined Superhero Films
9.content:
Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" is a masterclass in filmmaking that transcends the superhero genre, blending intense action, deep character exploration, and a thought-provoking narrative into one of the greatest films of its kind.

Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker is nothing short of legendary. His portrayal is both chilling and mesmerizing, capturing the essence of chaos and unpredictability. Ledger's Joker elevates the film to new heights, serving as a perfect counterpoint to Christian Bale's stoic and determined Batman. The dynamic between the two characters is electric, embodying the struggle between order and anarchy.

The film's screenplay is tightly woven, offering a gripping story with high stakes and unexpected twists. Themes of morality, sacrifice, and the blurred lines between heroism and villainy are explored with depth and nuance. The ethical dilemmas presented, particularly in the ferry sequence, leave a lasting impression, challenging viewers to consider their own values.

Hans Zimmer's score is another standout element, heightening the tension and drama with a haunting and relentless soundscape. Combined with Wally Pfister's stunning cinematography, Gotham feels alive and menacing, a character in its own right.

While the film is near-perfect, a few supporting characters, like Rachel Dawes, could have been developed further.

Overall, "The Dark Knight" is a near-flawless film that redefined what a superhero movie could achieve. It balances blockbuster entertainment with profound storytelling, making it a cinematic experience that remains impactful even years after its release.

9.title: greatest super hero movie ever !
9.content:
I got to see The Dark Knight on Wednesday night, the reason though why I'm writing this movie comment this late is because I didn't wanna just jump and say this movie was awesome, I wanted to think it through, still today, I can't stop thinking about this movie! The Dark Knight lives up to it's hype and goes beyond it, this is the Batman movie that goes where no other Batman movie has gone before. It gave us a real sold story, we are finally told why the villains are the way they are, how all the injustice in the world can get underneath Batman's skin, how you have to believe that people still have faith in good on Earth. Heath Ledger, I absolutely loved Jack Nicolson's performance in the 1989 film, when I first read that Heath was signed onto The Dark Knight, I was like "What are they, kidding?", once you see The Dark Knight... Heath was incredible! I'm not going to compare Jack and Heath's performance, because they were two different versions of the Joker, but Heath's Joker was definitely the more scary and intense of the two nominations. You didn't know what he was going to do next, he was so crazy, he was also so charismatic to the point where you could relate to his character, and the worst part is not only that he's crazy, he's driving Gotham crazy and treating everyone like little puppets on strings that he can control, and guess what, he is doing it so well with a smile on his face.

This was so much more than a Batman film, this was so much more than a comic book film, The Dark Knight truly delivers with drama, action, romance, horror, dark humor, the study of a psychopathic killer, a detective story. The force behind this epic movie is Christopher Nolan, who's previous film, Batman Begins, didn't really thrill me, but his incredible film making is truly shown in The Dark Knight, the shots that he got of Gotham City were absolutely fantastic and made you feel part of the city, part of the Batman story. One of the things that I absolutely loved about The Dark Knight is that normally with a comic book movie, you know it's not real, people don't dress up in costumes, and save the day, villains don't name themselves crazy names and dress in make up or crazy costumes, but The Dark Knight actually makes it seem incredibly real, like it could happen.

Bruce Wayne is still learning how to be in his double life of Batman and himself, he has lost Rachel to the new district attorney, Harvey Dent, he's inspiring others who are dressing up as Batman and are trying to take on the villains of the city themselves. But things are much worse when the Joker waltzes into town, and he's going to bring Hell upon Gotham City. Constantly playing with Gotham's mind and trying to get Batman to reveal himself, Batman has never dealt with such a psychopathic genius before. The Joker has named himself as the "Classy Villain that Gotham needs", he also has brought a new thought into Batman's head of them actually being more alike than different, that Batman completes him, the Joker would be nothing without him. But Batman is relying on Harvey Dent, who is Gotham's "White Knight" trying to put all of Gotham's scum in jail. But when the Joker plays Batman and Commissioner Gordon, Harvey and Rachel find themselves in very horrific position and Harvey must discover if he will die a hero or live long enough to become a villain.

All the performances are dead on in this movie, now everyone's going crazy over Heath Ledger's performance, but one performance I would also love to credit is Aaron Eckhart who plays Harvey Dent/Two Face, his performance was just as great as Heath's and made Two Face a human villain. You could understand his hatred and vengeance on what happened to him and why he became Two Face. I know that everyone is saying this but I truly mean when I say this is one of the best movies I have seen in a very long time. We had some great movies these past few years, but I think The Dark Knight is seriously something special, but I don't wanna build it up too much since some people go to the theater expecting my words to be the same as your own. In my opinion though this is not a great movie, I can't come up with a word describe how incredibly powerful this movie was, to be honest I would go above a 10 rating if I could; this is the Batman film that we have been waiting for. I've seen it twice in one weekend, I'm going to see it three times this upcoming week, I don't mind one bit. I can't wait for the sequel and I would just like to say RIP to Heath, wish he could have seen his breath taking performance as The Joker.

Few films have achieved the same level of critical acclaim and enduring popularity as The Dark Knight. Released in 2008, Christopher Nolan's sequel to Batman Begins stands as a testament to the power of storytelling, performance, and technical mastery. With its complex characters, thought-provoking themes, and visually stunning action sequences, The Dark Knight has captivated audiences worldwide and cemented its place as one of the greatest superhero films of all time.

The film follows the Caped Crusader's relentless pursuit of the enigmatic criminal mastermind known as the Joker, a role that Heath Ledger delivers with chilling intensity. Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is a masterclass in acting, capturing the character's chaotic energy, unpredictable nature, and profound nihilism. The Joker's presence serves as a stark counterpoint to Batman's unwavering commitment to justice, creating a dynamic that is as thrilling as it is thought-provoking.

Nolan's direction is impeccable, weaving together a complex narrative that explores the darker side of human nature, the blurred lines between hero and villain, and the very nature of the Batman mythos. The film is visually stunning, with cinematographer Wally Pfister capturing Gotham City in all its gritty realism and grandeur. The action sequences are expertly choreographed and executed, delivering a visceral thrill that is both exhilarating and grounded in reality.

The performances across the board are exceptional, with Christian Bale delivering a subtly nuanced performance as Batman, conveying the character's inner turmoil and unwavering determination. Michael Caine is equally captivating as Alfred Pennyworth, Batman's loyal butler and confidant. Morgan Freeman shines as Lucius Fox, the resourceful and brilliant technological genius who provides Batman with the tools he needs to fight crime.

The Dark Knight is not just a superhero film; it is a cinematic masterpiece that explores profound themes of morality, justice, and the nature of evil. It is a film that will stay with you long after the credits roll, challenging your perceptions and leaving you questioning the line between good and evil. With its complex characters, thought-provoking themes, and visually stunning action sequences, The Dark Knight is a must-see for any fan of cinema.

9.title: The Movie Was Epic
9.content:
The Dark Knight poses and plays with ethical conundrums, most of which seem designed to push Batman, his allies and all of Gotham over the brink. "Madness, as you know, is like gravity," the Joker says. "All it takes is a little push."

The Joker succeeds in transforming Dent into a vicious villain with (quite literally) a two-sided face, and then sits back as his pet project flips that coin (one side now charred and scarred) to determine who dies and who lives. "The only morality in an amoral world is chance," Dent says.

Batman argues that the world's not governed by chance, but by choices. And when Dent dies, Batman makes the movie's most interesting choice of all: He takes the blame for the people Dent killed. He becomes, unjustly, a fugitive hated by the very people he's protecting.

"Sometimes, truth isn't good enough," Batman says. "Sometimes people deserve more. Sometimes people deserve to have their faith rewarded."

The decision, like Dent himself, shows us two faces.

On one side of it, Batman creates a lie-a flat-out fabrication that patronizingly presumes he knows what's best for Gotham's citizens, and that they're too fragile or shortsighted to accept the truth. In an age when we are all wary of lies, deceptions and governmental cover-ups, this kind of fabrication (well-meaning though it may be) feels especially wrong and, in any case, always violates one of God's core commandments: Don't lie.

On the other, Batman takes Dent's sin on his own shoulders, leaving the DA, in Gotham's eyes, pure and spotless and clean. Sound familiar? It can be read, at some level, as an echo of the sacrifice Christ-utterly innocent, yet humiliated and judged on our behalf-made for us.

One more thing to chew on: Batman, in Bruce Wayne's mind, is not a hero, but an ideal-a symbol for something greater. People, he muses in Batman Begins, are corruptible. Ideals are not. It stands to reason, then, that he would want to push Dent from corruptible man to incorruptible ideal-a symbol of something greater. "Gotham needs a hero with a face," Wayne says. And so he gives that hero to the city, willingly destroying his own reputation in the process.

Without a doubt, then, The Dark Knight is mesmerizing and thought-provoking. It's guaranteed to become a critical darling while scooping up a bazillion dollars at the box office. But its dark side cannot be ignored. The Chicago Tribune leads its review with this warning: "Sensational, grandly sinister and not for the kids." The New York Daily News tells us, "The PG-13 rating seems tame; this sucker is rough." You're seeing it advertised on everything from cereal boxes to candy bars, but that doesn't make Knight's violence, it's aura of menace, any more digestible. It's not just kids who'll walk out of the film shaken.

When you see Harvey Dent's new look for the first time, you barely notice his still pretty-boy right side. The left side-charred, unblinking, horrific-seems to fill the screen. And the same could be said for this movie. Yes, it's undeniably well-crafted. But it's a harsh creation, and by all rights shouldn't have been named after the good guy. The Dark Knight is the Joker's court, and he's not looking for a laugh.

9.title: The Dark Knight is a movie that is primarily about the battle of Batman versus the Joker.
9.content:
The Dark Knight is a movie that is primarily about the battle of Batman versus the Joker. In this movie, Batman, or Bruce Wayne, is played by Christian Bale, and the Joker is played by Heath Ledger. The new district attorney for Gotham, Harvey Dent, who is played by Aaron Eckhart, is fighting crime in the court room, putting much of the mob in prison. He aids the Batman, as well as Lieutenant Jim Gordon (Gary Oldman) in trying to take down the Joker. The Joker tries to get under their skin, forcing them to do things they would not typically do.

One theme for The Dark Knight is the fight of good versus evil. Throughout the entire movie, the Batman is trying to stop the Joker from committing all of his crimes. The Joker even manages to turn the people of Gotham against the Batman, making it seem as if he is partly responsible for all of the bad that is happening. Harvey Dent was doing everything that he could to legally take down the Joker, and Bruce Wayne saw this as being very important. However, after the Joker killed Harvey's fiancée, Rachel (Maggie Gyllenhaal), Harvey turns bad, and starts to kill people himself. After the Joker was captured, this caused another evil for Bruce Wayne and Jim Gordon to fight. Harvey does end up dying, and Bruce Wayne has Jim Gordon lie and say the Batman was responsible for the people that Harvey killed, in order to preserve the image of Harvey Dent and all that he done for the legal system in Gotham.

Another film that is similar to The Dark Knight in theme is Spiderman. This film also uses a masked vigilante to fight crime in the city. A similarity is even though both Batman and Spiderman are trying to take down crime for the better of the city, they get made out to be the bad guy when things are not going so well.

One way that good versus evil is demonstrated in the film is when Harvey Dent gets his face burned after an explosion. The idea is introduced earlier in the film, when Harvey refers to people calling him "Harvey two face." The good versus evil is symbolized by Harvey's two sides of his face; the burnt side, and the non-burnt side. This is when Harvey took a turn towards a villain. He even has a quote within the film, where he says "You either die a hero, or you can live long enough to see yourself become a villain." Another symbol of the good versus evil theme is Harvey's coin. Throughout the film, Harvey used his coin, which has heads on both sides, to "make his own luck" as he states in the film. After the accident when he gets burnt, however, one side of the coin gets burnt as well. From then on, he used the coin in deciding whether people would get to live or die. The two sides of the coin symbolize the good versus evil theme.

9.title: The Dark Knight: A Masterpiece of Chaos and Brilliance
9.content:
"The Dark Knight" is not just a superhero movie; it is a cinematic triumph that transcends genres and expectations. Directed by the visionary Christopher Nolan, this film is a dark and gripping exploration of morality, chaos, and the nature of heroism, anchored by a truly unforgettable performance by Heath Ledger as the Joker.

From the opening moments to the jaw-dropping conclusion, "The Dark Knight" grips the audience in a vice of tension and suspense. Christian Bale returns as Batman, grappling with the consequences of his crusade against crime in Gotham City while facing a new and terrifying adversary in the form of the anarchic Joker.

Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of legendary. His performance is a revelation, a mesmerizing descent into madness that is both chilling and electrifying to watch. Ledger's Joker is a force of nature, a chaotic and unpredictable presence that challenges Batman's very essence and pushes Gotham City to the brink.

The supporting cast is equally stellar, with Aaron Eckhart delivering a nuanced performance as Harvey Dent, the idealistic district attorney whose fall from grace mirrors Gotham's descent into darkness. Gary Oldman shines once again as Commissioner Gordon, providing a steady moral compass in a city consumed by corruption and fear.

Visually stunning and thematically rich, "The Dark Knight" is a feast for the senses and the intellect. Nolan's signature style is on full display, with breathtaking action sequences, intricate storytelling, and a sense of moral ambiguity that lingers long after the credits roll.

What truly sets "The Dark Knight" apart is its willingness to ask difficult questions and explore complex themes. The film delves deep into the nature of good and evil, the power of choice, and the thin line that separates hero from villain. It challenges the audience to confront their own beliefs and values, leaving them breathless with its audacity and intelligence.

In conclusion, "The Dark Knight" is a triumph of storytelling and filmmaking that stands as a testament to the power of cinema. With its unforgettable performances, gripping narrative, and profound themes, this movie is a masterpiece that will be remembered and celebrated for generations to come. Christopher Nolan has crafted a modern classic that has redefined the superhero genre and set a new standard for excellence in filmmaking.

9.title: A Thrilling Battle Between Chaos and Justice

The movie masterfully blends action with psychological drama, focusing on the internal struggle of Bruce Wayne as he navigates the consequences of his vigilantism.

Ledger's Joker is chaotic and terrifying, a true agent of destruction who serves as a perfect counterbalance to Batman's sense of justice. His performance brings unpredictability and menace to every scene. The film also highlights Harvey Dent's (Aaron Eckhart) tragic arc, turning from Gotham's white knight into the disfigured and vengeful Two-Face, symbolizing the fragility of idealism in a corrupt world.

The themes of order vs. Chaos, the ethical dilemmas of power, and the nature of heroism are elevated by Hans Zimmer's score and Wally Pfister's atmospheric cinematography. Nolan's tight direction and narrative structure, along with thought-provoking philosophical questions, ensure that The Dark Knight remains a cinematic landmark, offering more than just action-it's a deep reflection on society, identity, and the cost of true justice.
