7.title: Not a bad movie, but not the masterpiece you'll read about here..
7.content: I was a fan of Christopher Nolan's "Batman Begins" because it bore re-watching and pulled the viewer through the salt-and-pepper psychologizing almost without effort (much the same way Michael Clayton hypnotizes the viewer). But this follow-up is at least 30 minutes, and several reversals-of-fortune too long and too many. Its strength lies in the two performances, from Bale and Ledger, not, contrary to widespread popular opinion, the special effects (the action in the Bourne Ultimatum was far more visually interesting/captivating with far fewer gadgets and complicated digital backdrops). But a measure of the movie's shambling structure in the last third is the fact that Ledger's continuing inventiveness wears thin after 90 minutes, so much so that I found myself thinking more about what he would do next than what was supposed to be happening in the story that no longer engrossed me. My guess is Nolan got one too many ideas and couldn't resist putting every last one of them on screen. Not a good formula for a suspense thriller, which needs a tight focus to perform as the work of the greats in this genre (Hitchcock, Ridley Scott) generally do. Too bad, since what Nolan is trying for is just more interesting than what the other directors in this franchise have been doing. Maybe next time?

7.title: Epic, Maybe a Little Too Epic
7.content:
Having just watched this on DVD, this is definitely a movie for the theaters. The pace, editing and action scenes really need that immersive experience to show best. At home with a repeat viewing, I start to ask myself questions. Questions like how did The Joker places himself and his men in the memorial ceremony without anyone noticing? And how did Gordon know he would need to take a bullet (or pretend to) for the mayor, then have a plan to fake his death in place to protect his family? And why even bother with a plot twist that has no real effect on the narrative? And how did Joker put bombs everywhere in the city without anyone noticing anyway? Or get into the hospital to talk to Dent unnoticed? I know, it's just a movie. But when it strives for hyper-realism, it becomes more important to deliver a plausible plot. At a certain point it is just rather convoluted; filled with good ideas but there's not enough time even in 2.5 hours to carry them all out. There's also a tendency for Nolan to have Gordon explain (with Dent in the hospital, in the very end) instead of either letting the audience think or showing the audience.

That's the bad. The good certainly outweighs all of those criticisms on the whole. Once the chaos begins unfolding with Joker forcing virtually every character into uncomfortable choices, a vast array of questions arise. This is the strong point of the film. The audience is asked to consider what makes a hero, and more importantly to consider the hero as an individual with conflicted motives. There's a beautiful inverse symmetry to Batman, who never truly wavered in his heroic intentions, assuming the role of outlaw, while Dent, who flipped to become a villain, is preserved as hero. Additionally, we are asked how far can one bend the rules in the interest of doing good. This in fact drives to the essence of Batman as vigilante wanting to make right while breaking all the rules. Joker, knowing the inherent contradiction, does his best to convince Batman they are no different. He doesn't succeed, but the question is one that needs to be considered.

On another note, the hospital scene with Dent and Joker is one of my favorites. It's here that Dent makes his transition to Two Face. Previously, he had claimed to make his own luck with his heads I win, tails you lose logic. But here he seemingly embraces the random chaos Joker espouses by letting heads be both live and die for Joker. Additionally, Joker's quote, "You know what I've noticed? Nobody panics when things go according to plan. Even if the plan is horrifying! If, tomorrow, I tell the press that, like, a gang banger will get shot, or a truckload of soldiers will be blown up, nobody panics, because it's all part of the plan. But when I say that one little old mayor will die, well then everyone loses their minds!" is a nice bit of social commentary as well. Is this movie overdone at times? Sure. But it's also quite rich and provocative for the audience. It manages to probe uncomfortable themes while ratcheting the action up several notches. That's a hard combo to pull off, and it's done skillfully here.

7.title: Action packed, good story line.
7.content: I have never been a fan of batman movies, but this one is an exception. There is a good story line to begin with and tons of action follow. However, besides the acting of the Joker (Heath Ledger) which might end up in an Oscar nomination or even award, I feel it could get some help elsewhere. The Bat-automobile transformation is somewhat awkward, I think, but that is of small details compared with other full blown effects. I am not sure there would be sequel to this movie since it seems to be the prequel of another one with the riddler (Jim Carrey), if I am not mistaken. The sound effect and all the violent parts could be too much for kids, so be ware if you bring them along.

7.title: Great....but #10 of top 250? Slightly Overrated
7.content:
I saw this before Batman Begins so I have no idea if it is a continuation from the previous one or is a totally new chapter of the story. I just heard everybody say how great it is so I want to witness myself if it is true. Frankly I think everyone praises it because Heath Ledger is in it and he is dead. Dead actors usually draw more people to the cinema, sadly.

The film is very long almost three hours. I feel Christian Bale is not quite suited as Batman, something about his looks I can not explain. The villains are better cast. I like Gary Oldman as Inpsector Gordon. I love Aaron Eckhart as two-faced. I sympathize his character as he turns against Batman only as he loves Rachel so much and he blames Batman for her death. He is still a good person even after he becomes two-faced.

Heath Ledger is great as the Joker but I think Jack Nicholson is better. At least the make-up is done very well and Heath looks great. I don't really feel the hatred between him and Batman (over the dead girl reporter? Seems silly. Why is she so important? I don't really see her play a significant part in the movie) in the interrogation room. The annoying music in the scene continues to drone insides my head and makes more impact to me but in the irritating kind of way.

I feel the atmosphere is very dark. Batman only appears at night in his dark suit so half the action happens at night and I can't quite well see it in 'proper light', lost interest after a while.

The day scenes is all talks in suits and no action. Nice scenery from the tall building with big windows. I feel bored in some parts and wish they could just talk faster.

It is an okay movie but I fail to see how it can make it to #10 spot in the top 250 films. Nolan is good but obviously over-rated. Maybe due to lack of capable directors discovered in this generation. Feel movies are all about the same. Maybe all the good movies have already been made before 2000. Will wait for Batman 3 and see.

7.title: darker than ever
7.content:
'The Dark Knight' is a new and interesting achievement in the career of Christopher Nolan, a director who always tries to do something different, something that surprises and takes films beyond the genres of patterns they are supposed to belong to. Although I do not share the superlatives and I do not think that 'Dark Knight' belongs to the top 10 or even top 100 movies of all times as it is placed now, there are enough interesting things to make it worth seeing.

It's dark times out there and our preferred movies sequels get darker also. 'Dark Knight' starts in a routine comics movie style, with a confusing first quarter an hour until we can make sense of the characters and we start understanding that it's more here than the standard stuff. Sure, we do get a great concentration of acting talents, and just having Michael Caine and Morgan Freeman play two supporting (but key) roles says enough. What is however remarkable is that this is a long film, and yet, tension and quality builds in time, and the last half hour is the most interesting of all - not because but despite all the special effects, acrobatics fights and car races. It builds into a destructive and apocalyptic vision, and the frightening thing is that in today's world such a vision is almost credible.

Amazingly for a comics movie, at some point in time we start to care about the characters. The evil character in the film is the most interesting as well, and we can only deplore the fact that Heath Ledger did not live to enjoy the success of this film which is due to a large extent to his acting talent. As the film all over, within the limits of the mask and of the convention, this is almost the best we can get.

7.title: Prophet of Doom
7.content:
Well, whats left to say? The only reason we are still talking about it is for you know who. Lets face it, Heath Ledger MAKES this film, whenever he isn't on screen it loses a lot of its rape-the-cat, drill-nails-through-your-forehead intensity that Hans Zimmer sees fit to emphasize with a razors-on-string section score. When I first saw it with that steadily rising buzz saw of a musical cue sounding in the beginning I thought I'd stumbled into the latest serial killer pic, not Batman part 6. PG-13 be damned, this should've been rated R. Think about it- we went from Adam West's 60's pop art psychedelic camp fest to Tim Burton/Joel Schumacher's black rubber gay S&M fetish to Silence of the Lambs meets the caped crusader, post 9/11.What a huge distance in just a few decades. Our pop culture seems to be becoming quasi-sociopathic to match our increasingly dire State of the Union & I cannot conceive of a society that found the 60's Batman show satisfying on anything but the most ironically detached level; what would they have made of the cynical 2008 audience that needs its actors to work themselves into nervous breakdowns portraying comic book characters? That laughs at pencil-through-the-eyeball gags & cheers on urban terrorism for dummies? And we certainly don't do traditional acting anymore either. Nothing less than a performer killing himself to pass our bullsh*t-ometers. Lemme tell you, its beyond disconcerting watching the publics' increasingly parasitic relationship with celebrities; It reminds of Kurt Cobain in fact, another rising star who revelled in death & damnation to the delight of hungry, hungry fans.

Jack Nicholoson's ('I warned him!') Joker has nothing on this incarnation- that was campy scenery chewing, Jack being Jack- this is a rag man in the gutter preaching brimstone & hellfire by way of Nietzsche,a perverse evocation for the terrorism age, confirming every one of our worst fears about the slippery facade of civilization. Every evil clown you've ever seen in the movies rolled into one lone, loving Satanic prophet of doom. Slinking, twitchy, greasy, with a rat's nest of thinning green hair and running make-up: there is something so insanely punk-rock nihilistic about a slap hazard clown face melting underneath the heat & the whole film feels seedier every time our freak clown takes centre stage (Was there EVER a time clowns were truly a symbol of innocence instead of this twisted, molester-under-the-bed inversion they are now? Pennywise,Captain Spaulding, Gacy, Slipknot, hard-core clown porn.....). Yet he's the most joyful, attractive, child-like person in the film, everyone else is weighed down by the weight of a collapsing world,they can't help but look small next to him.The defining shot of the movie finds Joker hanging out a car window shaking his head like a dog & breathing in the air,clearly happy to be alive.Words can't describe it.

Ledger tapped into something real here, underneath the glitz and flash our own burning Gotham. How exhilarating and depressing to hear your own worst doubts played out in mime face like a sick joke,to have the joy & sorrow to know you're not the only one thinking very dark thoughts about the future. So yes, we should honour Heath for showing us what we don't want to look at except through the fun house mirror of Hollyweird, where anything goes. You *should* admire a movie & its actors for having the guts to go to these places, to show us the writing on the wall so brazenly, but thats the thing with Hollyweird- if they get anything right at all its usually the most obvious side of the equation. Where's our anti-joker, our ray of real light when the dawn is darkest? Because it sure as hell isn't Batman.

7.title: entertaining but not great
7.content:
They could have cut about 40 minutes from this movie and made it much more enjoyable. There seemed to be at least two other points where the movie appeared to have wrapped up and it made me a bit antsy when it continued past the first logical ending.

The Scarecrow was completely wasted in this film. His appearance added little to the film.

The Batcycle was just plain silly. It looked completely unmaneuverable and ungainly. Is it too much to ask to have someone with at least a cursory knowledge of physics involved in the design of such gadgets? That being said, the movie had a nice dark feel to it. The casting was excellent. Heath Ledger gives a slightly unhinged performance which made the Joker more believable than he had been in past films. Aaron Eckhart makes a great Two Face though I found his makeup a bit gruesome for my tastes. I would have preferred something closer to the way Two Face was portrayed in the comics. Michael Caine and Morgan Freeman both give great performances as always. Bale is definitely the best Batman to date.

I still find I prefer Batman Begins to this film and I liked Iron Man more than both.

7.title: stranger
7.content: The film is not bad, but definitely not one of the best in history, removing all scenes with the joker from here will be a regular superhero film

7.title: Lives up to Most of the Hype...
7.content: I've heard far too much about this film and about how "awesome" it was in every way before seeing it and then I too was intoxicated by the experience. Before I go forward I'd like to explain my experience in the theater. The sound was turned up all the way, when a gunshot went off I winced and luckily there were no interruptions in the theater at all. Oh and one more thing, go see this in theaters, the fading to black, the obnoxiously loud noises, everything cannot be replicated outside of the theater. The camera angles don't really impress me but almost everything else does, the acting by everyone is pretty high and Nolan certainly shows off his ability to manipulate lighting, colors, etc. The dialogue's strong for the most part, if it isn't the acting carries the lines through. The films pretty well paced but I think it hangs over by 20-30 minutes. Stepping into this extra amount of time feels a little strange at first but it's still pretty darn engrossing and fun to watch and sets up the trilogy further so I can understand why it's in there. Ledger's performance doesn't make me awestruck but it does inspire me, his character has an aura in this film and there is a complete vision of the Joker but I don't feel that this performance completely trounces Nicholson's twenty years ago. Don't get me wrong, it's great but I don't think it's forty times better than Nicholson. Either way, a must see in theaters the experience is pretty awesome, and yeah you can say the films not very challenging but it really is a lot of fun.

7.title: Not so great, but good
7.content: When a movie is so hyped up it often tends to disappoint. But when I saw a review stating that the movie is actually up to the hype I expected an awesome ride for the money. There were indeed remarkable moments both technically and dramatically, and The Joker was an astonishing coup in concept and execution. The supporting cast was solid and at no point in the 2-1/2 hour flick did I start to muse about the actors themselves or the crew - the story (barely) managed to hold my attention throughout. Still, Burton's Batmans pale in comparison to Nolan's as the newer version is more realistic, fantastic, and dynamic. In the end I saw nothing new here, mainly a modern iteration of the Thor/Loki personae and conflict with a budget worthy of Asgard. Nice work, not great.

7.title: A admirable and memorable Batman and comics film, but not quite a masterpiece
7.content:
"The Dark Knight" is the best movie based on comics that I've ever seen. For once, impressive special effects and photography are matched by a screenplay that impressively examines the main figures as fully rounded human beings. All in all, I liked "Dark Knight", but I didn't think it was as masterful as some reviews suggested.

Heath Ledger's performance is as good as the hype; his Joker is intensely frightening. The suggestions that he wanted to be killed, specifically that he wanted Batman to kill him simplified his character. Apart from these shadowings, the film's portrait of him is immensely disturbing. I liked how the face off between Batman and the Joker didn't explore that they were two sides of one personality, evil as opposed to good, but forces in eternal opposition.

The screenplay served the film well in its complexity and depth. Gotham wasn't just dark, Gothic, and brooding: it resembled an actual contemporary city, with all its dangers and corruption. I also liked how the film examined the battle between good in evil in everyone, not just in Bruce Wayne and Harvey Dent.

Dent's characterization was also excellent, and portrayed admirably. "the Dark Knight's" portraits of Two Face and the Joker are among the strongest the characters have ever had in film or comics.

The film's Jim Gordon was moving too. But Bruce Wayne, alas, seemed one dimensional in comparison to the villains. I didn't feel that Bale was given very much to do in this film in terms of exploring Wayne's personality.

It would been much more interesting if Dent discovered that Wayne was also the Batman: it would have given the last part of the film even more force. I couldn't understand why Dent blamed Gordon for Rachel's death, for not saving her: was he complaining that Gordon didn't get to her fast enough? It would been much more dramatic to have Dent confront Batman and blame Wayne for not saving Rachel first, particularly regarding Wayne's feelings for her.

We found the film too long. I thought the Joker's arrest would be the climax and the ending. I was restless. My seat was a little uncomfortable, but that's not why I kept shifting in it. The movie would have benefited from tightening of pacing and some trimming, especially of the violent scenes.

My husband was upset by the movie's glorification of knives, and the Joker's relishing of sticking knives in people's mouths while terrorizing them. In the past months several teenagers and young people in the UK have been killed in knife attacks, and there is national campaign to confiscate knives and end knife crimes. We were very surprised that the Dark Knight received a 12 rating. I thought it should have been a R movie. I know that sadism is a part of the Joker's character, but the portrayal of it in the movie must be terrifying for young people.

7.title: The Dark Knight
7.content: Good Movie. Everybody acted very well in the movie, especially Heath Ledger's performance was excellent. VFX and BGM in the movie were excellent. Fight scenes in the movie were excellent. The movie had some unwanted scenes that made the movie somewhat lagging. The movie was interesting and thrilling but the movie lagged and bored a bit because of some unwanted characters and scenes. Good Movie.

7.title: Should not be PG13, -- R is more realistic rating--
7.content:
First this movie is really good, however its not appropriate for anyone in range of 13. Matter of fact even 17 is cutting too close.

The level of fear in this movie is that of Aliens. Except with people, not monsters. The joker is the classic psychopath, who cares only to torture people, not to achieve monetary or power goals. I thought this movie was a cross between Aliens, and Taxi driver. Except the joker plays the role of threshold-less fear creator.

Again if you are an adult, i mean over the age of 20, this is a good film to watch, but definitely not for people in there early or late teens. The MPAA really missed it on this one.

The first 15 minutes of this film is very disturbing, like "pulp fiction", but once that scene is done, the movie is more watchable.

7.title: Very good film
7.content:
I only gave it a 7 out of 10. I can't give it higher, if this is the theatrical cut, I should give it lower. There must be a better cut than this. Batman Begins if one of my all time fav movies, but I have issues with this one. Heath's Joker is amazing. The script is amazing. The Visuals are amazing. I even like how they added a little bit of things that annoyed me about the first one. Like using your companies R&D stuff without anyone knowing. Worst accountants EVA!

That being said, these things are the only problems I had with the movie. 1) The Cut. I know there is a longer version of this film out there. A lot of the scenes didn't make sense. The joker escapes from prison and the very next day he has already initiated another plan. WHAT? Give the guy a few days. Didn't he want to sleep? Eat? He had to buy all that stuff. The movie is full of that. Terrorist in real life take years of planning and 'nonactivity' to hatch a scheme. If Bale would have said "We haven't heard from the joker in a month..." and suddenly the Joker appears on TV hatching a scheme, I would have accepted that. And Katie holmes ruined Dawes character that bad that she didn't even get a funeral? 2) The henchmen. This isn't just my problem with this film, it is all batman films (except Begins) in general. WHERE DO THE BADGUYS GET THESE GUYS? Is there a human resource section? The joker must have went through what 50 guys this film. With a turnover rate like that, and the fact that he is burning all this money, who would join him? "Crazy" people? Just because you are crazy, doesn't mean that if the Joker says, "ok stand there like a hostage while a tied up hostage holds a gun to you. When the police come they will be caught off guard". What did the henchmen think will happen??? No matter what, there was only one result: All the henchmen would have died. If the police department had this many cracks in it, why didn't the joker's....department? And again, how did he come up with these guys?

Other than that, it was a good film. I can't see them ever topping it.

7.title: Certainly Dark
7.content:
Oh, jeez, I'm quite late, aren't I? Okay.

I recently reviewed 'The Avengers', so I'd say it's time to review the other movie commonly regarded as 'the best superhero movie ever'. It's been praised to Kingdom Come, it's a phenomenon. And what do I think?

It's not.

Christopher Nolan is a good director. There's no denying that - Inception was fantastic. Technically, this film is fantastic. Heath Ledger (R.I.P) delivers an extremely haunting performance as the Joker, practically redefining the definition of a good villain. Aaron Eckhart, as well, stands out for his portrayal of Harvey Dent. Michael Caine is, of course, awesome and Morgan Freeman certainly isn't too shabby either. Christian Bale's a great Bruce Wayne and a pretty darn good Batman for what he was given to work with. The effects are pretty good as well, particularly when Joker blows up the hospital. Cinematography is good, and the score is actually great.

So, where did this movie fall apart for me? I'll break it down:

1) The pacing. This movie is very long - about 2 and a half hours. I don't have a problem with long movies, but the movie really started to feel more like the last stretch of a marathon rather than entertainment.

2) The writing. Okay, this is a big one. People praise this movie as perfect, but I think they're overlooking some major plot holes. How did Batman and Rachel survive after they fell at least 30 stories and landed on a taxi? What happened to Joker after he got into Wayne's penthouse? The first one is just weird, but second one is a major point that's never addressed in the movie.

3) Rachel Dawes. She's extremely unlikable, boring, and enforces a huge misstep in most works of fiction: she dies so that the male hero can have something to fight for. It's terrible, but I felt nothing when she died.

4) Joker. I mean absolutely no disrespect to Heath Ledger's memory when I say this. In fact, it saddens me to it. I've had 4 years to reflect on what Christopher Nolan's Joker is, and I've come to the conclusion that he just feels like someone who dresses up LIKE the Joker and infuses his own philosophies into it. He's not funny, he's just extremely terrifying. Nolan made a huge misstep with this character.

5) The tone. This movie is dark. It's violent. And it's overtly so. Some say it's to reinforce how 'realistic' this Batman's world is supposed to be - I say it's a 14-year-old's idea of what mature is. And a lot of the time, it misses the mark on what a superhero movie is supposed to be - entertaining. The Dark Knight forgoes this and becomes a philosophical cop drama that takes itself too seriously.

In conclusion, this is a technically excellent movie hampered by plot holes, an overtly dark tone, and other flaws.

7.title: Good but WAY over-hyped
7.content: Honestly, the action scenes in this movie are absolutely amazing. It is far superior in this regard to Batman Begins. But I think everyone needs to stand back, take a deep breath and judge the movie on the movie, not on the fact that Heath Ledger unfortunaetly passed away earlier this year. I love Christian Bale as an actor but he was ordinary in this film. I wish they would take that mouth guard out when he is playing Batman. The constant self-serving 'justice' speeches got a little old as well, when is a super-hero just going to kill the damn bad guys? I think a little Boon Dock Saints needs to be added to some of these Super Hero scripts. Heath Ledger was good as the Joker, but he was not nearly as good as Jack Nicholson. I hate to be a sinic but if Heath was alive I don't think his role would be touted as Oscar worthy.

7.title: The best batman movie yet
7.content:
The Dark Knight is easily the best batman movie produced so far. The villains actually look scary and the atmosphere of Gotham is masterfully portrayed. This time round, the producers decided to use actors who actually knew their trade. A very chancy and unorthodox thing to do, however in retrospect, i think it safe to say that the move was clearly beneficial to the outcome of the film (they might be on to something here...).

I would recommend this film to most people. Especially to all who have been discouraged by watching the previous films as this one is so very different.

The rating of 7 out of 10 is just about what this film deserves, it is clearly worth seeing. I've seen surprisingly high ratings and overwhelming amounts of praise for the Dark Knight, but come on you guys, it wasn't THAT good...

7.title: Mildly Disappointing Considering Expectations and Hype
7.content:
I watched Batman Begins immediately before seeing Dark Knight, and Batman Begins was definitely more 'real' than Dark Knight, more gritty, and a more coherent, smooth screenplay. No doubt Heath Ledgers' Joker is a superb Villain - to go down in the history books as one of the best all time on the big screen, however he was misused and underused. He had a grasp on the character like no one else, yet they didn't have near the character development they should have for him, and they lost focus almost making the movie more about Harvey Dent (played with a bland performance by Aaron Eckhart) than the Joker. Bruce Wayne comes on the scene much less humble and down to earth than his character in Batman Begins, and Maggie Gyllenhaal's character was more annoying and less lovable than Katie Holmes' rendition. It felt like there was just too much money put into this that took the focus off of making the storyline tight, and instead was about how many different things can we do with the money.

Cinematography was good with several picturesque shots, stunt work was spectacular, and the Joker was insane and intoxicating, however without him the movie would be sub par. It's a shame.

7.title: Glad to see more realistic rating on this film finally.
7.content:
Yes, it's a great film. But to have been rating and sitting at the best rated film of all time on IMDb for such a long time? Maybe it was the publicity surrounding Heath, or just the collection of Batman fans.

I'm sorry but this film seems to have gone back to more tongue-in-cheek than I like, I'm used to seeing Batman has a dark almost sinister character. Others have told me that this is heading back to how it is in the comics and that the films have deviated. Well, blame Hollywood for polluting his character with the original Batmans.

Acting was OK (Heath was great), but I don't see why this Batman movie should be rated 'much' higher than the others.

By all means do watch this film, but don't expect to be blown away. Sorry but Jim's Carrey's portrayal of the Riddler was much more powerful than Heath's portrayal of the Joker.

7.title: A great sequel...Ledger stole the show
7.content: The Dark Knight is perhaps better than the original, Batman Begins, in my opinion, but as well as being that it's also a great chance for people to watch, remember and think about Heath Ledger. As the Joker he gives a superb last performance, stealing practically every scene which he featured inhe was both frightening and funny. The film in general is certainly more complicated than any other hero movie I've seen before; lots of goodies and baddies, plots and twists that made it a little difficult to keep up with for adults, let alone children. It's certainly something I'll have to see again when it comes out of DVD. It's still a great movie nonetheless and everyone should see it. Harvey Dent was a good introduction, giving a fresh angle to the plot, while Gary Oldman & Morgan Freeman reprise their roles well as Batman's allies. What more can I say without spoiling it? It has great action, breathtaking and well-thought of stunts and is destined to be a real hit for years to come.

7.title: Darker and Longer
7.content:
The second of the "Batman" movies starring Christian Bale. Michael Keaton, Val Kilmer and George Clooney have worn the bat suit before Bale, and Bale is much better in the role.

In both of Bales' films, the story line is darker and more complex than prior Batman films. The crime fighter faces villains who are more powerful than law enforcement, who are both out-gunned and hamstrung by concerns about civil liberties.

The Joker portrayed by the now-deceased Heath Ledger is at once funny and frightening. Ruthless and quick to kill, he creates chaos for the joy of disrupting society. There has been some deserved Oscar buzz about his work.

The film is about 2 and a half hours, and seems to run past a natural ending at about the 2 hour mark. The film is interesting and engrossing but it runs along the edge of too much and too long. Fans of the series will not be bothered by the length, but the action sequences are intense, layered and frequent. Most action films of this type find the climax earlier.

The action is complicated at times, and there is so much of it along with elaborate special effects, it is disorienting as the characters migrate from good to evil and maybe back again.

Less might have been more.

7.title: Gets An "A" for Effort
7.content:
I saw this movie when it first came out (naturally), and while I liked it, there was something wrong with it that I couldn't put a finger on. I saw it again, and got the same feeling. That time I was able to figure out this feeling came at the beginning of the 3rd act, but still couldn't figure out what was wrong. I just saw it for a third time, and finally figured it out: it was lacking in tension.

Don't get me wrong, there was plenty of it, but I felt it lacking in comparison to that of the second act. I thought the moment of highest tension was the confrontation between Batman and the Joker in the interrogation room, when Batman was teetering on the edge of breaking his one rule. After that, there was tension, but Batman's moment of crisis had passed, leaving the only question of whether he could stop the Joker's "social experiment".

But Mr. Nolan gets an "A" for effort. He really tried to outdo himself, and with the exception of that problem, he did. I will definitely come out for his next effort.

Oh yeah, one last thing: believe the hype about Heath Ledger's performance. As last performances go, this was a great one. I'm starting to think there maybe something to all this talk about a posthumous Oscar.

7.title: A great encapsulation of our times!
7.content:
*** Warning, this review will contain spoilers *** Not that this warning is really needed, since I seem to be one of the last to have seen this film.

What a great movie! In the vein of classics, this film makes you think while being absolutely entertaining. I had some reservations going into it, with so many people on YouTUBE idolizing the Joker and talking about the value of anarchy. But his film keeps a clear delineation of good and bad without making that delineation so narrow that the story sounds cliché'd. It is not a totally original plot nor is it a realistic film, but the direction, acting, and pacing make it feel fresh - allowing the writers to pack in a huge amount of themes without overloading the audience.

There are a few bad notes to the film which I'll mention first so I can then move on to the good notes. The most unrealistic aspect is the Joker's scheming. There are so many double and triple crosses that happen so quickly that he could not have possibly foreseen all that would happen. For example, after the Joker's semi chases Dent's armored car out of the tunnels (a tunnel exit the Joker was not planning Dent to take), how would he have known to have positioned 2 of his clowns with wires in just the precise spot at just the precise height to knock a police helicopter down? Or how could the Joker have predicted that his bomb at the police station would either kill or knock out every single police officer, yet leave him completely untouched, so he could stroll up to Lau and kidnap him? There's several examples of this sort of ESP that the Joker seems to posses even though he's portrayed as a normal person (albeit a totally crazy one). A second small quip was the Hong Kong scene. Batman flies from the IFC tower, then flies by the IFC tower, then lands on the IFC tower (although all are portrayed to be different buildings). Weird... Also, with so much chaos in Gotham, I think they would have called the national guard by then. And then there's the one faulty concept of "sometimes truth isn't good enough. Sometimes people deserve to have their faith rewarded." As a Christian, I believe truth sets you free and that faith is a gift from God, not something you can earn. But even with these faults, the film has such a surprisingly strong emotional pull with its characters you care about that the mistakes don't bog the movie down.

Now for the good... The production work, script, and acting are all top notch with even the most minor of characters getting just enough screen time or meaty enough dialogue that you remember them; even someone like the young police officer (whose wife is in the hospital) in the car who Gordon tries to disarm. While the Joker is by far the strongest and scariest villain I have ever seen, Nolan wisely avoids delving too much into his past. We end up understanding something of him without ever empathizing for him. Nolan keeps our compassion on his victims. I love the way ideas are addressed in the film and then played out in later scenes such as when Alfred tells Bruce they caught the bandit by burning the forest down, and then later there is Bruce using the cell phone sonar device to "burn down the city forest" if you will. I love how masses of people are shown giving into fear and then later courageously thinking outside of themselves. And so many themes almost effortlessly packed into this film: "The night is darkest before the dawn, but the dawn is coming."

What is civic duty?

Batman consistently taking on the blame of others to redeem them.

"You either die a hero or you live long enough to see yourself become the villain."

"Know your limits."

And many others. With so much going on and so many opposing and complementing messages, the movie encapsulates the Zeitgeist of the 2000's and its post modernism. It is a reflection both positive and negative of the attitudes of this generation. The Dark Knight is not a perfect film, but an excellent one nevertheless. It is a worthy follow up to Batman Begins and indeed surpasses it in scope and production. It is a perfect transition film between Begins and whatever Batman 3 will be.

7.title: Great film, with great cast.
7.content:
Superb acting, cinematography and very well directed. The plot constantly evolves and increases in tension. Great location shots, and fantastic cast. I genuinely don't think they can make the series anymore enigmatic. Looking forward to the future casts, and a high level of respect to the cast and director to push the story again, after the loss of Heath. Fantastic score and use of locations as well.

Shame about the nominations for an award or two, but worth every accolade it picks up. I'm wondering if Ben Affleck can still deliver as visual as our Christian, let's see.

Was the story too long, many have said yes, but I don't think so.

7.title: Not that good if you are really into a good movies
7.content:
Probably worse Batman movie ever just due to a fact that your barely see one during it.

All interesting and thrilling scenes of The Dark Knight are dedicated to Joker and besides them movie is just boring sequence of long dinner cliche talks regarding ambiguity of good and evil mixed with clumsy immemorable action scenes.

Never understood all the hype for it, probably it was created by teenagers who really appreciated the idea of evil being doing the good things sparing them from all the struggles of trying to be better person.

Heath Ledger is fantastic though, but it would be better if he was filmed as in Joker movie instead. Batman Begins and Dark Knight Rises are much better movies in the trilogy.

7.title: Batman Leaves Us Wanting More Joker
7.content:
Oh my! This film was so anticipated with so much hype and so much sympathy there is no way it wasn't going to break some kind of record. Should it be any surprise how many nominations and wins Heath Ledger racked up posthumously, the total is still coming in.

It should really go without saying the story here is that we're following Batman in his darkest character portrayal thus far. His nemesis the Joker is the bad guy played by Heath Ledger. We follow the Joker sort of leading Batman by the nose in this movie and we're almost pulled into the Joker's world Ledger does such a wonderful acting job here. There are lots of chases and explosions and action, it is an action movie after all. We are left wanting to see even more of the Joker on screen especially since this was his last role.

This is far and away the best of the Batman films so far. Who knows if the players can walk away from such a money maker, but I suspect they might. There will be more Batman, he's an icon so we know he will return. ***/****.

7.title: Not the second coming, but still a great movie
7.content:
Everyone has been acting like this is the greatest movie ever made or something. I thought it was good- I had a great time watching it, and appreciated the whole attempt to be deeper than a comic book film thing. I didn't think it was the second coming of Christ or anything though. I'm sure I am in the minority, and people will react like they do when you say that you thought Apocalypse Now was overrated and bloated, or that Quinten Tarantino sucks, for the most part.

Anyway, I'd say this is the best Batman movie yet. Christian Bale still has that horrible voice when he's Batman, and still does the whole Patrick Bateman/American Psycho thing when he's Bruce Wayne.

Heath Ledger's Joker sounds like Andy Dick or something. And here was my biggest problem. This was a good performance, but it was NOT a groundbreaking performance by any means. I think when posthumous actors have roles like this, people tend to over-blow it- kind of like they did with Brandon Lee in the Crow (another good performance, but not a performance for the ages, by any means).

I can appreciate the whole Zen/Anarchy/pseudo Fight Club philosophy stuff Ledger was going for, but he's no Frank Langella as Skeletor. I mean, it's definitely better than the whole Jack Nicholson paradigm, but he still just came off like a wannabe Tyler Durden/Bodhi from Point Break with schizophrenia. The real star of this movie is Aaron Eckhart, who is great as Harvey Dent/Two Face.

The cinematography and plot twists were really something to behold, and I applaud the filmmakers for continuing the standards set in 'Batman Begins' and not turning the Dark Knight into another mindless, popcorn munching summer blockbuster. The only really negative thing I can say about this film is that, for a film that takes itself so seriously, and clearly expects to be measured against truly great cinema, it just falls a little short. Not the second coming, but still a fun, "thought- provoking" (AHEM) movie. Score another one for Christopher Nolan and Goyer.

7.title: Disappointed with the PG nature of the film
7.content:
Ledger's Joker is well acted, though I would not suggest Oscar worthy as the popular media has, Bale's Bruce and Batman are again well played, Ekhart plays Dent well.

Caine, Freeman and Gylenhaal offer good supporting roles.

Where the Dark Knight fails is in the cut of the film. I would have preferred an R rating and making the film much darker than the current PG-13. There are scenes where the effect is completely lost because of implied violence; and whilst this is a useful mechanism under certain circumstances it does not work for this film.

Was the film re-cut to give a softer feeling after Heaths tragic passing in an effort to improve rating and hype one may wonder, depending on how cynical you are.

7.title: Good story, great production, BAD Batman!!!
7.content: My one big gripe with The Dark Knight is...well, the dark knight. Sure, there are a couple of other faults but as far as Batman goes, the movie is lacking. Worst of all is Christian Bale.Jesus! The guy does nothing but scream, snarl, and yell every line he has! His over-the-top Batman reminds me of my P.E. teacher! The costume is also got problems with too much circuitry and gadgets, it looks like a power rangers uniform. Even in the story line of the movie, Batman is less than important. But other than that, it's actually pretty good. Heath Ledger turns in a great performance as the Joker, although it isn't very accurate to the comics version. The vehicles and action scenes are well done although they are way too "Rambo/Terminator 2" for Batman in my opinion. Aaron Eckhart's Two-Face could use some work as well. His Harvey is okay, but the Two-Face is lacking any personality and comes off pretty stiff. The face prosthetics are excellent and is way better than the Batman Forever make-up. I love certain aspects of the story, like the Joker's social expiereiment with the two boats and the humor is great, but alas, it suffers from the same mistake Batman Begins did (although it isn't nearly as bad): the sad fact is the movie tries too hard to please the non-fan by wrapping Batman up with ridiculous action scenes and Die-Hardesque pacing. Basically the movie isn't a comic book movie, it's a second-rate action movie. It's the Lethal Weapon of Batman films.

7.title: not really a disappointment.Just not as good many say
7.content:
Let me start this way, I have been a BATMAN fan ever since I first read issue #1 way back in 1940. There was a BATMAN 15 episode serial as well, which I sat thru each episode, each every Saturday afternoon.

There were cartoon versions as well which I liked.

In the 1970's there was a comic BATMAN TV series It was a hoot. There even was a film which I saw more than once.

In the 1980's &'90's there were about 4 Batman films They like all the previous efforts were pure fun even stupid fun. A few years back we had the first part of the new Batman series of films It was a good film a wee bit serious but fun.

NOW we have THE DARK KNIGHT. This excellently acted well thought of film is just too serious for its own good.

Christopher & Jonathan Nolan fashioned a very serious screenplay & with Christoper's directing we have a sombre film.

Batman films are comic books brought to the large screen they are supposed to be fun, the are not real life, The audience is supposed to feel good at the exciting antics of the heroes & villains.

There is no humour in this very long action packed film. There are many special effect scenes, excellent CGI work ALL very professional.

Now for the cast. Christian Bale is our sombre almost dull hero. The others in the cast overshadow him. Aaron Eckart Is an excellent Harvey Dent/Two Face. The late lamented Heath Ledger is superb as the tormented joker. When Heath left us last year The acting community lost one of the future GREATS<

Gary Oldman is also very good as Lt.Gordon.

Maggie Gylennhaal is OK in here role, Its a nothing much role to begin with. Most major action films, seemingly action film must have a female in it.

Micheal Cain & Morgan Freeman are there usual fine selves in there roles.

Cillian Murphy has a few short minutes as the scarecrow.

Chin Han as some effective moments as well.

The production credits are all first rate.

I was hoping for a film that had more humour & WHERE WAS ROBIN

Robin always was a mainstay in the many previous ones.

7.title: Had very mixed feelings about it but still, not easy to dismiss
7.content:
This is a very twisted film. Yes, it's far better than the campy franchise of the Batman tale that Joel Schumacher churned out, but the movie has a decidedly downbeat spin on the Dark Knight and also its villains.

Here we really feel that being Batman is a curse, something that was sort of explored in Batman Forever. It is also weird to see something that is essentially pure fantasy turned into something so close to realism.

The message of the picture is pounded in your face. On one hand you get pure evil in the form of the Joker, played to exhaustion by the late Heath Ledger, but as the plot moves on, we are lead to believe that given the circumstances all people are selfish and could easily be every bit as evil as the Joker.

That evil is rubbed off on Harvey Dent, aka Two-Face. Aaron Eckhart almost puts Heath Ledger to shame as the crusading district attorney. Sorry, that his character explores only the dark side of his face.

One thing that did bother me was Rachel Dawes. Please forgive me but what happens to her didn't really feel as a big loss. But for plot purposes it was a great twist. I also missed Michael Caine, he was hardly present in the movie or for that matter, neither was Morgan Freeman.

As for Christian Bale, he handles Batman's conflict pretty well. Bruce Wayne's fate is wisely downplayed because we all know by now what he is and which one of the characters knows who he is.

So as far as the plot goes, very hard to sit through but the drama is excellent.

Everyone else in this film gave a terrible performance, not to mention Christian Bale basically wasn't even in this movie. It was completely focused on the Joker, which makes sense since Heath gave a performance worthy of an Oscar. It is without a doubt the best batman movie, but come on. That's not really saying anything... I mean look at the previous batman movies. Other than Batman Begins, which I think was actually better than this film, there haven't been any good Batman flicks. Unless you count Clooney's performance in Batman Forever.....in which he pulls out his "bat-credit card" and spouts the line, "I never leave the Batcave without it."

7.title: Mixed feelings
7.content: I'm in Thailand which has a release date of today, so I actually saw this film. My feelings are somewhat mixed. It does succeed as a hard action film, but was definitely too long. The joker character is truly terrifying this time around and the film's tone is appropriately violent and dark - both figuratively and literally, much of the action takes place at night. The script caters for the American audience by making the joker and his cronies less criminals and more terrorists - who are probably what Americans are most concerned about. This made it less appealing for me. Much better than average, but still not more than 7 out of 10.

7.title: Batman:The Dark Knight: Bruce Wayne: Come out into the Light
7.content: The Dark Knight pays homage to the Michael Keaton:Batman. A very dark venture into the twisted psychology's of the main characters. The Joker, (Heath Ledger) Harvey Dent, (Aaron Eckhart) and of course, Bruce Wayne, (Christian Bale) are all men whose souls have one thing in common; the desire to be perfect. This of course is impossible, because, being human makes one fallible. The trait, these three males also share, is the lack of the fear, of death. Unfortunately, this flick, spends too much time, dealing out, the death card. The Joker's personal card, is a playing card, with a joker, on the face. While the film is quite intense, there is too much murder, a foot, with little bloodshed. The rating of The Dark Knight is PG- 13, it may in fact, have been better served, with an R. The rating of any film, decides the audience, who can view said flicker, but in today's movie market, top box office billing is the driving force. The Dark Knight, is not intended for children, under 12 years of age. The question of reality verses fiction, in the mind of the young, is a defining factor, when trying to resolve this film, in the young mind. Listening to a conversation between two boys after viewing the film, brings out this question. "The Joker is a genius!" said one lad. I said, "The Joker, was a genius." The two boys said nothing in return, and walked away. So much for the understanding, of a film, intended for adults, by two youths. The fact, that the passing of Mr. Ledger, and his role, as The Joker, may be too much for children, to comprehend. Commissionair Gordon, (Gary Oldman) is the true hero, of The Dark Knight. He is portrayed as a man, with very, deep, family values. This quality, plants his feet firmly on the ground, and not with the death defying aspects of The Joker, Harvey Dent, or Bruce Wayne. When Gordon comes home, from a murderous night in Gothem, he is not alone. This factor separates him, from the rest of the main cast. The audience knows, that all of the rest of the main leads, are alone. The other problem with The Dark Knight, is the fact, that it is a sequel. When The Dark Knight, rides off alone, at the conclusion of the this film, the audience is not sure, what direction, this franchise will follow. With so many dying, the question is, who is left for a third?

7.title: Decent effort. Ledger outstanding, but Bale lacking
7.content: One of the best efforts at a batman movie which I've seen (though i still hold a special place in my heart for the Adam West version). As the joker, Heath Ledger is outstanding, the best villain of the trilogy by a mile. His manic personality is intermingled with shows of wit and ruthlessness while never going totally over the top. Morgan Freeman is solid, but seems to be coasting a little bit in this film when you compare to many other films he has done. The directing and screenplay remain consistently good throughout, though never outstanding. Sadly, for me at least, the movie fell down with the partnership between Bale and Caine. Neither convince me in anything they do and their chemistry together is very poor. Caine has always seemed overrated to me and Bale usually only shows flashes of his talent. Overall a decent watch, but probably not deserved of all the praise it has received. In my opinion though, I could watch it just for Heath Ledgers performance.

7.title: Atmospheric, yet also muddled & forced
7.content:
The Dark Knight is, like Batman Begins, an atmospheric piece of work that captures the filth of Gotham City very well. It is, however, not as good as Batman Begins since it seems to be a constant montage of anticipation of/and action sequences themselves.

The only aspect of The Dark Knight that was improved upon from Batman Begins are the action sequences. The ASL ( Average Shot Length ) in these sequences is a lot higher and we can now actually see what is going on in the fight scenes. There are still however a lot of fights later on in the film that feature a lot of amateurish shakycam camerawork, but it is common knowledge that Nolan's strength is not his action sequences, and the problem with The Dark Knight is that it nearly consists of wholly action sequences or the build up towards them. Car chases are still unremarkable while being filmed with low camera standpoints combined with inside shots of characters ( In the police vans ) we know nothing about. For some reason Nolan believes it to be necessary to show these unknown characters reactions to create some kind of cheap immersion.

The Dark Knight has pretty cinematography, sure. Like Batman Begins, it captures a visual atmosphere that complies with its overseriousness and dark tone. It is still not as atmospheric as the neo noir cinematography of Batman Begins, so the visuals might not be as fitting as they were in the previous entry, but standing alone it does provide some interesting images, such as the one of the Joker taunting Wayne to hit him in the middle of the street, or the entire trackingshot of the Joker attempting to blow up a hospital. It is all great to look at, but once again it doesn't quite capture that darkness and sleaze that Batman Begins did due to its Blade Runner-esque stills and smoke vents.

The acting is pretty good from most of the cast, except that Maggie Gyllenhaal is a significant step back from Katie Holmes's portrayal of Rachel. Much has been said about the praising of Heath Ledger as the Joker, who undoubtedly delivers an adequate performance albeit a bit overly theatrical. The tongue flicking, cue laughing, hair touching all becomes a little bit cliché after a while, but at least his antics are interesting to witness. His character in reality isn't very well written, as even though he isn't the typical 'Villain motivated by only money', he is still only motivated by one thing, which is chaos. The Joker is a psychopath with no honor to morals whatsoever, and the kind of writing for this simplistic psychopathic villain isn't really a stroke of genius on anybody's part, because his motivations are even lazier than the cliché money obsessed villains.

There is little room for character development due to the constant barrages of would be tension and action sequences. Only Harvey Dent has a character arc, and this arc is really once again the result of poor writing, as he changes from the idealistic hero of Gotham City to a revenge ridden monster due to one traumatic event. This is a character arc we have all seen before, and it is not original by any means. Not to mention the fact that he rips off No Country For Old Men's Anton Chigurh with his coin clip.

The Dark Knight is also muddled in its morality. It tries to create duality and discussions about right and wrong in its actions, but Nolan himself doesn't even seem to know what he wants here. The later stages of the film feature moral dilemma after moral dilemma which constantly forces the viewer into these life and death kind of situations. It really is a poor excuse for lack of storytelling and character to bring forth these cliché sequences constantly. It truly seems to believe it is telling something about human morality, but it is in fact only using these moments as disguise for the weakness in its writing & character.

Like Batman Begins, it constantly follows a montage like overly fast pace that decreases the audience's immersion significantly. This is coupled with a lot of irrelevant scenes such as Reese's attempted blackmail. There are a lot of over dramatic conversations in which the camera is constantly spinning around characters for some reason ( Much like in House of the Dead. Not that i am insinuating that The Dark Knight is as bad as that one, since that is ofcourse a great insult to the latter. However, these pretentious dynamics in camera movement do not have any place in this film. )

The Dark Knight has generally good acting, nice cinematography creating an atmospheric city albeit in lesser proportions than Batman Begins did, decent action sequences ( Especially for Nolan standards ), but it is also muddled in its view on dual morality. These situations are constantly repeated throughout the film which really makes it border on pretentiousness. The narrative isn't as complex and sophisticated as Batman Begins, but it still slightly succeeds as a reasonable film with a lot of visceral thrills.

7.title: A philosophical battle between order and chaos!
7.content:
The Dark Knight, directed by Christopher Nolan and released in 2008, stands as a monumental achievement in the superhero genre and cinema as a whole. This film not only redefined what comic book adaptations could be, but also pushed the boundaries of storytelling, character development, and thematic depth.

At the heart of the film is Heath Ledger's iconic portrayal of the Joker, a performance that earned him a posthumous Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor. Ledger's Joker is chaotic and unpredictable, embodying an anarchic philosophy that challenges Batman's moral code. The character is both terrifying and mesmerizing, with every scene he occupies pulsating with tension. His interactions with Batman, played by Christian Bale, are charged with a philosophical battle between order and chaos, heroism and villainy.

Bale's Batman is darker and more complex in this instalment, grappling with the consequences of his vigilantism and the moral dilemmas that come with it. The film explores themes of sacrifice, identity, and the fine line between hero and villain. The supporting cast, including Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent and Maggie Gyllenhaal as Rachel Dawes, adds layers to the narrative, with Dent's tragic transformation into Two-Face serving as a poignant commentary on the fragility of hope.

Nolan's direction is masterful, blending intense action sequences with a cerebral narrative. The cinematography by Wally Pfister is stunning, capturing Gotham City's grim atmosphere while elevating the film's emotional stakes. Hans Zimmer and James Newton Howard's score is haunting and exhilarating, perfectly complementing the film's tone and enhancing its dramatic moments.

One of the film's most striking aspects is its moral complexity. It doesn't provide easy answers; instead, it poses challenging questions about justice, the nature of evil, and the responsibilities of those who wield power. The ethical dilemmas faced by Batman and Dent resonate long after the credits roll, making The Dark Knight a thought-provoking experience.

Overall, The Dark Knight is a groundbreaking film that transcends its genre, blending action, philosophy, and unforgettable performances. It remains a benchmark for future superhero films and a compelling exploration of the duality of human nature. Whether viewed as an action-packed thriller or a deep moral exploration, it's a cinematic masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences around the world.

7.title: To Heath Ledger

Batman has human weaknesses and is still a superhero. This, I think, is what endears him to his fans. 'Batman Begins' brings that out beautifully. In 'The Dark Knight' the tension is not within Bruce Wayne, but outside. It is about how Gotham perceives him - the people of the city not liking him; blaming him for deaths, and so on. At this juncture, we see Joker, who apparently is challenging Batman at a moral level. Joker is a criminal for his own sake, not for money or anything else. Just as Batman is a protector of Gotham for his own sake. The plot does not bring out this moral dilemma or conflict of Batman, except in few instances. The plot is in conflict with itself in trying to create an action film and to create a moral war between the hero and the villain.

What makes the film out of the ordinary is Heath Ledger. His interpretation of the character and how he just seems to delve deep into that role is amazing. Few actors have lived out a character like that for the entire duration of a film.

The natural petulance of Christian Bale makes his ego and alter ego the most fascinating and complex of all film superheroes. 7.title: Loved this part of Batman
7.content:
I absolutely love The Dark Knight. It is my favorite superhero movie of all time, and I think it is one of the greatest movies ever made.

The Dark Knight is a dark, gritty, and realistic take on the Batman mythos. It is a character study of Bruce Wayne as he struggles to balance his vigilante persona with his civilian life. It is also a crime thriller that explores the themes of good vs. Evil, chaos vs. Order, and the nature of heroism.

The Dark Knight is beautifully shot, with stunning cinematography and memorable action sequences. The performances are all top-notch, with Christian Bale giving a tour-de-force performance as Batman/Bruce Wayne. Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker is one for the ages, and it is arguably the best villain performance in any superhero movie.

The Dark Knight is a masterpiece of modern cinema. It is a must-see for any fan of superhero movies, crime thrillers, or simply great movies.

Here are some of the things I love about The Dark Knight:

The performances: Christian Bale, Heath Ledger, Aaron Eckhart, and Gary Oldman all give incredible performances.

The story: The story is complex and engaging, with plenty of twists and turns.

The action: The action sequences are some of the best ever put to film.

The themes: The movie explores some complex themes, such as good vs. Evil, chaos vs. Order, and the nature of heroism.

The visuals: The movie is beautifully shot, with stunning cinematography.

The music: The score by Hans Zimmer is iconic.

I could go on and on about why I love The Dark Knight so much. It is simply one of the best movies ever made.

7.title: Amazing Work... for a Serious Superhero Movie
7.content:
The Serious Superhero Movie Movement has been going on for a while... from the Hulk reboots to the X-men franchise-- but none of them is anywhere as good as the Dark Knight (2008). Packed with solid production values and strong dramatic performances, the deal is sealed by the Seriously Psychotic Joker Character of Heath Ledger, who inspires equal amounts of fear and hate through the sheer unhinged power of his performance.

Written & directed more like a crime drama involving a serious vigilante rather than a comic superhero, the film manages to create and maintain an amazingly consistent and convincing pace and atmosphere. Gotham City feels like a real city threatened by crime although we never really see the crime syndicates and dirty cops at work; and the Joker feels like a criminal genius even though his level of dementia could never have allowed him to plan and lead like a crime boss. So the heightened level of realism can sometimes work against itself in places where the film still applied "superhero movie logic/ conventions"-- i.e. where superheroes/ criminals get things done too easily/ conveniently. I mean, I can accept that all of Batman's gadgets work-- but enter and leave Chinese airspace without authorization? Err, the last American aircraft that tried it in 2001 was captured on Hainan Island.

Doesn't really break any genre conventions-- the characters are still stereotypes despite the great characterizations, and the imaginative script still led to an ending stinking of post-cold war propaganda ("we need a common enemy/threat to unite us", blah X 3 is not really that smart/ meaningful-- see Watchmen, etc.)-- but it certainly made for a great ride.

7.title: Not the Film we deserved, but the one we Needed.
7.content:
A sequel to Batman Begins, The Dark Knight blew fan and critic expectations out of the water when if first hit theaters in 2008. It's been a cultural phenomenon and a fan favorite ever since. Not to mention it's regarded as one of the greatest movies OF ALL TIME.

Personally, I find this movie to be a teensy bit overrated. Don't get me wrong this movie is still excellent, but there are some problems with it. I like to usually start with the bad in my reviews, to get it over with.

The first thing is that I don't think Christian Bale's version of Batman fits the character very well (not his fault, it's the writing). I just don't see this guy as Bruce Wayne, or the Caped Crusader. He doesn't seem cold, distant or strict enough. It might also be the terrible voice that takes away from it a bit. Though that in and of itself can be a criticism of the trilogy as a whole.

The next sin the film commits is what a lot of Christopher Nolan films seem to do. The film is drastically over-complicated with at least four other sub-plots, that are very hard to follow, mostly because the dialogue is so quiet yet the music is so LOUD.

My last flaw of the film worth mentioning is some pacing problems. After the very start of the film, it drags on for a bit, then picks up, then drags on for a bit. Then the last act goes for a way too long, creating the notorious 4th act of the Dark Knight.

This movie is not nearly as pretentious as Batman Begins. One thing I really don't like about some movies is that they can really be pretentious, pretending to be bigger than they really are. The Dark Knight has little to no sanctimoniousness, and handle's it's dialogue and themes very well.

Speaking of very well let's move on with the good.

Heath Ledger's Joker is the highlight of this film. This is one of if not the greatest performance I've ever seen. He portrays a charismatic, yet extra unsettling version of the Joker who actually has a point half the time. That's one of the things that makes him interesting. Also his ambiguous past makes him mysterious and mythical. I could honestly go on for hours on how great of a villain the Joker is. Top 3 of all time for me.

The opening of the film is one of the best parts of the movie for me as well. It sets the tone for the rest of the movie, is filled with tension, fast paced, and introduces our beloved villain.

The acting all around in this movie is top notch, particularly Christian Bale (as Bruce Wayne), Michael Caine, Gary Oldman, Aaron Eckhart, Morgan Freeman, and Heath Ledger, just to name a few.

Rachel is written and handled a lot better than she was in the first movie. She actually seems to affect the plot and isn't as pretentious as she was in Batman Begins.

Aaron Eckhart as Two Face was one of the best casting choices. His performance believably shifted from a man trying to do the right thing, to a broken man who has lost is love and his dignity.

The best scene in the movie is the Interrogation scene. There is so much tension, we learn more about the Joker, and Batman doing what he does best, beating someone senseless, doesn't work on the Clown Prince of Crime.

Overall this movie is fantastic and worthy of most of the praise it receives. I give it a 9/10 with the title of "Excellent."

7.title: Nolan ups the ante!
7.content: The best super hero movie ever? Na...that would be Spiderman 2...but a pretty good super hero movie anyway? Yes! Chris Nolan has crafted an extremely dark, brooding film that takes the Batman franchise into hitherto unexplored territory. This is not to suggest that the film deviates from the pre-requisites of a summer blockbuster - big action set pieces & impressive SFX are woven into the narrative seamlessly. The matte painted, Gothic Gotham City that we have become accustomed to seeing in most Batman films is replaced by a very real, everyday American city that in fact adds to the creepiness by making the goings-on seem that much more identifiable. As the Joker unleashes terror on the city, its upto Batman & upright D.A. Harvey Dent to try & stop him. But can a man who has nothing to loose & is not motivated by greed be stopped? As Nolan explores issues of morality & conscience, the film descends into a nightmare world where the Joker is the puppeteer & the good guys his puppets. Though every actor excels, the film truly does belong to Ledger. While his sinister make-up and Nolan's very astute direction do help, credit has to be given to Ledger for the sheer energy and madness he brings to the role. The action, whenever it bursts forth, is indeed a big adrenaline rush. Of particular note is a stunning extradition sequence in Hong Kong & the Batcycle-Monster truck chase through the streets of Gotham that ends with a spectacular pay-off. The film however, does have its flaws. Most importantly the length. 20 minutes of trimming (particularly in the latter half) could have made it a much more streamlined product. Also, the excessively dark tone often weighs too heavy and makes one crave for the occasional relief. But gripes aside, 'The Dark Knight' is a rewarding night at the cinema - one that provides entertainment with a dollop of intelligence.

7.title: Lacks the punch of Begins, but The Dark Knight still delivers
7.content:
The Dark Knight is the second film in the Christopher Nolan trilogy of Batman films. Being a fan of the first film, Batman Begins, I had huge expectations for this I was expecting it to be just as good if not better then Begins. While The Dark Knight may lack the punch that Begins had, it's still a great film in its own right.

The Dark Knight is one of those films that does so much right but yet you feel that it could've been a better movie. I think the main problem with The Dark Knight is that it focus to much on the Joker and doesn't spend enough time on Bruce Wayne and Batman, while The Joker does make for a great villain, I still would've liked to see more time spent on Bruce Wayne and Batman.

Once again the acting in The Dark Knight is solid, everyone delivers great performances. Heath Ledger delivers the best performance in the film, delivering a Joker that is both creepy and fun. Ledger owns the role and is the best Joker we've seen in a Batman film yet, I don't think his performance in The Dark Knight will ever be topped. Once again Bale delivers a great performance as Bruce Wayne and Batman and had it not been for Heath Ledger's performance as The Joker, Bale would once again be the best actor in the film.

The story mostly works for The Dark Knight, having said that though I feel that the story wasn't as focused as it was in the first film. The story here focuses to much time on The Joker and not enough on other characters, the only character that I feel get's as much time as The Joker is Harvey Dent. I would have to say Dent is the best character in this film because you get emotionally invested in him, you feel for him and once you see what happens to him in the end, you can't help but feel bad for him because Dent could've became a hero in his own right. The story while not as good as Begins, does work overall.

The Dark Knight may not be as great as film as Begins, but it still delivers.

This review is dedicated in memory of Heath Ledger.

The scene then shifts to a parking garage where two criminal gangs are having a meeting when suddenly two people dressed as Batman arrive and a shootout ensues. Suddenly the real "Batman" (Christian Bale) enters the picture and not only subdues the criminals but also the Batman impersonators as well. Needless to say, it's only a matter of time before the Joker and Batman collide head on-and there will be a lot of chaos and mayhem along the way. Now rather than reveal any more I will just say that I honestly didn't think anybody could top the performance of Jack Nicholson as the Joker in the "Batman" movie of 1989. But I am here to say that Heath Ledger totally dominated the Joker persona like nobody else has ever done. He was truly excellent. Likewise, Christian Bale also performed quite well as Batman. Along with that, the movie itself was one of the better "Batman" films ever produced as well. That being said, I have rated it accordingly. Above average.

7.title: Rushed plot, too many important events occur offscreen
7.content:
I used to really like this movie, but the older I get, the more I see that the plot is incredibly rushed and way too packed (reminds me of the final season of Game of Thrones). All of the events occur too quickly...and even though it's a 2.5 hour movie, another 30 minutes should have been added for better transitions from one scene to the next. Worst of all, this movie completely lacks foreshadowing.

The kidnappings of Harvey Dent and Rachel....one minute they're kissing goodbye and the next minute they're tied down to oil drums with explosives...and they don't show us anything that happened in between? They at least could have shown Ramirez making a phone call to Maroni to give the audience a clue that something bad is about to happen. Nope, nothing. The "social experiment" scene where neither boat decides to blow each other up because "Gotham is full of people ready to believe in good"..... I can't find one single moment in the movie that even remotely foreshadows that. The guy with the bomb in his chest in the jail....where in the world he did come from? I don't remember seeing anything leading up to that.

It feels like DC expected fans to sit back and be entertained without caring much about the mechanisms of the plot. And obviously it worked. It even hooked me when I first saw it. Like most people, I mostly liked it because of the Joker. Looking beyond that, I now see that this is one of the most overrated movies of all time.

This movie has a 9.0 rating, but it is not because it has a well-constructed plot.

7.title: Na-na na-na na-na na-na na-na na-na na-na na! Dark Kniiiiiiight!
7.content:
The Dark Knight, the second installment of Christopher Nolan's Dark Knight trilogy. Box office skyrocketed, audiences worshiped it and critics gave it countless gold stars; it was easily considered the best of the Batman films.

Bruce Wayne/Batman, played by Christian Bale, is a superhero who joins forces with Gotham City Officer Jim Gordon, played Gary Oldman, and District Attorney Harvey Dent, played by Aaron Eckhart, to fight the underworld mob leaders, who are under control of the maniacal terrorist, The Joker-- played by the late Heath Ledger.

The plot seems simple, no? The Dark Knight is basically a series of events. While it's mostly events after events, they do flow nicely and fall into place for the next action for the characters to partake in. And most of all, you do want to know the outcome of the entire experience. It's also a tragedy story at best, especially for the character of Harvey Dent. After the entire left side of his face his burnt, the part where he screams in agony of his transformation after losing everything he loved, but all you hear is one musical note that gets uncomfortably louder.

The Joker is cool, but at times, I think he was too serious. I know that "well, that's how The Joker is". But, The Joker is supposed to be funny at times too. I only giggled a few times, but to be fair, he was terrifying. As The Joker should be anyway. I just thought they went a little too overboard of him being just a mass murderer.

My biggest problem with the movie? The dialogue. It's nice and stuff, but it sounds like something you'd hear in speeches. They don't sound like realistic words, they sound like speeches. "Batman stands for something more important"/"You either die a hero or you live long to see yourself become the villain"/"Your stand against organized crime is the first legitimate ray of light in Gotham in decades"/"Because he's the hero Gotham deserves, but not the one it needs right now."

I know they sound like adult choices of words, but there's a difference between realistic words and speeches. And whenever there's a "speechy moment" it's usually how Batman is noble or the importance of the characters and it's like every five minutes. The thing is, we already KNOW the importance of the characters, their needs and motivations. You don't need to give speeches about them, just let their actions speak for themselves and have them talk like normal people instead of talking about the situation.

Aside from that, the movie is just great. The action is great too. There's no crazy jump cuts and the shaky cam is used to a minimum, which is pretty rare you see in movies today. When you get past the preachy-ness, The Dark Knight is a great Batman film to watch and such a good action flick to entertain yourself with. See it and you won't be disappointed.

I usually only find the works of Marvel Studios so overrated. Heath Ledger does his job well, but despite his involuntary smacking, doesn't manage to match the comic book character of the Joker. Only his confusion about his origins is reminiscent of the Killing Joke Joker. I also find the characters a bit flat and too slick in typical Nolan fashion although the story could hardly be more dramatic. The Bale Bruce is portrayed more and more egotistically, although he only reaches the peak of narrow-mindedness in Rises.

In addition, Nolan has also scrapped the great setting from Batman Begins and simply renamed Manhattan Gotham, and I will never approve of the exchange of actors during ongoing film series. Entertaining work that suffers from a lack of atmosphere, changes too much from its predecessor here and there and misses the mark by far. I'd also like to say something about the Batpod... what is it and why do you have to use it to turn around on walls in such an extremely stupid way? I give Nolan credit for the "then you'll love me" performance, but even this moment doesn't come close to the "swear on me" performance from Batman begins, nor does the film have the charm and atmosphere of the Burton films, nor the presence of a Batfleck bat. The film is very entertaining in my eyes, but did not excite me as much as Batman 89 and Batman begins.

7.title: A Great Sequel
