Oh, one more complaint, which I honestly should knock it down to a 7 for, little to no blood. Many scenes that would have made great kill shots and the camera cuts away, do us a favor and make the next one R rated.

I had to roll my eyes every time I heard about how good Heath did as the Joker, but he was really great...though I thought the "why so serious", why did that become a catchphrase?, scene was one of the weakest in the film.

Overall a great film, even for people like me that hate superhero films. Everyone treating Maggie Gyllenhaal like she was the best looking woman in the whole city was pretty laughable, but it's easily overlooked. I wonder how future installments will fair without the amazing Ledger returning to his role of the Joker.

8.title: A good superhero movie but overrated
8.content:
Back when I originally saw "The Dark Knight" it was still in theatres and the hype was intense. Users on this site had made it the highest rated movie of all time and professional critics were also giving it high marks. I had been let down a bit after the hype for "Batman Begins" a few years earlier, so I was wary of the same thing happening again. Ultimately, there's no doubt that my reaction at the time was negatively influenced by the hype. Basically, I thought that the movie was merely decent and far from perfect. Having just rewatched the movie a decade later, my opinion has softened somewhat.

The movie picks up not too long after the events of "Batman Begins". As teased in the final scene of that movie, the focal villain this time around is the Joker, arguably Batman's most recognizable foe. With Batman cleaning up the streets of Gotham City, mob bosses are finding their iron grip on the populace loosening as others are becoming defiant as well, including the popular new District Attorney, Harvey Dent. Recognizing their vulnerable position, the Joker offers to rid them of Batman... for a price.

The script by Christopher Nolan and his brother Jonathan is a cut above most superhero movies. It's intricately plotted and has more dramatic heft than you might expect. Supposedly it was mainly inspired by the comic book stories "The Killing Joke" and "The Long Halloween", both top notch sources. Personally, I'm not sure that I'm completely on board with the Nolans' interpretation of the Joker but that may just be personal preference. I think you'd be hard-pressed to argue that it's not a vivid portrayal, regardless of whether or not it matches any preconceived notions that you may have about the character. However, as I see it, the script is not without its faults from a narrative perspective. At two and a half hours, the movie seems a bit bloated, which often happens in superhero movies when multiple villains are in the mix. Maybe some or most of the Two-Face storyline should have been left for the final chapter in the series. Also, I think that the movie was hampered a bit by its PG-13 rating, since the Nolans were broaching some themes with the Joker that could've benefited from less restraint. Lastly, the realistic tone of the film sometimes doesn't work so well when dealing with characters that are, let's face it, fairly outlandish.

When talking about the cast, it's hard to be objective about Heath Ledger's performance as the Joker, considering that he died about six months before the movie opened. No doubt this was one of the things that got everyone talking about the movie. In retrospect, even though I don't necessarily agree with this characterization of the Joker, I'd have to admit that Ledger contributed a standout performance in the role. When you consider that he posthumously won an Oscar, a Golden Globe and a BAFTA for this performance, its pretty clear that it was something special. Granted, awards voters likely wouldn't have been so generous in bestowing acting awards on a superhero movie if Ledger was still alive but that shouldn't take away from his transformation here. It's a completely different performance for him and is as impressive, in its own way, as his previous Oscar-nominated performance in "Brokeback Mountain".

Apart from Ledger, the bulk of the cast was made up of returnees from the first movie. Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Gary Oldman & Morgan Freeman were all up to their usual standards here. Meanwhile, Maggie Gyllenhaal took over the Rachel Dawes role from Katie Holmes and I think that it was a change for the better. The other notable new addition was Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent. I'd say that he's got the right look for the part but I was never a big fan of his acting in general. The large supporting cast features some recognizable faces as well, including Eric Roberts and, in small roles, Cillian Murphy, Anthony Michael Hall & William Fichtner. Overall, not a bad cast at all.

From a visual standpoint, the movie looks quite good. Director Christopher Nolan decided to shoot some of the scenes in IMAX format and the results were stunning. The action setpieces were also nicely handled. If I have one complaint about the visuals it's that the CGI for Two-Face isn't quite convincing, which makes me wonder if they could have done any better with makeup/prosthetics. The score by James Newton Howard & Hans Zimmer is also well done, with my preference being for Zimmer's tense Joker themes.

As of this writing, "The Dark Knight" sits at #4 in IMDb's top rated movies list. While I certainly believe that the movie has merit, I don't think that it belongs anywhere near that lofty perch. So, I would advise you to watch it with tempered expectations or else you may find yourself reacting overly negatively towards it as a result, as I initially did.

8.title: Plot
8.content: The Dark Knight is a 2008 superhero film directed, co-produced, and co-written by Christopher Nolan. Featuring the DC Comics character Batman, the film is the second part of Nolan's The Dark Knight Trilogy and a sequel to 2005's Batman Begins, starring an ensemble cast including Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Heath Ledger, Gary Oldman, Aaron Eckhart, Maggie Gyllenhaal and Morgan Freeman. In the film, Bruce Wayne/Batman (Bale), Police Lieutenant James Gordon (Oldman) and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Eckhart) form an alliance to dismantle organized crime in Gotham City, but are menaced by a criminal mastermind known as the Joker (Ledger) who seeks to undermine Batman's influence and create chaos.

8.title: An Excellent Movie!

This was truly an awesome movie.

8.title: Heath Ledger's Swan song
8.content:
Dark as night and nearly as long, Christopher Nolan's new Batman movie feels like a beginning and something of an end. Pitched at the divide between art and industry, poetry and entertainment, it goes darker and deeper than any other Hollywood movie.Mr. Nolan has found a way to make Batman relevant to his time — meaning, to ours — investing him with shadows that remind you of the character's troubled beginning. That's nothing new, but what is surprising, actually startling, is that in The Dark Knight, which picks up the story after the first film ends, Mr. Nolan has turned Batman into a villain's sidekick.

That would be the Joker, of course,this character is one of the most heinous of the villains that has ever existed in any comic book.This character represents a theory about existence that part of me believes that all people wish we could embrace, in our own way. Don't start thinking I'm crazy just yet. Hear me out, as I explain one of the most intricate and complicated people who has ever appeared in fiction.

The Joker is a catharsis about the dark side of a part of us that we don't acknowledge – the part that doesn't want to obey the little niceties of society. There is a reason that characters like Gregory House and Eric Cartman are so popular. They represent the idea that we all, in some way, wish we could be a part of. They don't obey society's rules. They don't follow the set way of thinking. They do their own thing, and to hell with everybody else. Let's be honest, all of us wish that we could do that. But the Joker is part of the darker side of that way of thinking. Not only does he not want to follow the rules of society, but also he actively seeks to destroy the rules of society as we understand them. In his mind, chaos is the only actual truth in the world.We cannot deny the fact that Joker imprint strong impact on our conscious and subconscious existence.

It is ridiculous how much praise "The Dark Knight" truly deserves. Even the most elaborate descriptions feel like they're still not doing the movie justice. The film is for Batman fans, for Christopher Nolan fans, for fans of good storytelling, for fans of good writing, for fans of amazing cinematography, for fans of some of the strongest acting performances ever to be filmed, and for fans of action, crime, or dramatic films; long story short, the film can and probably will be enjoyed by anyone.

It is one of the only films to come out in recent years that not only lives up to the hype, but leaped over it and actually deserves every ounce of it. By the time you get to the end credits, you'll immediately want to see it again and you'll be just as excited the second time(and possibly third time) through. It's that good. These fingers can continue to praise this movie until they're purple from typing so much, but they'll leave it at this; it really was the movie of 2008. If it wasn't the greatest superhero film up until that point, it was at least the most captivating. It truly feels timeless and the type of film that'll stand up to greatness for eternity.

8.title: The Dark Knight review
8.content:
'The Dark Knight' is definitely one of the best superhero films out there. With the most phenomenal villain on screen. Batman vs The Joker. This is the second of the Christopher Nolan Batman trilogy: the first being 'Batman Begins', the third 'The Dark Knight Rises'.

A new villain has come to Gotham, one crazier and extreme unlike any other that Batman (Christian Bale) has seen before. In his crazed make-up and his purple suit, The Joker (Heath Ledger) resembles a mad man with nothing to lose and only chaos to gain. Meanwhile, there's a new hero in town, the District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart), who will do anything to clean the streets of Gotham, a knight in shining armour determined to take the Mob down and all the criminals in his city. But The Joker is determined in his acknowledgement of Batman being his perfect half to "complete" him, he wants to continue a warp of madness in the city that messes everything up for Dent, forcing a clean city to turn on its head.

I truly think this is a brilliant film. It is quite a long one, but there is so much to the plot that you become emotionally invested, warped into Gotham. There is so much meaning and drive to the plot that brings this film to light. The director is obviously essential in making this trilogy as phenomenal as it is. The brilliant use of sound and lighting makes the audience feel tense in the crucial places. But we cannot forget the outstanding cast of this film. Personally, I think Christian Bale is one of the best Batman's. With Michael Caine and Morgan Freeman on his side as Alfred and Lucius Fox retrospectively, who can't appreciate the characters? Additionally, the magnificent Gary Oldman as Gordon, the officer trailing the streets with Batman in the shadows on his side. However, I've left best till last, the brilliance of the villain can never be forgotten. Heath Ledger brings The Joker into a different, creepy, unnerving light. Every word is listened to in tension. His laughs echo through the film in remembrance of Gotham's crash. He becomes the antagonist and brings this phenomenal cast to a close.

I would definitely recommend watching this film. You become warped into Gotham with Bruce Wayne's new chaotic life where The Joker personally victimises Batman. The film is a whirlwind of action and special effects excellently executed for the audience to escape into. You really don't know what can happen with The Joker in the mix.

8.title: As good as a superhero movie can be
8.content:
As the title suggests, I think this is probably the best superhero movie we've been blessed with. What happens when an actual good director with a great cinematic vision and the aspiration to convey deeper themes picks up a movie idea that is inherently childish and unrealistic, like a superhero one? Well, this movie (and trilogy).

It has a grown man in a hyper-advanced bat-themed suit, a grown man in clown make-up, a guy who can still see and speak despite getting half his face burnt, and we're meant to take them all seriously when they start acting like deep and realistic villains/anti-heros/vigilantes. Yeah, okay. You also have to take the people of Gotham seriously when they can't figure out Bruce Wayne is Batman despite him being practically the only person in the city rich enough to afford that kind of gear.

Those are basically the theoretical flaws which may bring sophisticated viewers to rate more mature movies higher... however, I am not that sophisticated. I applaud the depth that the director has tried to bring to a franchise which, as involved as it is in telling pretty mature stories about vengeance, justice and corruption, is pretty much viewed as "just" a superhero comic for children. Heath Ledger's acting is obviously legendary and the movie's elements' all-round are well-executed and of high quality.

The main villain from this movie is interesting and the reason this movie in particular is the highest rated one in the franchise. His relationship to the protagonist, and aspirations and worldview in general, are quite interesting and even unique though obviously pretty extreme.

I removed one point due to the fact that you have to suspend your logic and blindly believe in some aspects in this story. Some of it was mentioned already with the bat-obssessed billionaire and what he can do in battle as a result of his gear. The other point I removed because, after all, this is quite a linear storyline that can be simply described as - hero vs villain, with some other crooks on the side. The suspense comes mainly from what Joker is planning which is interesting, cruel and unexpected, but there are hardly any twists or more mysteries to be uncovered in this work. It is, above all, a movie that relies on action such as fights, rather than mystery or psychological depth, to entertain and keep viewers compelled.

I don't think The Dark Knight (2008) does much wrong at all. It's just that other movies are better than it, as they are less linear and more captivating for me as a bigger fan of deeper mysteries and suspense than of fights and superheroes. So an 8 only felt natural.

8.title: The Joker Dictates The Narrative
8.content:
Firstly I acknowledge the masterful way this movie is put together, the acting and the action, as all others have described.

The Joker leads to story throughout this blockbuster thriller, leaving everyone struggling to comprehend and catch up with his deranged vision of power. When he is finally in police custody, and is in the interview room, batman appears from nowhere (?), to question, torture and threaten the criminal. But we find the Joker once again chatting, laughing and taunting the caped crusader. He leads the conversation, while ignoring any pain or fear he might feel. He arouses Batman's curiosity, laughs at his naive understanding of justice, and then taunts him with titbits of information. He controls the conversation. Meanwhile the Joker has magically orchestrated all kinds of mayhem. Somehow, not explained, he planted buildings, hospitals, ferries with explosive leading police, batman and the public clueless as to what he is really doing. He has organised trucks, weapons cables and traps perfectly, despite everyone, including crimes bosses, hating and opposing him. Moving though the shadows with his small dedicated band of clowns he does whatever he wants with his signature brand of "funny terrorism". How does one pack enough hidden explosives to blow up a hospital, undetected, and then walk into the building on high alert in his garish costume? It strains credibility in a disturbing way.

This was my main reaction to the story, it is a disturbing vision of a city torn apart by greed, mania and revenge. Fortunately the world we live in is not that bad. Maybe the meta narrative is about the twisted, two faced nature of Man, his deep corruption, and yet the ultimate triumph of the forces of Good over Evil. Indeed the movie throws up questions like, who can you trust, who can be turned into an evil monster, how much power should even a good person have? And how can such a dishevelled person organise so well?

I liked the movie but found it a disturbingly dark fantasy of violence.

8.title: Best Movie so far I've seen
8.content:
The Dark Knight, directed by Christopher Nolan, is one of the most groundbreaking superhero films ever made. The movie transcends the typical superhero genre by delivering a deeply philosophical narrative, exploring complex themes like justice, morality, and chaos. What truly sets The Dark Knight apart is the Oscar-winning performance by Heath Ledger as the Joker, a portrayal so chilling and unpredictable that it redefined villainy in cinema.

The film is not just about action-packed sequences, although the stunts and visuals are remarkable. Nolan crafted a story that dives into the psychology of both hero and villain, making the audience question the fine line between good and evil. Christian Bale's Batman struggles with his inner demons, while Ledger's Joker brings anarchy to Gotham, forcing Batman to confront the chaos head-on. The tension between these two forces creates a gripping narrative from start to finish.

Moreover, the cinematography, sound design, and Hans Zimmer's iconic score elevate the film to a level rarely seen in superhero movies. Nolan's choice to ground the movie in a more realistic setting and his focus on human emotions and ethics make The Dark Knight a cinematic classic.

8.title: How it's done

Nolan's move to a dark origin instead of the campy tongue in cheek that Burton liked, moved this story and franchise forward in ways that led to the new invigoration of super hero movies today. It was this style of brooding storytelling that energized fans the world over again for this franchise. It was a surprise and so well done. While I did enjoy the Burton films, I was also a lot younger and didn't appreciate really good honest storytelling. This honest origin story paved the way for good super hero movies like Iron Man and Ant Man. Yes, I said Ant Man. Hell, even Deadpool used this style in a way that captured the fans emotions and hearts, while breaking down the 4th wall...but that is a review for another day.

8.title: The Ultimate The Dark Knight review
8.content:
I wanna use the Roger Ebert's review on The Dark Knight, "Batman" isn't a comic book anymore. Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" is a haunted film that leaps beyond its origins and becomes an engrossing tragedy. It creates characters we come to care about. That's because of the performances, because of the direction, because of the writing, and because of the superlative technical quality of the entire production. This film, and to a lesser degree "Iron Man," redefine the possibilities of the "comic-book movie." "The Dark Knight" is not a simplistic tale of good and evil. Batman is good, yes, The Joker is evil, yes. But Batman poses a more complex puzzle than usual: The citizens of Gotham City are in an uproar, calling him a vigilante and blaming him for the deaths of policemen and others. And the Joker is more than a villain. He's a Mephistopheles whose actions are fiendishly designed to pose moral dilemmas for his enemies.

The key performance in the movie is by the late Heath Ledger, as the Joker. Will he become the first posthumous Oscar winner since Peter Finch? His Joker draws power from the actual inspiration of the character in the silent classic "The Man Who Laughs" (1928). His clown's makeup more sloppy than before, his cackle betraying deep wounds, he seeks revenge, he claims, for the horrible punishment his father exacted on him when he was a child. In one diabolical scheme near the end of the film, he invites two ferry-loads of passengers to blow up the other before they are blown up themselves. Throughout the film, he devises ingenious situations that force Batman (Christian Bale), Commissioner Gordon (Gary Oldman) and District Attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) to make impossible ethical decisions. By the end, the whole moral foundation of the Batman legend is threatened.

Because these actors and others are so powerful, and because the movie does not allow its spectacular special effects to upstage the humans, we're surprised how deeply the drama affects us. Eckhart does an especially good job as Harvey Dent, whose character is transformed by a horrible fate into a bitter monster. It is customary in a comic book movie to maintain a certain knowing distance from the action, to view everything through a sophisticated screen. "The Dark Knight" slips around those defenses and engages us.

Yes, the special effects are extraordinary. They focus on the expected explosions and catastrophes, and have some superb, elaborate chase scenes. The movie was shot on location in Chicago, but it avoids such familiar landmarks as Marina City, the Wrigley Building or the skyline. Chicagoans will recognize many places, notably La Salle Street and Lower Wacker Drive, but director Nolan is not making a travelogue. He presents the city as a wilderness of skyscrapers, and a key sequence is set in the still-uncompleted Trump Tower. Through these heights, the Batman moves at the end of strong wires, or sometimes actually flies, using his cape as a parasail.

The plot involves nothing more or less than the Joker's attempts to humiliate the forces for good and expose Batman' secret identity, showing him to be a poser and a fraud. He includes Gordon and Dent on his target list, and contrives cruel tricks to play with the fact that Bruce Wayne once loved, and Harvey Dent now loves, Assistant D.A. Rachel Dawes (Maggie Gyllenhaal). The tricks are more cruel than he realizes, because the Joker doesn't know Batman's identity. Heath Ledger has a good deal of dialogue in the movie, and a lot of it isn't the usual jabs and jests we're familiar with: It's psychologically more complex, outlining the dilemmas he has constructed, and explaining his reasons for them. The screenplay by Christopher Nolan and his brother Jonathan (who first worked together on "Memento") has more depth and poetry than we might have expected.

Two of the supporting characters are crucial to the action, and are played effortlessly by the great actors Morgan Freeman and Michael Caine. Freeman, as the scientific genius Lucius Fox, is in charge of Bruce Wayne's underground headquarters, and makes an ethical objection to a method of eavesdropping on all of the citizens of Gotham City. His stand has current political implications. Caine is the faithful butler Alfred, who understands Wayne better than anybody, and makes a decision about a crucial letter.

Nolan also directed the previous, and excellent, "Batman Begins" (2005), which went into greater detail than ever before about Bruce Wayne's origins and the reasons for his compulsions. Now it is the Joker's turn, although his past is handled entirely with dialogue, not flashbacks. There are no references to Batman's childhood, but we certainly remember it, and we realize that this conflict is between two adults who were twisted by childhood cruelty — one compensating by trying to do good, the other by trying to do evil. Perhaps they instinctively understand that themselves.

Something fundamental seems to be happening in the upper realms of the comic-book movie. "Spider-Man II" (2004) may have defined the high point of the traditional film based on comic-book heroes. A movie like the new "Hellboy II" allows its director free rein for his fantastical visions. But now "Iron Man" and even more so "The Dark Knight" move the genre into deeper waters. They realize, as some comic-book readers instinctively do, that these stories touch on deep fears, traumas, fantasies and hopes. And the Batman legend, with its origins in film noir, is the most fruitful one for exploration.

In his two Batman movies, Nolan has freed the character to be a canvas for a broader scope of human emotion. For Bruce Wayne is a deeply troubled man, let there be no doubt, and if ever in exile from his heroic role, it would not surprise me what he finds himself capable of doing.

8.title: Nolan plays 3-dimensional chess in the most intelligent superhero film you will ever see
8.content:
Writing a synopsis for this film is quite the challenge. Any description will not do justice to the sheer experience of how the events materialise and collide on the screen. I can, however, provide a basic set-up. Batman (once again played by Christian Bale) has helped to clean up the streets of Gotham. His influence has been so impactful that hotshot DA Harvey Dent (played by Aaron Eckhart) has been able to rise through the ranks without being wiped out by Gotham's criminals. In the courts of law, Dent prosecutes just as effectively as Batman doles out vigilante justice on the streets. But just as it seems the net is fully closing in, a wild card appears and threatens to drive the entire city into its worst crisis yet.

This wild card is named Joker (played by Heath Ledger). He is a dangerous, murderous criminal who has more than a taste for the theatrical. By initially operating alongside what remains of the criminal entities of Gotham, he finds a way of injecting new life into the bloodstream of its darkest forces. But he is more than just a criminal. He is "an agent of chaos". He can not be reasoned with; he can not be intimidated. He is a nihilist who intends to destroy Gotham purely for his sport.

Game changed. With the 2nd installment of the Christopher Nolan Batman series, we are exposed to one the most mentally stimulating, philosophically dense films ever put to celluloid. Almost the entire run-time operates as a philosophical puzzle wrapped in a moral dilemma. Characters are constantly forced to make choices which focus on either their own interests or the interests of the greater societal good. Underlying this are fundamental questions relating to fate: do the decisions that we make matter? Do we have any control? And is the road to hell finally paved with good intentions?

The screenplay of "The Dark Knight" has received the highest accolade that it is possible to bestow: it has entered popular culture. "Why so serious?", "You either die a hero or live long enough to become the villain", "He is not the hero we deserve, but the hero we need", "Some people just want to see the world burn". Not since The Godfather have so many quotable one-liners entered the public consciousness. There is something in the writing of this film which encapsulates fundamental truths about human experience. It resonates, powerfully. And the Nolan brothers, the scriptwriters, demonstrate just how insanely gifted they are in writing lines that strike the right note.

Talking about striking the right note, no review of this film ought ever to be written without expounding upon Heath Ledger's preternatural performance as Joker. Analysing his approach to this film is the equivalent to deconstructing Picasso. Yes, this is beyond technique, this is art and Ledger provides the "Guernica" of acting turns in this role. Giving just a flavour of his achievement, he exudes dark charisma with fascinating facial tics. He also employs vocal cadence which lulls with a superficial playfulness, all the while, suggesting malice and mortal danger. His death so soon after the making of this film is one of cinema's great tragic losses. Only James Dean and River Phoenix can be held up as similar examples of such immense acting talent being taken in the prime of its existence.

Directorially, this film sees Nolan fully realise his gift for delivering a big-budget style. This is something he has now become renowned for. It must be said that there is some strange camera-work in the first act of the film, cameras constantly spinning in a circular arc is not generally an engaging look. But this is jettisoned quickly enough and, instead, we get some sumptuous spectacle. The immortal scene of Joker outside the hospital has to be the highlight, but sonar vision, Batman flying through the high-rise buildings of Hong Kong and the final Batman, Joker stand off deserve to be mentioned also.

Now onto the plot. The sheer ambition of it is breathtaking. It presents constant twists and turns and is replete with diabolical scenarios that the characters have to contend with. It is awe-inspiring in its scope and originality. Yet... I think it goes too far. After just one of Joker's "games", you'd expect half the city to have had a nervous breakdown. Yet they are continually put through the ringer with psychological torture built upon further psychological torture. It is almost impossible not to become inured by this as a viewer.

Then there is the perennial Nolan issue of balancing a focus on hearts and minds. Personally, I was mentally riveted throughout but, emotionally, I became disengaged during key parts of the film. This is the danger when you have two writers who are so clearly fascinated by concepts: you lose touch with flesh and blood reality. And I don't mean this as a criticism of the suspension of disbelief, which is, once again, very much required for this film, I mean it in the sense of having a true understanding, or even interest in, the emotional aspects of one's characters.

I will avoid major plot spoilers here, but there is a particular choice Batman makes which, although designed to demonstrate nobility, would essentially indicate that the man is completely devoid of feeling. I understand the symbolism: as Joker is the agent of chaos, Batman is the agent of order. Everything he does is designed to keep Gotham City functioning in as harmonious a manner as possible. But while Joker can afford to be an allegorical symbol, and Heath Ledger clearly understood this, the human centre of this film can not. Batman must maintain his humanity, otherwise his value is diminished. For me, Batman is at his most fascinating when he is human, all too human. Turning Batman into a cartoon diminishes him (ahem... "Batman & Robin") but so does turning him into an abstraction.

Nevertheless, this film is a triumph of original, intelligent, visually exuberant storytelling. It is, undoubtedly, one of the most impressive films ever made. But I contend that there's more to great art than being impressive. I believe that great art connects with the heart and the mind. You must feel the experience deep within you, not solely be mesmerised by the content of its intellectual prowess. It is for this reason that I regard "The Dark Knight" as a brilliant film but not necessarily a great one, or, to put it another way, the film we deserve but not necessarily the film we need...

8.title: Dark k(N)ight of the Soul
8.content:
(Note: this is a pretentious essay, if you want a standard review read the thousands of others)

The 2008 summer blockbuster & sixth Batman film surprised many with its bleak vision of a crumbling American landscape (Gotham here) beset by two opposing forces of pure will, aiming to re-mold the charred urban wasteland in their own image.

Superhero films are a dime a dozen in our brave new world, but Chris Nolan attempts to one-up them with his new take on the caped crusader: quasi-realism. His Bats, disregarding pretty boy Hollywood exterior, is more damaged goods than valiant hero (much like Christian Bale IRL ha ha)more walking wounded than champion of the few, something shared by the whole cast.

In its two archetypal bogeymen Batman & Joker, we see not so much hero & villain as wannabe Nietzschean over-men, two soul-mates liberated of the slave mentality that besets our Gothamite rabble; one walking-GPD rich & the other rising from ash clogged gutters- both driven by demons projected onto the besieged cityscape.

This is Batman for the 9/11 era: no more glitz or gay rubber of the Joel Schumacher/Tim Burton schools, terrorism has downgraded the conversation into something more severe. Shades of grey & hard decisions abound, with that collective sense of teetering on some unfathomable edge worse than ever (in no small part due to the soundtrack - like straight razors cutting up a string section)

Only the post modern probings of Alan Moore's master thesis WATCHMEN (itself something of a Holy Grail) matches the scope found here; of note particularly is its rather obvious examination of the shared plight of Bats & Mr. J, two heads of Harvey Dent's scarred silver coin (& of course, in nowhere but the two-party country of the film's origin do we find such a binary nation).

Batman & Joker are textbook psychotics (if we are to run with the conclusions of Dark Knight's heart of darkness)toddlers trapped in the intellect of adulthood. Batman is the Ego to Joker's ID, his quest to clean up the streets as flat out batsh*t as Joker's sermon of brimstone & hellfire.

Joker is so much easier to understand & revile then the seemingly admirable intentions of deeply messed-up Bruce Wayne, and yet,If Batman & Joker represent equal sides of the same coin then Thesis + Antithesis= Synthesis.Both sides of the movie's duality make it possible for the other to exist: If Batman killed Joker during the disappointing climax, he would no doubt create him again with just his mission statement alone.

Batman would also have to kill himself if he killed Joker, defusing the escalation both figures have brought upon crime wave Gotham (....assuming both sides aren't emboldened by the psychotic actions of our sick costumers & rise up to take their place. Monkey see monkey do, as the film's hockey mask wannabes demonstrate) Batman didn't kill Joker- not so much out of his awesome dedication to morality & the good fight but because he couldn't kill himself; he doesn't want to stop playing Cops & Robbers (he too, would follow Depression addled Americans into permanent unemployment)

His spoiled palette only savours the thrill of the Cause, not the plebeian mores of the slaves below. Joker's savage tastes meanwhile co-inside, preferring the wisdom of the Abyss to the hypocritical masses living above. Both live or both die to maintain proper balance & both hold their subjects in secret & not-so-secret contempt, terrorists of the first order who make their mutual destructions seem like a ball; Joker especially with his 'anarchy for dummies' platform, exploring that on-going, uniquely American dilemma of extreme bootstrap individuality in our Global age, finally turned on its head to expose the rotten belly beneath.

Batman arrives at stalemate, not relinquishing the mantle of hero yet, determined to play martyr & sacrificial lamb/jihad leader as long as he can avoid the implications of truly succeeding in holy war (and paving the way for the sequel 'natch).

....Enter third wheel Harvey Dent, Superego, midway point between titans, the Gotham District Attorney waging a battle of his own with big talk & bigger plans, daring to reach for the sun but balking at the price when his moment arrives.Failing to either throw in with the light or dark, Yin or Yang leaves all hostage to the Jokers & Bruce Wayne's of the planet.

White Knight Harvey Dent ends the film literally torn in two by awesome extremes he deftly skated prior, losing his foothold when the game gets too real, the vanity behind his bluster exposed.His symbolic scarring remains forever a reminder of being pulled in two directions at once.

Predictably, our fallen knight sinks back into victim mentality, the lesser way favoured by the plebes he sought to transcend, raging at the stars that he could've lost so much & holding all accountable in his rush to vengeance except himself.

Binary is Blase.

8.title: A Cinematic Triumph of Darkness and Heroism: The Dark Knight
8.content:
"The Dark Knight," directed by Christopher Nolan and released in 2008, redefined the superhero genre and elevated it to unprecedented heights. This dark and brooding masterpiece stands as a testament to the power of storytelling, pushing boundaries and challenging viewers' perceptions of heroism and morality.

At the heart of the film is the iconic Batman, portrayed by Christian Bale with unparalleled intensity and conviction. Bale's portrayal captures the tormented soul of Bruce Wayne, a vigilante driven by a desire to protect Gotham City from the forces of chaos and corruption. Opposite him, Heath Ledger delivers a legendary performance as the Joker, a chaotic and unpredictable antagonist who becomes the embodiment of anarchy.

"The Dark Knight" transcends the confines of a typical superhero film. It explores complex themes such as the nature of good and evil, the blurred lines between hero and villain, and the sacrifices one must make for the greater good. The screenplay, penned by Nolan and his brother Jonathan Nolan, delves deep into the psychological and moral dilemmas faced by the characters, creating a rich and thought-provoking narrative.

Visually, the film is breathtaking. Nolan's masterful direction, coupled with Wally Pfister's stunning cinematography, immerses viewers in the gritty and atmospheric world of Gotham City. The practical effects and meticulously choreographed action sequences further enhance the film's realism, making every moment feel visceral and impactful.

Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker stands as one of the greatest performances in cinematic history. His chilling and captivating interpretation of the iconic villain is nothing short of mesmerizing. Ledger's commitment to the role and his ability to convey the Joker's chaotic nature with both dark humor and genuine menace create an unforgettable character that haunts the film.

"The Dark Knight" is not merely a spectacle of action and suspense; it is also a character-driven drama that explores the complexities of its protagonists. The film delves into the personal struggles of Bruce Wayne, his internal battles, and the moral dilemmas he faces as he grapples with his own demons. The supporting cast, including Gary Oldman as Commissioner Gordon and Aaron Eckhart as Harvey Dent/Two-Face, delivers exceptional performances that further elevate the film's emotional depth.

Furthermore, Hans Zimmer's iconic score adds another layer of intensity and grandeur to the film. The haunting and pulsating music perfectly captures the tone and atmosphere of the story, heightening the tension and amplifying the emotional impact of each scene.

In conclusion, "The Dark Knight" is a groundbreaking and extraordinary film that transcends the superhero genre. With its complex characters, thought-provoking themes, and exceptional performances, it remains a cinematic triumph. Christopher Nolan's visionary direction and the unforgettable portrayal of the Joker by Heath Ledger have left an indelible mark on cinema, cementing "The Dark Knight" as an enduring masterpiece that continues to captivate audiences worldwide.

8.title: Batman pushed to his extreme limits.
8.content:
Batman begins was good but this one is truly amazing. Right of the mark the fight choreography is slower and better. Punches now feel like they carry a lot of weight when delivered by Batman. After two great opening action sequences we get some exposition between Alfred and Bruce Wayne explaining the situation Gotham is currently in and what Rachel is up to now.

Not needing to setup so many characters this time allows the film to go into a much more intense direction and really push each character to the extreme. Batman's ambition in this film is very ambitious, to take down the entire mob which still controls Gotham city. To achieve this he teams up with Jim Gordon and Harvey Dent. Gotham is still a very sick and frightened city even though Batman has given it some hope. If Batman represents order then the joker is chaos and anarchy. You know this clash is going to unleash carnage and you get the feeling now that none of the characters are safe. Not Rachel or Gordon or Harvey. The Joker's plan partly involves making Gotham turn against Batman, almost to prove to him that there are no true heroes. The Joker of course gets his own score and it's a very tense uncomfortable piece of music as you'd expect.

The costumes continue to look great. Batman is given a new batsuit which looks great in the dark street lights of Gotham. The Joker has a grungy look to him and the film overall has a dark look to it, even in scenes with colour if that makes sense, brightness and colour are two different things. The world of Gotham is one in which largely men wear suits, it would look completely wrong if in the middle of the Harvey Dent press conference for instance there was a man in a pair of shorts and t-shirt there like you get in real life on a summers day.

I'd say the overall tone of this film is not the most hopeful and the lighting really reflects that. Shot on location it holds onto it's more realistic look, expect lots of helicopter shots of sky scrappers and towers at both day and night. Wayne Manner is also gone in this film, Batman swaps it for a penthouse, the bat mobile is also replace by a motorbike adding a greater sense of danger and vulnerability for our hero. In this world of corrupt police officers and vicious gangsters Alfred and Fox are reliable as ever, giving Batman moral guidance.

The only negative I have for the film is the Imax v 35mm give the film different aspect ratios, some viewers may find it distracting the way it keeps switching between the two. I personally like the Imax full screen look the most.

Without spoiling too much Batman is completely pushed to his physical and psychological limits, it's such a compelling story and there just seems to be no way that our heroes could win.

There's some amazing practical effects, and stunts in this film, it's really surprising to see how much was done practically, it's one of the reasons it all looks so gorgeous in 4k, the highlights, the shadows, everything. There's no real B plot either, it's just relentless.

Gordon in a way is the other real hero in this story, you have to really love his character, Garry Oldman is brilliant. He's just as brave and good as Batman just without his strength or technology.

8.title: Thought provoking and genuinely great!
8.content:
This was also a great film! It explored some interesting themes and particularly the impact you can have and the unforeseen consequences when you interfere with the natural order of things. Almost like the butterfly effect, one action somewhere can cost dearly later on.

The joker was a greatly created villain with an ambiguous backstory and it was intriguing because although he was caught, he still won, ruining Harvey, Gotham's saviour. Perhaps it was not as enjoyable as Batman begins (personally) but it explored deeper themes and required more thinking, making for a better watch. The Joker really stole the show as the best character in the movie,

Harvey's decline into what he vowed to destroy was poignant and I feel like the quote 'you ever die a hero or live long enough to become the villain' was what resonated most with me about this movie. The thin and often unclear line between good and evil, having morals and a sense of justice does not mean you're right and the ability of the joker to showcase this so heavily throughout the film just made it a great watch.

I feel like this film was less about Batman, and more about questioning what good and evil really is, how fragile we are as a society and how interfering with the natural order of things can cause anarchy.

8.title: Positive Elements
8.content: The Dark Knight is a complex film with a myriad of messages. But at its most basic, the question it poses is this: To what lengths do good people go in order to conquer the worst sort of evil? Must they become a little evil themselves along the way? "You got rules!" a broken mob boss tells Batman. "The Joker—he's got no rules!" It's a pesky truism our heroes struggle with from the get-go. None of them escape unsullied. "You either die a hero or live long enough to see yourself become the villain," says Dent. But it's when they refuse to compromise that the movie soars.

8.title: Set a standard for its generation
8.content:
The Dark Knight might be overrated and the perfect hipster sensation, but we can't deny it set a new standard for superhero movies. Christopher Nolan's realistic and mature approach is exactly what the Batman franchise needed after years of embarrassing renditions. The dark and captivating tone of the Tim Burton movies is partly brought back, but instead of his trademark gothic, almost expressionist landscapes, Nolan goes for a more modern and raw setting. The writing is solid if we consider the average of superhero movies. They couldn't resist throwing in a bunch of campy moments as well as the mandatory (uninteresting) love story, but there is still a significant quality gap between this and all other DC movies. Batman gets kind of overshadowed by the villains, but I guess that's actually what made the film strong anyway. Not that we could have taken a billionaire in a bat costume seriously anyway. Now that I think about it, all the good Batman movies were built around a charming villain ("Batman Returns" above all). I wish they expanded on Harvey Dent's psychological transformation a bit more though, as he literally changes into a bad guy overnight. A gradual change would have turned him into a much deeper and well-rounded character, but I guess no-one was really interested isn't it.

While "Batman Begins" ended up being a bit too boring and slow-paced in its ambitiousness, "The Dark Knight" reaches a better balance overall without turning into the nonsense that was "The Dark Knight Rises". The only problem is, like in other Nolan movies, the confusing and disorienting direction of the action scenes. The action does not play a primary role in this movie, but they don't spice things up as they were supposed to.

8.title: The dark cinematic
8.content:
As a fan of superhero movies, I recently watched Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight" and was blown away by its masterful storytelling, stunning cinematography, and powerhouse performances.

The film follows Batman (played brilliantly by Christian Bale) as he battles the Joker (a truly iconic performance by the late Heath Ledger), a twisted and malevolent force of chaos and anarchy. The cat-and-mouse game between the two characters is intense and gripping, with the stakes growing higher with each passing scene.

Nolan's direction is nothing short of brilliant, with his use of practical effects and stunning visuals creating a gritty and realistic tone that is both dark and grounded. The action sequences are thrilling and well-choreographed, while the quiet moments between characters are filled with tension and emotion.

The film's themes of justice, morality, and the nature of good and evil are explored in a thought-provoking and nuanced way, making "The Dark Knight" not just a thrilling superhero movie, but a work of art that speaks to the human condition.

Overall, "The Dark Knight" is a triumph of filmmaking that deserves its place as one of the greatest superhero movies ever made. Its impact can be seen in the numerous films that have followed in its wake, and it remains a testament to the power of cinema to inspire and captivate audiences.

8.title: The Dark Knight (2008): A Cinematic Masterpiece that Redefined the Superhero Genre
8.content:
Christopher Nolan's "The Dark Knight," released in 2008, stands as a monumental achievement in the world of cinema and is often hailed as one of the greatest superhero movies ever made. This gripping film not only solidified Nolan's reputation as a visionary director but also redefined the superhero genre by elevating it into a realm of complexity, moral ambiguity, and psychological depth rarely seen before.

At the heart of "The Dark Knight" is the eternal struggle between good and evil, personified by Batman (Christian Bale) and the Joker (Heath Ledger). The film skillfully delves into the intricate dynamics between these two iconic characters, presenting them as opposite sides of the same coin. Batman, draped in darkness and driven by an unwavering sense of justice, represents the struggle to maintain order in a chaotic world. On the other hand, the Joker emerges as an agent of chaos, a force that seeks to expose the fragility of morality and push society to its limits.

Ledger's portrayal of the Joker is nothing short of legendary. His posthumous Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor was a testament to his extraordinary talent. Ledger's Joker is simultaneously mesmerizing and terrifying. With his chilling mannerisms, enigmatic laughter, and iconic lines like "Why so serious?", he crafted a character that lingers in the minds of audiences long after the credits roll. Ledger's dedication to immersing himself in the role is palpable, and his performance is undoubtedly one of the film's defining features.

Bale's Batman, too, shines with complexity. Nolan's decision to ground the character in realism and explore the psychological toll of being a vigilante brings a new dimension to the caped crusader. Bale captures Batman's internal struggle between his public identity as Bruce Wayne and his alter ego, while also grappling with the moral quandaries of his actions. Bale's nuanced portrayal ensures that the audience is not just witnessing a superhero but a flawed, human protagonist.

"The Dark Knight" isn't merely about its titular characters; the supporting cast also plays a vital role in shaping the narrative. Gary Oldman's Commissioner Gordon embodies unwavering integrity in a city plagued by corruption. Aaron Eckhart's Harvey Dent starts as the white knight Gotham needs, showcasing the potential for redemption, only to be tragically transformed into the villainous Two-Face. Michael Caine as Alfred and Morgan Freeman as Lucius Fox lend emotional depth and technological prowess, respectively, grounding the fantastical elements of the story in a plausible reality.

Nolan's direction and storytelling prowess are evident throughout the film. He crafts a tense and relentless narrative, masterfully utilizing the visual language to convey emotion and suspense. From the stunning IMAX shots capturing the grandeur of Gotham City to the exhilarating practical effects used in the high-stakes action sequences, every frame feels meticulously crafted. The plot's intricate web of deception, moral dilemmas, and unexpected twists keeps the audience engaged and guessing until the very end.

The film's thematic richness also contributes to its enduring impact. Nolan explores complex moral questions about the nature of heroism, the thin line between chaos and order, and the extent to which society's values are tested in the face of adversity. These themes resonate on multiple levels, inviting viewers to reflect on their own understanding of justice and the human condition.

Hans Zimmer's haunting score deserves special mention. The dark and pulsating music perfectly complements the film's tone, serving as an auditory representation of the psychological battles waged by the characters. The Joker's theme, a cacophony of dissonant notes, captures his chaotic essence, while the solemn chords associated with Batman reflect his internal struggles.

In conclusion, "The Dark Knight" is a cinematic masterpiece that transcends its genre. Christopher Nolan's directorial brilliance, combined with exceptional performances, intricate storytelling, and thought-provoking themes, delivers an unparalleled movie experience. The film's impact on popular culture is immeasurable, leaving an indelible mark on the superhero genre and inspiring subsequent films to strive for depth and complexity. Over a decade since its release, "The Dark Knight" remains a testament to the power of storytelling and the heights that cinema can achieve.

8.title: Batman
8.content:
Sometimes folks look for trouble. And sometimes trouble comes a calling all on its own.

For a while, it seemed as though life in Gotham City was looking up. Gotham's finest, led by straight-arrow Lt. Gordon, was squeezing the city's crime syndicates. Harvey Dent, a new and fearless district attorney, stalked the courtrooms. Batman prowled the city's darkest alleys. Mob bosses stopped meeting at night, afraid they'd be pinched.

Thenlike the flu, like a hailstorm, like a crowbar to the side of the head—comes the Joker. No baggage. No backstair. No greedy motive. Just a leering, cackling demon of chaos. He crashes a high-level mob meeting and offers his services as the city's very own bat exterminator. What does he want? Nothing. Everything. What does he ask for? Half the mob's money.

So begins perhaps the deepest, bleakest summer blockbuster ever, an explosion-riddled saga about order and anarchy, about good and evil, and about the line we draw between the two.

The Dark Knight is a complex film with a myriad of messages. But at its most basic, the question it poses is this: To what lengths do good people go in order to conquer the worst sort of evil? Must they become a little evil themselves along the way?

"You got rules!" a broken mob boss tells Batman. "The Joker—he's got no rules. It's a pesky truism our heroes struggle with from the get-go. None of them escape unsullied. "You either die a hero or live long enough to see yourself become the villain," says Dent. But it's when they refuse to compromise that the movie soars.

Dent starts as a bright knight—a blond, bold DA who aims to clean up Gotham's streets for good. Though there are ever-so-slight indications that he's not altogether wonderful (the boys at the station call him "Two Face"), he's sincere about his crime-fighting calling—a sincerity that wins over even billionaire-celebrant Bruce Wayne. "Gotham needs a hero with a face," Wayne says. One might say Dent and Batman are two sides of the same coin, Dent the unsullied face of incorruptibility and Batman the black-caped heavy. Dent even sacrifices his career and good name at one point to keep Batman out on the streets—a favor Batman returns.

Lt. Gordon, once Gotham's only honest police officer, has a wee bit of company nowadays, but he's still arguably the film's finest, prepared to sacrifice his own life for both his city and family.

Lucius Fox, head honcho at Wayne Enterprises, continues to play Q to Batman's Bond, keeping him supplied with a host of critical Cozmo's and gadgets. But while he's willing to cook the books to keep Batman's identity a secret, there are ethical places he won't go—at least not for very long. When the Dark Knight creates a gigantic sonar net by tapping into all of Gotham's cell phones (a hefty invasion of privacy), Fox tells him that either the machine goes or he does. "Spying on 30 million people isn't in my job description," he says—though he acquiesces to use it for one specialized mission.

The most heroic guy of the bunch (go figure) is Batman himself, willing to sacrifice everything that's precious to him for the sake of the city. He never, ever kills, and he rigidly keeps this special vow even when the Joker more than deserves death.

The citizens of Gotham also show a bit of gumption. When the Joker pits average Joes and Janes against convicted killers and thieves in a death match of sorts, they manage to resist their selfish urges and risk everything to do the right thing. Humanity and its higher conscience survives even as the world burns down around it—much to the Joker's dismay.

8.title: The Dark Knight
8.content:
Christian Bale returns in The Dark Knight and continues the success of Batman Begins. With the tone and casting largely unchanged, it's a winning formula that delivers again.

The late Heath Ledger's turn as The Joker is an absolute treat. Manic, frantic and jumpy, the colourfully-dressed Joker is at every turn the antithesis of an otherwise black and serious city. From his devious introduction to his demented demise, he's a new sort of evil who creates craziness just because he can, and spreads anarchy for the hell of it. His irreverence brought an injection of humour and colour that makes the hefty 152 minutes whizz by, not least because Ledger is clearly in his element.

The wider BatBale arc continues apace, with themes of heroism (and not), and the lingering question of Batman's identity. Nolan isn't frightened to ask difficult questions of his protagonist. Is he really a force for good? Is he actually a hero?

The story blends Harvey Dent/Two-Face (Eckhart) seamlessly into the mix. His transformation from Dent to Two-Face is absolutely authentic and raises more questions about the true nature of good and evil, and the thin line that separates them.

Gyllenhaal has the unenviable task of replacing Katie Holmes as Rachel Dawes, and a disappointing combination of writing and performance strips Dawes of her mettle. Gyllenhaal's Rachel is reduced to the comic trope of love interest-cum-damsel in distress. The Holmes Rachel of Batman Begins was Bruce Wayne's moral compass and a champion for good, while this new Rachel serves only to entice Batman into making emotional decisions and battling for her affections. Gone is the kick-ass DA of 2005, and that is a shame.

Despite this niggle, an otherwise sparkling cast (including returning legends Caine, Freeman and Oldman) deliver another spectacular film, bolstered again by phenomenal visuals. The hospital scene is funny, chilling and mesmerising all at once, with special effects that are almost impossible to top.

No need for Dent to toss his coin here – The Dark Knight is a huge success.

8.title: The Joker making the difference!
8.content:
The Batman franchise is in many respects comparable to the James Bond franchise. Both films are about a hero, a villain and gadgets.

There are differences too.

In James Bond movies the villain is external (often in the earlier films the Soviet Union) while in the Batman movies the villain is corrupting the system from within. Of course far less an action movie compare this with a film like "It's a wonderful life" (1946, Frank Capra) with the character of Henry Potter being just such a kind of villain.

James Bond movies are situated in high society while Gotham city in the Batman movies is a very depressing place to be, making the Batman movies dystopian stories, just like for example "Blade runner" (1982, Ridley Scott).

Not an unimportant difference with the James Bond movies is the absence of the sexy Bond girl. Often Batman does have a love interest, but most of the time this is more of a girl next door. This is consistent with Batman himself who is (only) a parttime hero and an ordinary guy the rest of the time.

Given the absence of a Bond girl an important differentiating factor between Batman films is the character of the villain.

In "The dark knight" the character of the villain is really superb. Late Heath Ledger delivers a great performance as the Joker. He is not afraid that one of his predecessors playing this character is the famous Jack Nicholson in "Batman" (1989, Tim Burton). He even surpasses him and would become the second actor winning an Oscar posthumously after Peter Finch for "Network" (1976, Sidney Lumet). In my opinion the performance of Ledger is on par with the performances of Al Pacino in "Scarface" (1983, Brian de Palma) and Anthony Hopkins in "The silence of the lambs" (1991, Jonathan Demme). Maybe in part because of the performance of Ledger the character of the Joker later was able to become the lead character in its own film "Joker" (2019, Todd Phillips).

The Joker is all the more creepy because he is partly criminal, partly psychopath and thus very unpredictable. The comparisons I made above with Al Pacino (playing a criminal) and Anthony Hopkins (playing a psychopath) were not by accident.

By the way clowns in the role of villain are not uncommon. Think for example of "It" (2017, Andy Muschietti).

Also characters laughing all the time (often caused by some scars) are generally not trusted. The term "diabolical grin" illustrates this mistrust very well. Look also at "The man who laughs" (1928, Paul Leni) where the main character incidentally is all but a villain.

Superhero films often have their roots in comic books. Batman, one of the more darker superhero's, is no exception. The interpretation by Tim Burton (1989 - 1992) still pays tribute to these roots. The interpretation of Christopher Nolan is moving away from these comic roots into the direction of the noir genre. In the introduction to this review I did describe Gotham city as dystopian not unlike "Blade runner" (1982, Ridley Scott). This maybe true for the first episode "Batman begins" (2005, Christopher Nolan) but in "The dark knight" Gotham city is above all cold and sterile with all those skyscrapers.

In "The dark knight" both Batman and the Joker have has a youth full of trauma's. One of the themes of the film I suspect is the very different way in which they try to come to terms with these trauma's.

5.title: Let's be realistic.
5.content:
I settled on a 5/10 for The Dark Knight. I appreciated the story structure and all the notes they hit... I just don't think they played them loudly. I don't like re-casting, and the replacement of Katie Holmes/Rachel and the original Barbara Gordon actress (yes, her too, didya notice?) is awkward and distracting. The lack of ANY blood in the film to complement the multitude of beatings and killings (to sustain a PG-13 rating) nullifies the tension that should be present in some brilliantly conceived scenarios. I didn't believe for a second that the victims of several hostage situations (mass or otherwise) would actually lose their lives, because it's blisteringly apparent from the onset that this film is a PG-13, and would never disturb its audience beyond the minimum necessary plot points.

The Joker is actually underwritten. Ledger was game and his performance solid, but honestly: Throw the makeup and stringy hair on 75% of capable actors out there, and you have the same product. I think Jack Nicholson's output is ultimately more interesting, and I think that Tim Burton's original film, although imperfect, is still the most entertaining in the pantheon.

I realize that to hardcore Batman fans, this is a wet dream having the grittiness of the graphic novels transposed to the big screen (if they say so; I say it came close), but riddle me this: If the same script was fashioned into a non-superhero flick, let's say Heat II, and had the same strong performances and production values, would the lack of Batman fan loyalty still rocket it to its current position on the IMDb Top 250?

5.title: Not the greatest film ever made
5.content: Time for a corrective. As I write this review, The Dark Knight is, according to IMDb voters, the Best. Film. Ever. At the risk of incurring a hail of brickbats, I must demur. Yes, Heath Ledger delivers an excellent performance, as does Gary Oldman as Lieutenant--er, COMMISSIONER Gordon--and it's always a pleasure to watch Michael Caine and Aaron Eckhart. But The Dark Knight is an overlong, over plotted, logically flawed, and philosophically confused film that cannot (and should not) be mistaken for great art. Compared to most comic book movies, it's not bad. Compared to La Regle du Jeu, it ain't so hot. The film's first half is actually quite good, and seems to come to a timely conclusion somewhere around the eighty minute mark. Unfortunately, this being a summer blockbuster, there's another 70 plus minutes to go, and the film's second half is a distinct letdown. Instead of ending on a neat and tidy note, The Dark Knight spirals off into a muddled mess of bizarre plotting (how DID that prisoner get the bomb sewn into him?), illogic (how does Harvey escape the hospital explosion--and why is he apparently impervious to pain?) and confusing action (too many ass-kickings in too little time). I don't expect 100% logical consistency from my genre product, but there are so many flaws and elisions of simple common sense in Christopher Nolan's screenplay that utter frustration sets in around the two-hour mark. By the end of the film, we're expected to believe that, for some reason, the residents of Gotham now need to revile Batman rather than reward him for his good work, setting up a police pursuit into the sunset that presumably will end with our hero receiving a ticket for speeding on the Batcycle. So let's tell it like it is: in terms of 2008 comic book flicks, The Dark Knight is inferior to both Hellboy II (which at least is charming and amusing) and Hancock (which raises far more interesting questions about the nature of the super hero).

5.title: It's not really that great of a movie
5.content: I'm so relieved that I'm not the only one who doesn't think this movie is great. I saw this first in the theater, and to be honest, probably would've given it a bit higher rating...if I would've reviewed it then. But........I just watched it again on cable and it doesn't hold up as well outside of the movie theater with it's huge screen, dark room and loud speakers. First off...what I liked. Heath Leadger was fantastic as the Joker and could've done so much more with it if the writing and plot had been better. The movie should've focused on a battle of wits and balls between Batman and Joker. That would've been more interesting. I liked Morgan Freeman. I enjoy his character. I like that there wasn't some big distracting relationship for Batman/Bruce. I even enjoyed some of the explosions. I hate Christian Bale as Batman/Bruce. He just doesn't emote anything. Also...HE HAS THE WORST BATMAN VOICE EVER....EVER....EVER!!!! The movie was way too long and had way too many subplots going. I could've lived without the whole Harvey Dent thing. Why introduce Two Face just to kill him off? It made no sense. Then again, a lot of the subplots made no sense. The movie takes itself too seriously. There's really no humor either. I realize the whole idea was to make it dark, but sheesh, c'mon. There were too many just shoved in there explosions going on. It felt like two movies being rammed into one. It's just too much. Too many things going on that don't really gel together. I guess I'm tired of movies that offer more in explosions and chases than solid story telling and characters you can give a damn about. I honestly could not sit through this movie again. If I do anything, I'll watch it free on demand and fast forward to the Heath Leadger scenes. He did so much with what he was given to work with.....which wasn't any where near what it could have been. All in all...this movie doesn't live up to the hype.

5.title: Overlong, overfunded, overstaffed, overrated---merely okay.
5.content:
I suppose many people might be offended by the simple suggestion that this movie could be anything less than "the best movie ever" or perhaps just "the best movie of 2008", that it was merely okay, for superhero action drivel.

But to me, that's what it was. It's the old good vs evil thing, the good billionaire dons latex suit to fight the evil for no apparent reason other than that he's the good guy, and the bad guy being ridiculously-over-the-top so, with a similarly solid rationale. Then there is the another good guy who has to experience a biographical kink in the form of a girlfriend blown to pieces and some cosmetically challenging facial events, and he becomes the semi-good guy. Lots of explosions, pseudo- technology, vehicles driving above the speed limit, lots of fighting, the end.

I never really understood the appeal of the Batman franchise, which turned a unremarkable set of comic books (uh, "graphic novels") into an unremarkable series of movies. Yet, many people seem to love it, and consequently another one of those hit the streets, bigger, better, more expensive, and this time with an IMDb rating that even made me curious.

To be sure, there are many interesting and impressive aspects of the movie. The director, for one---I very much enjoyed Memento, and give Nolan a lot of credit for it. The cast of The Dark Knight is nothing short of impressive, with certified talent such as Caine, Ledger, Oldman, Bale, and Eckhardt. And, of course, the special effects are great, the fights are well-choreographed and fast-paced, the cinematography is excellent, and so on. It is, no doubt, a technically well-executed action flick, which I suppose is all that it wants to be, and probably all most of the people seeing it in the cinema expect it to be.

But it is also other things. Overlong, for instance. The trivial comic-book plot does not sustain 150 minutes of interest, its self-indulgent repetitiveness becoming boring quickly, the little character development happening in cartoonish hit-you-over-the-head-with-hamfisted-symbolism style, the rest being fights, battles, destruction, and some more fights. The range of excellent actors that make up the cast remains woefully underused, although we do get so see some excellent acting, most notably from Ledger and Oldman. Ledger's Joker, in particular, does not require a very broad range, but it's far out in the crazy and psychopathic part of the spectrum, and Ledger manages to turn a fairly ridiculous and cartoonish villain into a three-dimensional and utterly creepy character, which is testimony to his acting ability. By and large, however, one does get the feeling that performance per talent ratio isn't a very good one, and that this crowd could have been put to better use in a more grown-up production with less of a focus on expensive action sequences.

Overall, this movie is way over-hyped for what it is, it's not among the top ten movies of all time in my book, but then neither is "Shawshank Redemption" or "The Empire Strikes Back". It does have its moments, though, but it could easily be cut down to 90 minutes.

5.title: Distinctly average and surprisingly rather dull
5.content: It is odd to spend more than two hours watching a film and it slowly dawns on you that you are not particularly bothered how it ends and, if anything, rather wish it would end sooner rather than later. The Dark Knight is that kind of film. Exactly why I lost interest or even when, I'm not too sure, but lose interest I did. This is Christopher Nolan's second stab at Batman as well as Christian 'Rant' Bales, and although all the elements are there, it is simply not as good. Naturally, this being another slug, blast and punchfest - tho' despite it's reputation for being dark, thankfully not a bloodfest - many, many viewers have lauded this as a 'masterpiece', 'the best movie of 2008 so far', 'far surpasses Begins'. No, it isn't and no it doesn't. All I can say is that these people have not seen many 'masterpieces' or many films in 2008. The Dark Knight, in that way which Hollywood has made its sugary own, attempts to flatter the audience by including a 'moral dilemma' and it does so not once, but rather often. This time we are invited - the 'we' being the popcorn-chewing Saturday night crowd who think thought is a luxury - to reflect on moral ambiguity and how relative rather than absolute the notions of good and evil can be. And each time this viewer sighed a little: as the saying goes, you can put lipstick on a pig, but it is still a pig. We get any number of high falutin speeches about heroes and villains but, in truth, is just so much codswallop. In truth this film is just another blockbuster, and, at that, it is not even as good as many other blockbusters. If you want to meditate on the reality of good and evil, of heroes and villains, by all means make a film doing so, but in The Dark Knight it is all, for this viewer at least, all very phoney. Apart from that, this film is a tad confusing, there are too many characters, the plot, or at least what there is of it, really does not bear repeating, the suspense is curiously unexciting, and too often the film drags. The old actors are there, and all with the very honourable exception of the late Heath Ledger, seem to be acting by numbers. (This was, I think, Ledger's last film, and his early death is sad. Undoubtedly he was very talented.) And having said all that, there is not much more to say. It's not bad, it's not particularly good. As part of the series, it stands tall, but then the series is not all that outstanding. See it if you want to, and if, after reading this, you decide not to, well, sorry, but you won't be missing much at all.

5.title: The Dark Truth
5.content: What is going on with all of these maximum ratings for a barely average film? According to IMDb, this is the best film of the decade so far. Not one sane person could argue that this is justified. Have the studios finally managed to get the masses to 'believe the hype'? I was a bit skeptical about this film, due to the hype, and especially because I wasn't impressed with Batman Begins, but I must admit, the heist in the first five minutes was excellent, and I thought my skepticism was unwarranted. But then Batman turned up and began speaking like a wrestler with throat cancer, and it continued to go down hill from there. What I didn't expect this film to be was tedious. But it was. It was far too long and bored my pants off me. There was no character development, the story was convoluted and over-complex and it was far too long. But my my main problem, and this goes against nearly every reviewer here, even those who weren't impressed, I thought Heath Ledger was absolutely awful! Who are these people calling for a posthumous Oscar? There is nothing I despise more than a 'look at me' performance. Ledger did all the tricks required to portray a 'crazy guy', including shifting his eyes up, down, left and right at every opportunity, and ingeniously, due to having his mouth cut as a child, he keeps licking around the inside of his mouth, which rather than being an impressive feat of method acting is actually as irritating as watching a fat man eat chips with his mouth open. His performance was utterly self-indulgent and it seems like all you sycophants fell for it. The only decent acting performance in this film is Eckhart. Caine and Morgan bore, and Bale, with his 'employ me for movie trailers' voice barely has one dimension. I would have rated this film higher if it hadn't taken itself so seriously, but as it stands it is a pretentious hyped-up and tedious movie. At last, the dark truth.

5.title: It's been said already but this is way overrated.
5.content:
Well, this film is the most overrated movie I can remember but that doesn't mean it sucks at all. It's well made, with great shots and good acting (at least by Morgan Freeman, Michael Caine, and Heath Ledger). The action scenes are filmed more coherently than Batman Begins and that pencil trick was awesome.

Still, there are too many ridiculous scenes (like flying out of a window with a cable attached to a plane and cell phones turning into radar machines) and completely unnecessary plot lines. Do I really care if Commissioner Gordon plays dead for half the film and his wife gets mad at him or some Chinese guy is hording the criminal's cash? No. Give us more confrontation between the hero and villain. Lastly, the dark themes this film deals with are taken a little too seriously for a movie about a superhero of sorts. He wears a cape and a mask and fights crime as a symbol... don't try and get me emotionally involved in any THEME greater than that. Develop the characters and make me care about them. The animated "Batman and the Mask of the Phantasm" did a better job with that.

Whatev, i've rambled long enough. It's still a very enjoyable movie and if I see it again i'll probably like it more but there's no way this deserves all the praise it gets. I'd really give it a 6.5 out of ten but we can't do .5s and this definitely does not belong in the top movies of all time. Too bad because it might be worthy of a 7 or 8 had it not been hyped up like it was the gift of Zeus.

5.title: Is The Dark Knight that good... really? 'Fraid not.
5.content:
The Dark Knight is an extraordinary mish-mash lacking logic and cohesion.

Technically, the film is well made. That is, it looks and feels like a blockbuster, though a solid score is sorely lacking.

On the plus side, Michael Caine and Gary Oldman add gravitas to an otherwise ordinary ensemble.

And sadly, a fine actor will be remembered, not for the likes of moving and sensitive performances seen in Brokeback Mountain and Candy, but rather an excellent make-up job, an over-active tongue and a silly voice. As farewell performances rate, Heath Ledger's Joker sits alongside Peter Sellers' Fiendish Plot of Dr Fu Manchu.

To remind yourself how super hero movies should be made, dust off your copy of Spiderman II (from which it borrows) or Superman The Movie (from which it should've borrowed).

5.title: Are you kidding?
5.content:
To think that this movie belongs in the top 100 movies of all time let alone the top five is ludicrous. You bet, it' quite a spectacle. But spectacle doesn't make a great movie. There's one truly great character and everyone knows it's Heath Ledger's Joker. That was a magical paring of great writing and great acting.

But what happened to the rest of the movie? Besides The Joker the film is merely almost good. That is if you like exceedingly dark and depressing movies that have little if anything to feel good about. It's mildly suspenseful at times but much of the action is telegraphed. Let's see some more stupid police who can't see another Joker getaway coming from a mile away.

I'm no wimp -- I can be engrossed by and accept wholesale carnage when it's in something like "Saving Private Ryan" -- but this is yet another movie in which it doesn't matter how many faceless civilians and police die just as long as there can be lots of shooting and car crashes and the stars are OK.

And what of poor Batman? Christian Bale does a creditable job in the role, yet this is really a movie about The Joker. The hero and who he is isn't nearly as well explored as the villain.

Besides Ledger the two old pros, Michael Cain and Morgan Freeman, play the most interesting characters. Gary Oldman does a decent job as James Gordon. The problem is we're never given any reason to doubt him yet there is this undercurrent to the character that maybe he's not really working for the good guys.

The scene where Batman hunts The Joker as SWAT teams come crashing into the building is one of the most confusing messes I've seen. There's no clear idea what's happening and why and The Joker's final capture is anticlimactic. The turn to the dark side by character Harvey Dent is poorly developed and in the final scenes, lacking much logic. And the suspension of logic -- especially when it comes to the evil doing of The Joker -- just goes too far.

In the end, despite Batman's expected saving of the child, the movie simply peters out with a muddled message and Batman zooming off on his motorcycle in the direction of -- we can only presume -- another sequel.

If you want a dark, action-packed film then see "Quantum of Solace." It's not a great film -- not nearly as good as "Casino Royal" -- but it's a fair shot better than "The Black Knight."

5.title: Easily the most overrated movie of all time
5.content:
